projects.title: Salary Management
projects.description: High-performance HR salary management & compensation analytics platform built to manage 10,000+ employees across countries with sub-40ms API responses. Powered by a Turborepo + pnpm monorepo with Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, and PostgreSQL.
projects.fullDescription:
Salary Management is a full-stack HR compensation and workforce analytics platform built to manage salaries for 10,000+ employees across multiple countries and answer "how do we pay people?" with sub-40ms API performance.

• Monorepo Architecture (Turborepo + pnpm): Organized into apps/web (Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query, Recharts, shadcn-style UI), apps/api (NestJS on Express REST API), packages/db (Prisma schema with pg driver adapter, migrations, and deterministic 10,000-row Faker seed), and packages/shared (shared Zod schemas, DTO types, and constants).

• Core Screens & Workflows: URL-persisted employee directory (/employees) with search, multi-filter, salary range, sorting, and pagination; transactional Excel/CSV bulk importer (/employees/import) supporting up to 10,000 rows with ready/problem row previews; unified add/edit forms (/employees/new, /employees/:id/edit); compensation insights (/insights) computing min, P25, median, mean, P75, and max per country, department, or job title; and interactive pay spread histograms (/pay-spread).

• Engineering & Data Integrity: Salaries are stored strictly as whole-number integers in each employee's local currency, with all insights grouped per currency. Percentiles and histogram bands are computed directly in PostgreSQL using percentile_cont and width_bucket, delivering 6–40ms responses at 10,000 rows.

• Quality & Deployment: Automated CI pipeline running build, typecheck, unit tests, and isolated E2E API tests against a dedicated test database, deployed across Neon (PostgreSQL), Render (NestJS API), and Vercel (Next.js web).
projects.challenges: Scaled PostgreSQL salary queries and statistical insights (min, P25, median, mean, P75, max via percentile_cont and histograms via width_bucket) to respond in 6–40ms across 10,000+ employee records., Eliminated floating-point currency bugs and mixed-currency distortion by enforcing whole-number integer salaries in local currency and grouping all analytics strictly per country/currency., Unified validation and type safety across Next.js and NestJS using a shared Zod schema package in a Turborepo monorepo with transactional Excel/CSV bulk imports and isolated E2E database testing.

projects.title: Workforce Ultimate
projects.description: Modern, high-performance enterprise workforce, project management, and organizational collaboration platform inspired by Jira, ClickUp, and Linear. Built with Next.js 16 (Turbopack), React 19, and Supabase.
projects.fullDescription:
Workforce Ultimate is a modern, high-performance enterprise workforce, project management, and organizational collaboration platform inspired by Jira, ClickUp, and Linear. Built on Next.js 16 (App Router & Turbopack), React 19, TypeScript, and Supabase (PostgreSQL with RLS & Realtime), it delivers an enterprise-grade suite structured across four evolutionary phases:

• Phase 1 — Foundation & Core Architecture: Sub-second page compilation with Turbopack and dynamic streaming SSR; secure Supabase authentication with session persistence; native English and Arabic bilingual localization (i18n) with dynamic RTL layout switching; and seamless dark/light mode toggling.

• Phase 2 — Core MVP & Workforce Hierarchy: Granular 5-tier Role-Based Access Control (Owner, Admin, HR, Managers, and Employees); workspace invitation system with single-use/multi-use invite codes and 1-click joining; company timezone auto-detection and custom branding; comprehensive project & task pipelines (todo, in_progress, review, done); and estimated vs. actual labor time tracking with approval workflows.

• Phase 2.5 — Essential Operations Hub: End-of-day daily work logs (hours, blockers, mood ratings); performance evaluations with company OKRs and employee goal cycles; in-app and email real-time event notifications; instant universal search; and interactive operations analytics.

• Phase 3 — Real-Time Collaboration: Multi-tier real-time chat with public channels, private coworker channels, leadership management channels, and 1:1 direct messages; dynamic sender identities with role badges; Supabase Storage attachments and threaded comments; company audit trail logs; HR bonus/disciplinary tracking; and integration webhooks (GitHub commit sync, Gmail).

• Phase 4 — Scale & Polish: Full Progressive Web App (PWA) with desktop/mobile installability, Service Worker app-shell offline caching, and Web Push notifications; multi-tier TanStack Query caching presets and offline mutation queue; asynchronous background jobs engine; and executive workforce reporting with 1-click CSV exports and printable PDF reports.
projects.challenges: Architected a strict 5-tier Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) with Supabase PostgreSQL Row Level Security (RLS) policies and real-time multi-channel communication across public, private, and leadership channels., Engineered a multi-tier TanStack Query caching system with a Service Worker offline queue and Web Push notifications, delivering resilient PWA offline capability and slashing redundant queries., Delivered full bidirectional (RTL/LTR) Arabic/English localization with automatic timezone detection and an executive reporting engine with 1-click CSV export and PDF printing.

languages.title: JavaScript
languages.description: Core language for building dynamic, interactive, and high-performance web applications using modern ES6+ features.

insights.title: 01. Variables: let, const, and var
insights.content: Declare variables with const by default, let when reassignment is needed, and avoid var due to function scoping and hoisting.

blocks.text: JavaScript provides three variable keywords. `const` creates a block-scoped binding that cannot be reassigned (though referenced objects remain mutable). `let` creates a block-scoped binding that can be reassigned. `var` is function-scoped, allows redeclaration, and is hoisted with `undefined`.

insights.title: 02. Primitive Data Types
insights.content: JavaScript has seven immutable primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, and symbol.

blocks.text: Primitives represent single immutable values stored by value rather than by reference. Unlike objects, calling methods on primitives (like `.toUpperCase()` on a string) temporarily wraps them in an object wrapper behind the scenes without mutating the original value.

insights.title: 03. typeof Operator and Type Inspection
insights.content: Use typeof for primitives and functions, and pair it with null and Array.isArray checks for accurate runtime type detection.

blocks.text: The `typeof` operator returns a lowercase string describing a value's type. Historically, `typeof null` evaluates to `"object"`, and arrays also return `"object"`. Combining `val === null` and `Array.isArray(val)` handles those edge cases reliably.

insights.title: 04. Type Coercion and Explicit Conversion
insights.content: Prefer explicit conversions with Number(), String(), and Boolean() over relying on implicit coercion quirks.

blocks.text: JavaScript automatically converts types in mixed expressions—for example, `+` concatenates when either operand is a string, whereas `-` or `*` coerces operands to numbers. Using explicit constructors `Number()`, `String()`, and `Boolean()` makes intent unambiguous.

insights.title: 05. Strict (===) vs Loose (==) Equality
insights.content: Always default to strict equality (===) to compare value and type without unexpected coercion.

blocks.text: Loose equality (`==`) triggers abstract type coercion before comparing—causing surprises like `0 == ""` being `true`. Strict equality (`===`) returns `false` immediately if types differ. For `NaN` or `-0` vs `+0`, use `Object.is()` or `Number.isNaN()`.

blocks.code:
console.log(0 == "");        // true (coerced)
console.log(0 === "");       // false (different types)
console.log(null == undefined);  // true
console.log(null === undefined); // false
console.log(Object.is(NaN, NaN)); // true

insights.title: 06. Template Literals and String Interpolation
insights.content: Backtick strings support embedded expressions with ${...}, multi-line formatting, and tagged template functions.

blocks.text: Template literals use backticks (`` ` ``) instead of quotes. You can interpolate any JavaScript expression inside `${...}`, preserve line breaks naturally, or prefix a template with a tag function for custom escaping or formatting.

insights.title: 07. Essential String Methods
insights.content: Manipulate and query strings immutably using trim, slice, includes, split, padStart, and replaceAll.

blocks.text: Because strings are immutable, every string method returns a new string. Modern JavaScript includes ergonomic methods like `.includes()`, `.startsWith()`, `.replaceAll()`, `.trim()`, `.padStart()`, and `.at()` for negative indexing.

insights.title: 08. Numbers, NaN, and Number Methods
insights.content: Handle IEEE-754 floating-point numbers safely using Number.isNaN, Number.isFinite, and numeric separators.

blocks.text: JavaScript `number` is a 64-bit IEEE-754 float. Always use `Number.isNaN()` instead of global `isNaN()` because global `isNaN("hello")` coerces first and returns `true`. Numeric separators (`1_000_000`) improve readability, and `Number.isFinite()` guards against `Infinity` and `NaN`.

blocks.code:
const budget = 1_500_000;
const badCalc = 0 / 0;

console.log(Number.isNaN(badCalc));    // true
console.log(Number.isNaN("hello"));    // false
console.log(Number.isFinite(budget));  // true
console.log(Number.parseInt("42px", 10)); // 42
console.log(Number((0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2))); // 0.3

insights.title: 09. Math Object Utilities
insights.content: Perform rounding, clamping, powers, and pseudo-random range generation with built-in Math methods.

blocks.text: The `Math` namespace provides static methods for common mathematical tasks: `Math.floor`, `Math.ceil`, `Math.round`, `Math.trunc`, `Math.min`, `Math.max`, and `Math.random()`. Combine `Math.floor` and `Math.random` to pick random integers in an inclusive range.

insights.title: 10. BigInt for Arbitrary-Precision Integers
insights.content: Represent integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER accurately using the n suffix or BigInt().

blocks.text: Standard `number` loses integer precision above `2^53 - 1` (`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`). `BigInt` stores arbitrarily large integers accurately. Note that you cannot mix `BigInt` and `number` directly in arithmetic operators without explicit conversion.

insights.title: 11. Arithmetic, Assignment, and Increment Operators
insights.content: Use arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %, **), compound assignments, and understand prefix vs postfix increment.

blocks.text: JavaScript supports standard arithmetic plus exponentiation (`**`) and remainder (`%`). Prefix (`++x`) increments and returns the new value, whereas postfix (`x++`) returns the previous value before incrementing.

insights.title: 12. Logical Operators and Short-Circuiting
insights.content: && and || evaluate lazily and return the actual deciding operand, not necessarily a boolean.

blocks.text: In JavaScript, `a && b` returns `a` if `a` is falsy; otherwise it evaluates and returns `b`. Similarly, `a || b` returns `a` if `a` is truthy; otherwise `b`. The `!` operator negates and converts to boolean (`!!val` coerces any value to boolean).

insights.title: 13. Nullish Coalescing (??) and Logical Assignment
insights.content: Use ?? to fall back only on null or undefined, preserving valid falsy values like 0, false, or empty strings.

blocks.text: Unlike `||`, which falls back on any falsy value (`0`, `""`, `false`), `??` only falls back when the left side is `null` or `undefined`. Logical assignment operators (`??=`, `||=`, `&&=`) combine conditional checks with assignment cleanly.

insights.title: 14. Optional Chaining (?.)
insights.content: Safely access nested properties, array indices, and optional methods without throwing TypeError on nullish references.

blocks.text: Optional chaining (`?.`) short-circuits and evaluates to `undefined` if the target before `?.` is `null` or `undefined`. It works for property access (`obj?.a`), bracket notation (`arr?.[0]`), and method calls (`fn?.()`).

insights.title: 15. Conditionals and the Ternary Operator
insights.content: Branch execution with if/else if/else statements and write concise value expressions with the ternary operator.

blocks.text: `if / else if / else` controls statement execution flow. When you simply need to choose between two expressions (such as assigning a value or rendering UI text), the ternary operator `cond ? a : b` is cleaner—just avoid deeply nested ternaries.

insights.title: 16. switch Statements and Fallthrough
insights.content: Match a single expression against multiple strict cases using switch, remembering break or return to prevent fallthrough.

blocks.text: `switch` compares the expression using strict equality (`===`). Without `break` or `return`, execution falls through into subsequent `case` blocks—which is occasionally useful for grouping multiple cases together.

insights.title: 17. for, while, and do...while Loops
insights.content: Iterate a known number of times with for, repeat while a condition holds with while, or run at least once with do...while.

blocks.text: `for` loops bundle initialization, condition, and step update in one header. `while` checks the condition before each iteration, whereas `do...while` executes the loop body first and checks the condition afterward.

insights.title: 18. for...of and for...in Loops
insights.content: Use for...of to iterate values of iterables (arrays, strings, Maps) and for...in only for enumerable object keys.

blocks.text: `for...of` works on any iterable (`Array`, `String`, `Set`, `Map`) and yields values directly. `for...in` iterates over enumerable string keys including inherited prototype keys, so for plain objects `Object.keys()` or `Object.entries()` with `for...of` is usually safer.

insights.title: 19. break, continue, and Labeled Statements
insights.content: Exit loops early with break, skip the current iteration with continue, and break out of nested loops using labels.

blocks.text: `continue` skips to the next iteration of the innermost loop, while `break` terminates the loop immediately. Labeling an outer loop lets `break outer;` exit multiple nested loops cleanly without extra flag variables.

insights.title: 20. Function Declarations vs Function Expressions
insights.content: Function declarations are fully hoisted, while function expressions stored in const/let follow Temporal Dead Zone rules.

blocks.text: A function declaration (`function add(a, b) {}`) is hoisted completely and can be invoked before its line of definition. A function expression (`const add = function(a, b) {}`) assigns a function value to a variable and is only callable after evaluation.

insights.title: 21. Arrow Functions and Concise Bodies
insights.content: Write concise callbacks with arrow syntax, wrapping returned object literals in parentheses so braces aren't parsed as a block.

blocks.text: Arrow functions provide compact syntax and implicit returns for single expressions. Note two key behaviors: returning an object literal requires parentheses `=> ({ ... })`, and arrow functions inherit `this` lexically instead of creating their own.

insights.title: 22. Default, Rest, and Spread Parameters
insights.content: Assign fallback parameter values, collect variable arguments with ...rest, and expand arrays into arguments with ...spread.

blocks.text: Default parameters trigger when an argument is omitted or explicitly `undefined`. Rest parameters (`...args`) gather remaining arguments into a real array (replacing the legacy `arguments` object), while spread syntax expands an iterable at call sites.

insights.title: 23. Arrays: Creation, Indexing, and Array.isArray
insights.content: Create ordered collections, read elements from either end using .at(), and verify arrays with Array.isArray().

blocks.text: JavaScript arrays are dynamically sized, zero-indexed ordered lists. Use `arr.at(-1)` to read the last element cleanly without `arr[arr.length - 1]`, and use `Array.isArray()` instead of `typeof` to detect arrays reliably.

insights.title: 24. Mutating Array Methods
insights.content: Understand push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, and sort—all of which modify the original array in place.

blocks.text: Mutating methods alter the underlying array reference directly. `push`/`pop` operate on the end (`O(1)`), `shift`/`unshift` operate on the start (`O(n)`), `splice` inserts/removes at any index, and `sort()` sorts lexicographically unless given a comparator `(a, b) => a - b`.

blocks.code:
const items = [10, 2, 30];
items.push(40);        // [10, 2, 30, 40]
items.splice(1, 1, 5); // replace index 1 -> [10, 5, 30, 40]
items.sort((a, b) => a - b); // numeric sort!

console.log(items); // [5, 10, 30, 40]

insights.title: 25. Non-Mutating Array Methods: map, filter, slice, flatMap
insights.content: Transform, filter, and extract array subsets immutably by chaining pure methods that return new arrays.

blocks.text: `map` transforms each item 1-to-1, `filter` keeps items matching a predicate, `slice` extracts a shallow sub-range, and `flatMap` maps and flattens one level deep in a single pass—leaving the original array untouched.

insights.title: 26. Array Reduction and Search Methods
insights.content: Aggregate values with reduce and locate or test elements efficiently with find, findLast, some, and every.

blocks.text: `reduce` folds an array into a single value (sum, object map, grouped array)—always pass an explicit initial value to avoid errors on empty arrays. `find`/`findIndex` stop at the first match, while `some` and `every` short-circuit boolean checks.

insights.title: 27. ES2023 Immutable Array Methods: toSorted, toReversed, with
insights.content: Sort, reverse, splice, or replace an index without mutating the source array using ES2023 change-by-copy methods.

blocks.text: ES2023 introduced safe immutable counterparts to mutating methods: `toSorted()`, `toReversed()`, `toSpliced()`, and `with(index, value)`. They are ideal for React/Redux state updates where accidental mutation causes subtle bugs.

insights.title: 28. Objects: Literals, Shorthand, and Computed Keys
insights.content: Build clean object literals using property shorthand, method shorthand, and dynamic bracketed keys.

blocks.text: Object literals support concise `{ name }` shorthand when variable and key names match, compact method syntax `greet() {}`, and computed property names `[dynamicKey]: value` for keys known only at runtime.

insights.title: 29. Destructuring Arrays and Objects
insights.content: Extract values into variables with renaming, defaults, nested patterns, and rest collecting.

blocks.text: Destructuring unpacks elements from arrays by position and properties from objects by key. You can rename variables (`{ id: userId }`), provide default values (`= "N/A"`), and capture remaining items with `...rest`.

insights.title: 30. Spread (...) and Shallow Cloning
insights.content: Clone and merge arrays or objects concisely with spread syntax, keeping in mind that nested objects remain shared references.

blocks.text: Spread syntax (`{ ...a, ...b }` or `[...arr]`) creates a shallow copy: top-level properties are copied, and later keys overwrite earlier ones. Nested objects still point to the same reference unless cloned deeper.

insights.title: 31. Object.keys, Object.values, Object.entries & fromEntries
insights.content: Convert objects into arrays to filter or transform key-value pairs, then rebuild objects with Object.fromEntries.

blocks.text: `Object.keys`, `Object.values`, and `Object.entries` return an object's own enumerable string-keyed properties. Combining `Object.entries()` with `.filter()`/`.map()` and `Object.fromEntries()` lets you transform objects cleanly using array pipelines.

insights.title: 32. JSON.stringify and JSON.parse
insights.content: Serialize JavaScript values to JSON strings and parse JSON safely, knowing which types JSON drops or transforms.

blocks.text: `JSON.stringify` converts objects/arrays into JSON text—omitting `undefined`, functions, and Symbols, and converting `Date` to ISO strings. Always wrap `JSON.parse` in `try/catch` for untrusted input, and optionally pass a replacer or reviver.

insights.title: 33. Date Basics and Intl.DateTimeFormat
insights.content: Work with timestamps and ISO strings using Date, and format dates cleanly for any locale using Intl.DateTimeFormat.

blocks.text: JavaScript `Date` stores milliseconds since the Unix epoch (note that month indices are 0-based). Instead of manual string concatenation, use `Intl.DateTimeFormat` for locale-aware, timezone-safe formatting.

insights.title: 34. Error Handling with try, catch, finally, and throw
insights.content: Throw descriptive Error instances, catch runtime failures gracefully, and run cleanup logic reliably in finally.

blocks.text: Always `throw new Error("message")` rather than raw strings so stack traces are preserved. The `finally` block executes regardless of whether `try` succeeded or `catch` handled an error, making it ideal for closing resources or resetting loading flags.

insights.title: 35. DOM Selection, Manipulation, and Event Listeners
insights.content: Query elements with querySelector, update text safely with textContent, and attach interactive listeners with addEventListener.

blocks.text: Use `document.querySelector` / `querySelectorAll` with CSS selectors to locate elements. Prefer `textContent` over `innerHTML` for untrusted strings to prevent XSS attacks, and register handlers with `addEventListener` so multiple listeners don't overwrite each other.

insights.title: 36. Execution Context and the Call Stack
insights.content: Understand how JavaScript creates execution contexts in two phases and tracks active function frames on a LIFO call stack.

blocks.text: Every script and function call creates an Execution Context with a creation phase (hoisting bindings, setting `this`) and an execution phase. Function frames are pushed onto the single-threaded Call Stack (LIFO) and popped upon `return`; unbounded recursion overflows it.

insights.title: 37. Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
insights.content: let, const, and class are hoisted to the top of their block but stay uninitialized in the TDZ until their declaration runs.

blocks.text: All declarations are registered before execution, not just `var`. However, `var` is initialized to `undefined`, whereas `let`/`const`/`class` remain in the Temporal Dead Zone from block entry until evaluation—accessing them early throws a `ReferenceError`.

insights.title: 38. Lexical Scope and the Scope Chain
insights.content: Variable lookup resolves outward based on where functions are written in source code, not where they are invoked.

blocks.text: JavaScript uses lexical (static) scoping: an inner function sees variables in its own scope, then its enclosing parent scopes up to the global scope. Shadowing occurs when an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as an outer one.

insights.title: 39. Closures and Encapsulated Private State
insights.content: A closure lets an inner function retain live access to outer variables long after the outer function has returned.

blocks.text: Closures are foundational for data privacy, function factories, event handlers, and React hooks. Note that closures capture variable bindings (references), not snapshots—which is why `let` inside `for` loops creates a fresh binding per iteration.

insights.title: 40. IIFE and the Module Pattern
insights.content: Immediately Invoked Function Expressions create isolated scopes to avoid polluting the global namespace or run async setup.

blocks.text: An IIFE runs right after definition: `(function() { ... })()`. Before ES Modules, IIFEs powered the Module Pattern; today, async IIFEs `(async () => { ... })()` remain handy in CommonJS scripts or browser snippets without top-level `await`.

insights.title: 41. The this Keyword Across Call Sites
insights.content: Regular functions bind this dynamically by how they are called, while arrow functions capture this lexically.

blocks.text: Four rules govern `this` in regular functions (highest precedence first): `new` binding, explicit (`call`/`apply`/`bind`), implicit (`obj.method()`), and default (`undefined` in strict mode). Detaching a method (`const fn = obj.method`) loses implicit `this`.

insights.title: 42. call, apply, and bind
insights.content: Invoke functions immediately with a custom this via call/apply, or create a permanently bound function with bind.

blocks.text: `fn.call(ctx, a, b)` invokes `fn` with `this = ctx` and comma-separated args. `fn.apply(ctx, [a, b])` takes an array of args. `fn.bind(ctx, a)` returns a new function with `this` (and optionally leading args) permanently locked.

insights.title: 43. Object Property Descriptors
insights.content: Control whether properties are writable, enumerable, or configurable using Object.defineProperty.

blocks.text: Every object property has metadata flags: `value`, `writable`, `enumerable`, and `configurable`. Setting `enumerable: false` hides internal metadata from `Object.keys()` and `JSON.stringify()`, while `writable: false` prevents reassignment.

insights.title: 44. Getters and Setters (get / set)
insights.content: Expose computed properties and validate assignments transparently using get and set accessor syntax.

blocks.text: Accessor properties look like normal property reads/writes to callers (`user.fullName`), yet execute getter/setter functions behind the scenes. They work in both object literals and ES6 classes.

insights.title: 45. Prototypes and the Prototype Chain
insights.content: Property lookup traverses an object's [[Prototype]] chain until found or reaching null.

blocks.text: Every object (except `Object.create(null)`) has an internal `[[Prototype]]` link inspectable via `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`. Methods shared on a prototype live once in memory rather than being duplicated per instance.

insights.title: 46. Object.create and Dictionary Objects
insights.content: Link prototypes directly with Object.create(proto) or build prototype-free lookup maps using Object.create(null).

blocks.text: `Object.create(proto)` constructs a new object with `proto` as its `[[Prototype]]`. Passing `null` creates a pure dictionary without `toString` or `constructor` inherited from `Object.prototype`, eliminating key-collision risks.

blocks.code:
const safeDict = Object.create(null);
safeDict.toString = "custom value"; // No conflict with Object.prototype!

console.log(safeDict.toString); // "custom value"
console.log("valueOf" in safeDict); // false

insights.title: 47. ES6 class, Constructors, and Methods
insights.content: Classes provide clean syntax over prototypes, enforcing `new` invocation and strict mode inside the class body.

blocks.text: ES6 `class` declarations are syntactic sugar over prototype-based constructors, with key safeguards: class bodies always execute in strict mode, classes are not hoisted into usability (TDZ), and calling a class without `new` throws a `TypeError`.

insights.title: 48. Inheritance with extends and super
insights.content: Extend parent classes with extends, invoke super() before accessing this in constructors, and call super.method() when overriding.

blocks.text: Subclasses inherit both instance prototype methods and static methods from their parent via `extends`. In a subclass `constructor`, calling `super(...)` is mandatory before referencing `this` because the parent initializes the instance.

insights.title: 49. Private Fields (#field), Static Members, and Static Blocks
insights.content: Enforce true runtime privacy with # fields and organize class-level state with static members and static {} blocks.

blocks.text: Fields and methods prefixed with `#` are genuinely private—inaccessible outside the class body even via bracket notation or `Object.keys()`. ES2022 `static { ... }` blocks run once at class definition time for complex static initialization.

insights.title: 50. Symbol and Well-Known Symbols
insights.content: Create collision-free object keys with Symbol() and customize built-in language hooks like Symbol.toStringTag.

blocks.text: Every `Symbol()` call produces a guaranteed unique primitive key that won't clash with string keys or appear in `for...in` / `JSON.stringify`. Well-known symbols (`Symbol.iterator`, `Symbol.toStringTag`, `Symbol.toPrimitive`) hook into built-in engine protocols.

insights.title: 51. Set and Modern Set Operations
insights.content: Store unique values with O(1) lookup and use ES2025 Set methods like union, intersection, and difference.

blocks.text: `Set` preserves insertion order and guarantees uniqueness using SameValueZero equality (so `NaN` equals `NaN`). ES2025 added native mathematical set methods (`union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetricDifference`, `isSubsetOf`).

insights.title: 52. Map vs Plain Objects
insights.content: Choose Map when keys are non-strings, insertion order matters, or frequent additions/deletions occur.

blocks.text: Unlike plain objects (whose keys are coerced to strings or Symbols), `Map` accepts any value—including objects and functions—as keys, tracks `.size` in `O(1)`, and avoids prototype key collisions.

insights.title: 53. WeakMap and WeakSet for Memory-Safe Metadata
insights.content: Attach private metadata or visited flags to objects without preventing garbage collection when those objects go out of scope.

blocks.text: `WeakMap` keys (objects or non-registered Symbols) and `WeakSet` values are held weakly: if no other reference to the object exists, the entry is garbage-collected automatically. Because GC timing is non-deterministic, WeakMaps are not iterable.

insights.title: 54. ES Modules (import, export, Dynamic import())
insights.content: Organize code with static named/default exports for tree-shaking, and use import() for lazy code splitting.

blocks.text: ES Modules (`import`/`export`) are statically analyzable, enabling bundlers to eliminate dead code (tree-shaking). Dynamic `import(specifier)` returns a Promise resolving to the module namespace object—ideal for route-level lazy loading.

insights.title: 55. Regular Expressions: Flags and Named Capture Groups
insights.content: Extract structured substrings cleanly using named capture groups (?<name>...) and matchAll().

blocks.text: Named capture groups expose matches on `match.groups` instead of fragile numeric indices. Combined with `String.prototype.matchAll()` and the `/g` flag, you can iterate every match along with its named parts.

insights.title: 56. Event Loop: Call Stack, Macrotasks, and Microtasks
insights.content: Microtasks (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) always drain completely after each synchronous turn before the next macrotask runs.

blocks.text: The Event Loop executes synchronous code on the Call Stack first, then drains the entire Microtask Queue (`Promise.then`, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`) before picking one Macrotask (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O) and repeating.

insights.title: 57. Callbacks and Inversion of Control
insights.content: Understand error-first callbacks, callback hell, and why Promises replaced nested callbacks for composable async flows.

blocks.text: Passing a callback hands control of when (and how many times) your continuation runs to another function—called Inversion of Control. Wrapping callback APIs in a `Promise` restores predictable single-settlement guarantees.

insights.title: 58. Promises: Creation, Chaining, and Error Propagation
insights.content: Chain asynchronous steps cleanly with .then(), handle rejections anywhere in the chain via .catch(), and finalize with .finally().

blocks.text: A `Promise` settles once as either `fulfilled` or `rejected`. Returning a value or another Promise inside `.then()` chains sequentially, while a rejection skips intermediate `.then()` handlers until the nearest `.catch()`.

blocks.code:
const fetchUser = (id) =>
  id > 0
    ? Promise.resolve({ id, name: "Mona" })
    : Promise.reject(new Error("Invalid ID"));

fetchUser(1)
  .then((user) => user.name.toUpperCase())
  .then((upper) => console.log("User:", upper))
  .catch((err) => console.error(err.message))
  .finally(() => console.log("Request settled"));

insights.title: 59. Promise.all, allSettled, race, and any
insights.content: Run async operations concurrently using the right combinator for fail-fast, resilient aggregation, timeouts, or fastest-success.

blocks.text: `Promise.all` fails fast if any rejects; `Promise.allSettled` waits for all and returns `{ status, value | reason }`; `Promise.race` settles with the first settled promise (great for timeouts); `Promise.any` resolves with the first fulfillment.

insights.title: 60. async and await with Structured Error Handling
insights.content: Write readable async logic with async/await while avoiding accidental sequential waterfalls when calls can run in parallel.

blocks.text: `await` pauses only the enclosing `async` function—not the JS thread. Wrap awaited operations in `try/catch` for error handling, and start independent promises together before `await Promise.all(...)` so they execute concurrently.

insights.title: 61. fetch API, Response Checks, and AbortController
insights.content: Always check response.ok with fetch and cancel stale or timed-out requests using AbortController or AbortSignal.timeout.

blocks.text: `fetch()` only rejects on network failures, NOT on HTTP 404 or 500 responses—so checking `res.ok` is essential. Pass `signal: controller.signal` (or `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`) to cancel in-flight requests cleanly.

insights.title: 62. URL, URLSearchParams, and FormData
insights.content: Parse, mutate, and encode query strings safely with URL and URLSearchParams, and build multipart payloads with FormData.

blocks.text: Avoid manual string concatenation for URLs and query parameters. The `URL` and `URLSearchParams` APIs automatically handle percent-encoding and parsing, while `FormData` seamlessly serializes form inputs and `File`/`Blob` uploads.

insights.title: 63. Browser Storage: localStorage, sessionStorage, and Cookies
insights.content: Compare persistence scopes and limits across localStorage, sessionStorage, and HTTP cookies.

blocks.text: `localStorage` persists across browser restarts per origin (~5MB, string-only via JSON). `sessionStorage` is scoped to a single tab session. Cookies are small (~4KB) and sent automatically on HTTP requests—use `HttpOnly` cookies for sensitive auth tokens.

insights.title: 64. Event Bubbling, Capturing, and Event Delegation
insights.content: Attach a single listener to a parent container using event.target.closest() instead of binding listeners to every child.

blocks.text: DOM events travel down during capturing, hit `event.target`, and bubble back up to `document`. Event delegation leverages bubbling so dynamic child items work automatically with minimal memory overhead.

insights.title: 65. Debouncing and Throttling
insights.content: Debounce waits until bursts stop (search inputs); throttle caps execution rate (scroll/resize handlers).

blocks.text: High-frequency events like `input`, `scroll`, and `mousemove` can degrade performance. `debounce` resets a timer on every call and executes once idle; `throttle` guarantees at most one execution per time interval.

insights.title: 66. Memoization and Function Caching
insights.content: Cache expensive pure function outputs by argument key using a Map to avoid redundant recomputation.

blocks.text: Memoization trades a small amount of memory for speed on pure functions with repeated inputs. Use a `Map` (and bound cache size in long-lived apps) so cache memory doesn't grow unboundedly.

insights.title: 67. Currying and Partial Application
insights.content: Transform multi-argument functions into single-argument chains or pre-fill leading arguments for reusable specialized functions.

blocks.text: Currying turns `f(a, b, c)` into `f(a)(b)(c)`, while partial application fixes a subset of arguments upfront. Both let you build specialized helpers (like loggers or tax calculators) from generic functions.

insights.title: 68. Functional Composition (pipe and compose)
insights.content: Build readable data-transformation pipelines by chaining small single-purpose functions with pipe or compose.

blocks.text: `pipe(...fns)` passes a value left-to-right through a sequence of unary functions, while `compose(...fns)` evaluates right-to-left. Keeping each step pure makes pipelines easy to test and reuse.

insights.title: 69. Deep Cloning with structuredClone
insights.content: Deep-copy nested objects, Maps, Sets, Dates, and even circular references natively with structuredClone().

blocks.text: Unlike `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))`—which drops `Date` types, `Map`, `Set`, `undefined`, and fails on circular references—`structuredClone()` performs a true native deep clone (note: functions and DOM nodes still cannot be cloned).

insights.title: 70. Custom Error Subclasses and Error.cause
insights.content: Create domain-specific Error subclasses and preserve root-cause errors across layers using the ES2022 cause option.

blocks.text: Subclassing `Error` allows callers to check `err instanceof ValidationError`. Passing `{ cause: originalError }` (ES2022) lets you wrap low-level network or DB errors in high-level domain errors without losing diagnostic context.

insights.title: 71. Iterators and the Iteration Protocol (Symbol.iterator)
insights.content: Make any custom object work with for...of, spread (...), and destructuring by implementing [Symbol.iterator]().

blocks.text: An object is iterable if it implements `[Symbol.iterator]()` returning an iterator object with a `.next()` method yielding `{ value, done }`. Implementing this protocol enables seamless integration with built-in JS syntax.

insights.title: 72. Generators (function*, yield, yield*) and Lazy Sequences
insights.content: Pause and resume execution on demand with function* generators to produce infinite or memory-efficient lazy sequences.

blocks.text: A generator function (`function*`) returns a Generator (which is both an iterator and iterable). Execution pauses at each `yield` until `.next()` is called, and `yield*` delegates to another iterable or generator.

insights.title: 73. Async Iterators and for await...of
insights.content: Consume asynchronous data streams sequentially using Symbol.asyncIterator and for await...of.

blocks.text: Async iterables implement `[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` whose `.next()` returns a `Promise<{ value, done }>`. `for await...of` awaits each chunk automatically—ideal for Node streams, Web Streams, and paginated APIs.

insights.title: 74. Async Generators for Paginated APIs
insights.content: Combine async/await with yield in async function* to fetch paginated pages lazily only as the consumer requests them.

blocks.text: An `async function*` lets you `await` network calls and `yield` batches cleanly. If the consumer breaks out of `for await...of` early, remaining pages are never fetched.

insights.title: 75. Proxy Traps (get, set, has, apply, construct)
insights.content: Intercept fundamental object operations like property reads, writes, `in` checks, and function calls using Proxy.

blocks.text: `new Proxy(target, handler)` wraps an object or function to intercept operations via handler traps (`get`, `set`, `has`, `deleteProperty`, `apply`, `construct`). Common uses include schema validation, logging, and negative array indexing.

insights.title: 76. Reflect API and Safe Proxy Forwarding
insights.content: Pair Proxy traps with matching Reflect methods and pass receiver to preserve proper `this` binding for getters and prototypes.

blocks.text: `Reflect` provides function-based equivalents for every Proxy trap (`Reflect.get`, `Reflect.set`, `Reflect.has`). Forwarding `(target, prop, receiver)` guarantees getters on prototypes resolve `this` to the proxy, not the raw target.

insights.title: 77. Building Fine-Grained Reactive State with Proxy
insights.content: Implement Vue-style dependency tracking and change notifications by intercepting property reads and writes via Proxy.

blocks.text: Modern reactivity systems wrap state objects in a `Proxy`. The `set` trap compares old vs new values with `Object.is` and triggers subscribed listeners only when a property actually changes.

insights.title: 78. WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry
insights.content: Hold non-retaining object references with WeakRef and run optional cleanup callbacks after garbage collection via FinalizationRegistry.

blocks.text: `WeakRef.prototype.deref()` returns the target object if still alive or `undefined` after GC. `FinalizationRegistry` schedules a cleanup callback post-collection—useful for caches or external resource handles, though never rely on it for critical determinism.

insights.title: 79. Memory Leaks, Retention Paths, and Garbage Collection
insights.content: Prevent common JS memory leaks caused by forgotten timers, detached DOM nodes, global caches, and unremoved listeners.

blocks.text: JavaScript's mark-and-sweep GC frees objects unreachable from roots (global, active stack). Leaks happen when live closures, global Maps, `setInterval`, or `addEventListener` unintentionally hold references to large objects or detached DOM trees.

insights.title: 80. Trampolines for Stack-Safe Deep Recursion
insights.content: Convert tail-recursive functions into iterative thunk loops with a trampoline so deep inputs never overflow the call stack.

blocks.text: Most JS engines (except Safari/JavaScriptCore) do not enforce Proper Tail Calls. A trampoline invokes thunks (`() => fn(...)`) in a `while` loop, keeping call stack depth constant `O(1)` even for hundreds of thousands of steps.

insights.title: 81. ArrayBuffer and Typed Arrays (Uint8Array, Float32Array)
insights.content: Process binary protocols, audio, WebGL buffers, and image bytes efficiently using fixed-type views over ArrayBuffer.

blocks.text: `ArrayBuffer` allocates raw contiguous bytes; Typed Arrays (`Uint8Array`, `Int32Array`, `Float32Array`) provide fast typed views over that buffer. ES2024 also added resizable `ArrayBuffer` and `buffer.transfer()`.

insights.title: 82. DataView and Binary Endianness
insights.content: Read and write heterogeneous multi-byte binary fields with explicit big-endian or little-endian ordering via DataView.

blocks.text: Unlike Typed Arrays (which use host CPU endianness), `DataView` lets you specify `littleEndian` per read/write at arbitrary byte offsets—essential for parsing network packets, PNG headers, or binary file formats.

insights.title: 83. TextEncoder and TextDecoder (UTF-8 Binary Conversion)
insights.content: Convert strings to UTF-8 Uint8Array bytes and decode byte streams back into strings accurately, including multi-byte characters.

blocks.text: `TextEncoder` encodes JS strings into UTF-8 `Uint8Array` bytes, and `TextDecoder` decodes bytes (with optional `{ stream: true }` for chunked streaming) back into text without corrupting multi-byte UTF-8 sequences.

insights.title: 84. Web Streams API (ReadableStream, TransformStream)
insights.content: Stream and transform chunks incrementally with backpressure support using ReadableStream and TransformStream.

blocks.text: The WHATWG Streams API lets browsers, Bun, and Node process large payloads chunk by chunk via `pipeThrough()` without buffering entire files into memory. `ReadableStream` is also async-iterable with `for await...of`.

insights.title: 85. Web Workers and Transferable Objects
insights.content: Offload CPU-heavy work off the main UI thread with Web Workers and transfer ArrayBuffers in O(1) zero-copy.

blocks.text: Web Workers run in isolated OS threads communicating via `postMessage`. Normally messages are structured-cloned, but passing `[buffer]` in the transfer list transfers ownership instantaneously with zero copy (detaching it from the sender).

insights.title: 86. SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics
insights.content: Share memory across workers safely without data races using atomic operations like Atomics.add and Atomics.compareExchange.

blocks.text: `SharedArrayBuffer` allows multiple threads to read/write the same memory region. `Atomics` provides indivisible read-modify-write instructions (`Atomics.add`, `load`, `store`, `waitAsync`) to prevent race conditions.

insights.title: 87. BroadcastChannel for Cross-Tab Synchronization
insights.content: Synchronize auth logout, theme changes, or state updates across open tabs and workers of the same origin.

blocks.text: `BroadcastChannel` creates a lightweight pub/sub bus shared by all windows, tabs, iframes, and workers on the same origin—simpler and cleaner than abusing `localStorage` `storage` events.

insights.title: 88. IndexedDB Transactions and Object Stores
insights.content: Persist large structured datasets, blobs, and indexed records offline in the browser using IndexedDB.

blocks.text: `IndexedDB` is an asynchronous, transactional NoSQL database built into browsers. Schema upgrades happen inside `onupgradeneeded`, and reads/writes execute within `readonly` or `readwrite` transactions.

insights.title: 89. MutationObserver and IntersectionObserver
insights.content: Detect viewport visibility for lazy loading without scroll listeners, and observe DOM tree mutations asynchronously.

blocks.text: `IntersectionObserver` notifies you when elements enter or leave the viewport (replacing expensive `scroll` + `getBoundingClientRect()` loops). `MutationObserver` batches DOM node/attribute changes into a microtask callback.

insights.title: 90. ResizeObserver and PerformanceObserver
insights.content: React to element-specific box size changes with ResizeObserver and capture Core Web Vitals or long tasks via PerformanceObserver.

blocks.text: Unlike `window.onresize`, `ResizeObserver` watches individual element dimensions (including container query or flex shifts). `PerformanceObserver` passively streams browser performance entries like `largest-contentful-paint` and `measure`.

insights.title: 91. requestAnimationFrame and Frame-Synced Loops
insights.content: Schedule visual DOM/Canvas updates before each display repaint and use delta time for refresh-rate independence.

blocks.text: `requestAnimationFrame` aligns callbacks to the monitor's VSync (60Hz/120Hz) and pauses automatically in background tabs. Computing movement from `timestamp - lastTime` ensures identical animation speed across 60Hz and 144Hz screens.

insights.title: 92. queueMicrotask vs setTimeout vs requestIdleCallback
insights.content: Pick the right scheduling primitive for urgent post-turn work, macrotask yielding, or low-priority background work.

blocks.text: `queueMicrotask` runs before browser rendering/macrotasks—ideal for batching state updates. `setTimeout(fn, 0)` yields to let the browser paint and handle input. `requestIdleCallback` defers telemetry or non-urgent work until idle frames.

insights.title: 93. Intl APIs: NumberFormat, RelativeTimeFormat, and Segmenter
insights.content: Format currencies, relative times, locale sorting, and grapheme clusters natively without heavy third-party libraries.

blocks.text: The `Intl` namespace covers far more than dates: `Intl.NumberFormat` formats currencies/units, `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` formats `"2 days ago"`, `Intl.Collator` sorts strings properly per locale, and `Intl.Segmenter` splits graphemes/words accurately (crucial for emoji and Arabic).

insights.title: 94. Object.groupBy and Map.groupBy (ES2024)
insights.content: Group iterables cleanly by string key or arbitrary object/boolean key using ES2024's built-in groupBy methods.

blocks.text: `Object.groupBy(items, callback)` creates a null-prototype object mapping string/Symbol keys to arrays. `Map.groupBy(items, callback)` returns a `Map`, allowing non-string keys (booleans, objects, numbers) without key stringification.

insights.title: 95. Promise.withResolvers (ES2024) and Promise.try (ES2025)
insights.content: Extract resolve/reject handles cleanly with Promise.withResolvers and normalize sync/async throws with Promise.try.

blocks.text: `Promise.withResolvers()` returns `{ promise, resolve, reject }` directly without wrapping outer variables inside `new Promise(...)`. `Promise.try(fn)` safely wraps a function that might throw synchronously or return a Promise.

insights.title: 96. Array.fromAsync and ES2025 Iterator Helpers
insights.content: Materialize async iterables with Array.fromAsync and chain lazy .map/.filter/.take pipelines directly on any iterator.

blocks.text: ES2024 `Array.fromAsync` collects async iterables into an Array. ES2025 Iterator Helpers add `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.take()`, `.drop()`, and `.toArray()` to `Iterator.prototype`, evaluating lazily without allocating intermediate arrays.

insights.title: 97. RegExp /v Flag (Unicode Sets) and Lookbehind Assertions
insights.content: Match multi-codepoint emoji sequences and perform set subtraction with /v, plus context-aware lookbehinds (?<=...).

blocks.text: Lookbehind assertions (`(?<=...)` and `(?<!...)`) assert preceding text without consuming characters. The ES2024 `/v` flag upgrades `/u` with set operations (`--` difference, `&&` intersection) and string properties.

insights.title: 98. Top-Level await and Module Graph Execution
insights.content: Await async initialization directly at module top level in ESM, understanding how it blocks dependent modules.

blocks.text: Top-level `await` (ES2022) lets an ES module await async configuration, DB connections, or dynamic imports before exporting. Sibling independent branches in the module graph continue loading concurrently, while direct importers wait.

insights.title: 99. Prototype Pollution Prevention and Object Immutability
insights.content: Guard merge helpers against __proto__/constructor injection and lock objects with Object.freeze or Object.seal.

blocks.text: Recursive object merges on untrusted JSON can mutate `Object.prototype` if keys like `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype` aren't rejected. Use `Object.hasOwn`, block dangerous keys, or use `Map` / `Object.freeze()`.

insights.title: 100. Explicit Resource Management (using) and Modern Decorators
insights.content: Clean up deterministic resources automatically at scope exit with using / Symbol.dispose, and instrument classes with Stage 3 decorators.

blocks.text: Explicit Resource Management introduces `using` and `await using`, which automatically invoke `[Symbol.dispose]()` or `[Symbol.asyncDispose]()` when a block exits (even on thrown errors). Stage 3 Decorators standardize wrapping classes, methods, and accessors.

interviewQuestions.title: var, let, const — Scope, Hoisting & Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
interviewQuestions.content: var is function-scoped and hoisted with undefined; let and const are block-scoped, hoisted without initialization, and live in the Temporal Dead Zone until evaluated.

blocks.text:
• var is function-scoped (or global-scoped), can be re-declared, and is hoisted and initialized to undefined.
• let and const are block-scoped ({ ... }), cannot be re-declared in the same scope, and const prevents reassignment of the binding (not mutation of objects).
• Hoisting & TDZ: let and const declarations are hoisted to the top of their block, but remain uninitialized in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) from block entry until the declaration line executes—accessing them early throws a ReferenceError.

interviewQuestions.title: Closures, Lexical Environment & Stale Closures in Async Code
interviewQuestions.content: A closure is a function bundled with its lexical environment, allowing access to outer variables even after the outer function returns.

blocks.text:
• Lexical Environment: Scope is determined by where a function is written in source code, not where it is called.
• Closure: When an inner function retains a live reference to variables from its outer lexical scope after the outer function has returned.
• Stale Closures: In async callbacks (timers, event listeners, React effects), a closure can capture an outdated primitive value or state snapshot if dependencies or refs are not updated.

interviewQuestions.title: this Binding, call / apply / bind & Arrow Functions
interviewQuestions.content: Regular functions determine `this` dynamically at call time; arrow functions inherit `this` lexically from their enclosing scope.

blocks.text:
• Default / Implicit Binding: In a method call `obj.fn()`, `this` is `obj`. Detached (`const fn = obj.fn; fn()`), `this` is `undefined` in strict mode (or global).
• Explicit Binding:
  - `fn.call(ctx, arg1, arg2)` invokes immediately with comma-separated args.
  - `fn.apply(ctx, [arg1, arg2])` invokes immediately with an array of args.
  - `fn.bind(ctx, arg1)` returns a new bound function without invoking it.
• `new` Binding: Creates a fresh object and binds `this` to it.
• Arrow Functions: Have no own `this`, `arguments`, or `super`—they capture `this` lexically from the outer scope and cannot be rebound with `.call/.apply/.bind`.

interviewQuestions.title: Prototype Chain, Inheritance & ES6 Classes vs Prototypes
interviewQuestions.content: JavaScript uses prototypal inheritance; ES6 classes are syntax sugar over prototype delegation with a few stricter semantics.

blocks.text:
• Prototype Chain: Every object has an internal `[[Prototype]]` link. Property lookups walk up the chain until found or reaching `null` (`Object.prototype`).
• What IS syntax sugar: Methods defined on a `class` are placed on `ClassName.prototype`, and `extends` wires up `SubClass.prototype.[[Prototype]]` to `SuperClass.prototype`.
• What is NOT pure sugar:
  - Classes cannot be called without `new` (throws TypeError).
  - Class bodies always execute in strict mode.
  - Class declarations are not hoisted like function declarations (they stay in TDZ).
  - Class methods are non-enumerable by default.

interviewQuestions.title: Event Loop: Call Stack, Microtasks, Task Queue & async/await
interviewQuestions.content: The event loop drains the entire microtask queue (Promises, queueMicrotask) after each call stack turn before picking the next macrotask (setTimeout, I/O).

blocks.text:
• Call Stack: Executes synchronous frames LIFO.
• Microtask Queue: Holds Promise `.then/.catch/.finally` callbacks, `await` continuations, and `queueMicrotask`. Completely drained after synchronous code finishes and before the next macrotask or render.
• Task (Macrotask) Queue: Holds `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, DOM events, and I/O callbacks (processed one task per event-loop tick).
• async/await Patterns: Always wrap awaited calls in `try/catch` for error handling, and use `Promise.all` / `Promise.allSettled` for independent requests instead of sequential `await` inside loops.

interviewQuestions.title: Equality (== vs ===), References, Shallow vs Deep Copy & Array Methods
interviewQuestions.content: === checks value and type without coercion; objects are compared and copied by reference, requiring structuredClone or deep cloning for nested structures.

blocks.text:
• == vs ===: `===` (strict equality) compares both type and value without coercion. `==` performs type coercion (`0 == false`, `'' == 0`, `null == undefined`).
• Truthy / Falsy: Only 8 falsy values exist: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`.
• References & Copying:
  - Shallow copy (`{ ...obj }`, `Object.assign`, `[...arr]`) copies top-level properties only—nested objects still share references.
  - Deep copy: Use `structuredClone(obj)` (handles Dates, Maps, Sets, circular refs). `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` drops `undefined`, functions, and Symbols.
• Functional Array Methods: `map` (transform), `filter` (subset), `reduce` (accumulate), `find` (first match), `some` (any match), `every` (all match).

interviewQuestions.title: DOM Events, Event Delegation & Reflow vs Repaint
interviewQuestions.content: Event delegation attaches one listener to a parent using bubbling; reflow recalculates layout geometry while repaint redraws visual styles.

blocks.text:
• Event Delegation: Attach a single listener to a common ancestor instead of N child listeners, leveraging event bubbling (`event.target.closest('.item')`). Ideal for dynamic lists and lowers memory overhead.
• Reflow (Layout): Triggered when element geometry changes (width, height, margin, padding, font-size, DOM insertion/removal, or reading layout properties like `offsetHeight` / `getBoundingClientRect` after writes — layout thrashing).
• Repaint: Triggered when visual appearance changes without affecting layout (color, background-color, visibility, box-shadow).
• Best Practice: Animate `transform` and `opacity` to stay on the compositor thread and skip both reflow and repaint.

interviewQuestions.title: Debouncing vs Throttling & requestAnimationFrame
interviewQuestions.content: Debounce waits until activity pauses; throttle limits execution to fixed intervals; requestAnimationFrame syncs visual updates with the display refresh rate.

blocks.text:
• Debouncing: Delays execution until `N` ms have passed since the *last* call. Best for search inputs, form validation, and window resize handlers.
• Throttling: Guarantees execution at most once every `N` ms regardless of how many events fire. Best for scroll tracking, mousemove, and button spam protection.
• requestAnimationFrame (rAF): Schedules a callback right before the browser's next repaint (~60fps/120fps). Use it for smooth JS animations or DOM measurements synchronized with frames, rather than `setInterval`.

interviewQuestions.title: Fetch, AbortController, CORS, Web Storage vs Cookies & Web Workers
interviewQuestions.content: AbortController cancels stale in-flight requests; CORS is enforced by browsers via server headers; Web Workers offload heavy computation off the main UI thread.

blocks.text:
• Fetch & AbortController: Pass `controller.signal` to `fetch()` to cancel outdated requests (e.g., rapid search typing or component unmount) and prevent race conditions.
• CORS: Enforced by the browser. Frontend cannot bypass CORS; the backend must return `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` (for cookies).
• Web Storage vs Cookies:
  - `localStorage` (~5–10MB, persists across sessions, JS-accessible — never store sensitive secrets).
  - `sessionStorage` (cleared when tab closes).
  - `Cookies` (~4KB, sent automatically with HTTP requests; support `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite` flags for secure auth).
• Pure Functions, Memoization & Web Workers: Pure functions avoid side effects and are trivial to test. Memoize only expensive calculations with stable inputs (over-memoizing adds memory & comparison overhead). Use Web Workers for CPU-heavy tasks (CSV parsing, image processing, large sorting) so the main thread stays responsive.

interviewQuestions.title: REST API Design, Empty States & Production Debugging
interviewQuestions.content: Handle HTTP status codes explicitly, render intentional empty/error UI states, and trace silent production errors using source maps, telemetry, and network inspection.

blocks.text:
• REST API Design & Status Codes:
  - Resource-oriented nouns (`/api/employees`), proper HTTP methods (`GET`, `POST`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`), pagination, and consistent error payloads.
  - Status codes: `200/201/204` (success), `400/422` (validation), `401/403` (auth/permissions), `404` (not found), `409` (conflict/duplicate), `429` (rate limit), `5xx` (server errors).
• When API returns no data: Distinguish between `200 []` (valid empty state → show clear empty state UI + CTA), `204 No Content`, and network/5xx errors (show retry UI, never crash on `undefined.map`).
• Troubleshooting Production Errors Not in Console:
  1. Check Network tab & server logs (silent failed requests, CORS, or 4xx/5xx swallowed by `catch`).
  2. Use Error Monitoring (Sentry / Datadog) with uploaded Source Maps to de-minify stack traces.
  3. Verify environment variables, build flags, service worker stale caches, or React Error Boundaries.

interviewQuestions.title: Promise Combinators: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any
interviewQuestions.content: Promise combinators coordinate concurrent async operations with distinct short-circuiting rules for fulfillment and rejection.

blocks.text:
• Promise.all(iterable): Resolves when all promises fulfill; rejects immediately on the first rejection (fail-fast).
• Promise.allSettled(iterable): Waits for every promise to finish and returns status objects ({ status: 'fulfilled' | 'rejected' }) without rejecting.
• Promise.race(iterable): Settles with the very first promise that either fulfills or rejects (useful for timeouts).
• Promise.any(iterable): Resolves with the first fulfilled value; rejects with an AggregateError only if every promise rejects.

interviewQuestions.title: Promise.withResolvers() (ES2024) and the Deferred Pattern
interviewQuestions.content: Promise.withResolvers() returns { promise, resolve, reject } directly, eliminating outer-variable boilerplate when resolving a Promise outside its executor.

blocks.text:
• Problem Solved: Historically, creating a deferred Promise required declaring `let resolve, reject` outside `new Promise((res, rej) => ...)`.
• ES2024 Solution: `Promise.withResolvers()` cleanly destructures `{ promise, resolve, reject }` in one call.
• Use Cases: Bridging callback/event APIs (WebSocket handshakes, stream queues, request deduplication) to async/await.
• Note: Microtask timing and rejection semantics are identical to `new Promise()`.

interviewQuestions.title: Promise.try() (ES2025) for Normalizing Sync and Async Errors
interviewQuestions.content: Promise.try(fn, ...args) invokes a callback immediately and wraps synchronous returns, synchronous throws, and returned Promises into one Promise chain.

blocks.text:
• Sync-vs-Async Hazard: Calling `fn().catch(...)` crashes if `fn` throws synchronously before returning a Promise.
• Why Not Promise.resolve().then(fn): That defers `fn` to the next microtask, whereas `Promise.try(fn)` executes `fn` synchronously in the current turn like an `async` function body.
• ES2025 Benefit: Guarantees all errors—sync or async—route into `.catch()` without extra try/catch boilerplate.

interviewQuestions.title: Generators, Async Iterators (for await...of) & Array.fromAsync()
interviewQuestions.content: Generators produce lazy sequences via yield; async generators combine await and yield to stream paginated or chunked data with for await...of or Array.fromAsync().

blocks.text:
• Generator Functions (`function*`): Pause execution on `yield` and resume on `.next()`, returning `{ value, done }`. `yield*` delegates to another iterable.
• Async Generators (`async function*`): Yield Promises resolved one step at a time, ideal for paginated APIs, SSE, or Web Streams.
• `for await...of`: Consumes async iterables sequentially, awaiting each step cleanly.
• `Array.fromAsync()` (ES2024): Awaits an async iterable (or iterable of Promises) and resolves to a standard Array.

interviewQuestions.title: ES2025 Iterator Helpers & Lazy Evaluation vs Array Chains
interviewQuestions.content: ES2025 adds .map(), .filter(), .take(), .drop(), .flatMap(), and .toArray() onto Iterator.prototype, enabling single-pass lazy pipelines without intermediate arrays.

blocks.text:
• Eager Array Chains: `[].filter().map()` allocates a full intermediate array at each step and processes every element upfront.
• Lazy Iterator Helpers: Operations run element-by-element on demand only when consumed (via `.toArray()`, `.reduce()`, `for...of`, or spread).
• Infinite & Large Streams: Methods like `.take(n)` and `.drop(n)` let you safely slice infinite generators or huge `Map`/`Set` iterators.
• Note: Call `.values()` on an Array (`arr.values().filter(...)`) to enter the lazy Iterator pipeline.

interviewQuestions.title: Object.groupBy() vs Map.groupBy() (ES2024)
interviewQuestions.content: ES2024 introduces native Object.groupBy() and Map.groupBy() to partition iterables by callback keys without manual reduce() boilerplate.

blocks.text:
• Object.groupBy(items, cb): Coerces returned keys to strings/symbols and returns a null-prototype object (`Object.create(null)`), preventing collisions with `toString` or `constructor`.
• Map.groupBy(items, cb): Preserves non-string keys (booleans, numbers, objects) by returning a `Map`.
• Note: Both group references to the original elements (shallow grouping) and accept any iterable, not just Arrays.

interviewQuestions.title: Native Set Algebra Methods in ES2025
interviewQuestions.content: ES2025 adds built-in mathematical set methods—union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, and isDisjointFrom—to Set.prototype.

blocks.text:
• Composition Methods (return a new Set): `union`, `intersection`, `difference`, and `symmetricDifference`.
• Predicate Methods (return a boolean): `isSubsetOf`, `isSupersetOf`, and `isDisjointFrom`.
• Interoperability: They accept any Set-like object (implementing `size`, `has()`, and `keys()`), such as another Set or custom collections, without mutating either input.

blocks.code:
const frontend = new Set(["js", "ts", "css"]);
const backend = new Set(["ts", "go", "sql"]);

console.log([...frontend.intersection(backend)]);       // ["ts"]
console.log([...frontend.difference(backend)]);         // ["js", "css"]
console.log([...frontend.union(backend)]);              // ["js", "ts", "css", "go", "sql"]
console.log([...frontend.symmetricDifference(backend)]);// ["js", "css", "go", "sql"]
console.log(new Set(["ts"]).isSubsetOf(frontend));      // true

interviewQuestions.title: Import Attributes & JSON Modules (ES2025)
interviewQuestions.content: Import Attributes (using the `with` keyword) explicitly declare non-JavaScript module types such as JSON, preventing MIME-type confusion vulnerabilities.

blocks.text:
• Security Motivation: If a server accidentally serves a `.json` file with a JS MIME type, a bare `import` could execute attacker-controlled code.
• Syntax: `import data from './file.json' with { type: 'json' }` instructs the runtime/bundler to parse the resource strictly as JSON.
• Dynamic Support: `import(url, { with: { type: 'json' } })` supports runtime conditional loading.
• Note: The older `assert` keyword was superseded by `with` in the finalized ES2025 specification.

interviewQuestions.title: Top-Level await in ES Modules: Execution & Pitfalls
interviewQuestions.content: Top-level await lets ES modules pause their own evaluation until an awaited Promise settles, delaying execution of dependent importer modules.

blocks.text:
• How It Works: Only valid in ES modules (`.mjs` or `type: 'module'`), not CommonJS. Sibling modules without a dependency on the awaiting module continue loading concurrently.
• Execution Blocking: Importer modules wait for the exported module's top-level `await` to settle before executing their own body.
• Pitfalls: Overusing top-level `await` on slow network calls delays app startup, and circular dependencies involving top-level `await` can deadlock module evaluation.

interviewQuestions.title: Modern RegExp: RegExp.escape(), Named Groups & Pattern Modifiers (ES2025)
interviewQuestions.content: ES2025 adds RegExp.escape() to sanitize user strings for dynamic regexes and inline modifiers (?i:...) to scope flags to sub-patterns.

blocks.text:
• RegExp.escape(str) (ES2025): Safely escapes metacharacters (`.`, `*`, `+`, `?`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `^`, `$`, etc.) so dynamic user input is matched literally.
• Inline Pattern Modifiers (ES2025): `(?ims-ims:pattern)` toggles `i`, `m`, or `s` flags only inside a specific group.
• Named Capture Groups (`(?<year>\d{4})`): Accessed via `match.groups.year` instead of brittle numeric indices; ES2025 also allows duplicate group names across alternative `|` branches.

interviewQuestions.title: Non-Mutating Array Methods (ES2023) & Array.prototype.at()
interviewQuestions.content: toSorted(), toReversed(), toSpliced(), and with() return new copied arrays without mutating the original, simplifying immutable state updates.

blocks.text:
• Mutating vs Non-Mutating: Classic `.sort()`, `.reverse()`, and `.splice()` mutate arrays in place—a common bug source in React/Redux state.
• ES2023 Immutable Equivalents: `.toSorted()`, `.toReversed()`, `.toSpliced()`, and `.with(index, value)` always return a shallow copy.
• `.at(index)` (ES2022): Supports negative indexing (`arr.at(-1)`) cleanly on Arrays, Strings, and TypedArrays.
• Remember: `.toSorted()` without a comparator still sorts elements as UTF-16 strings!

blocks.code:
const nums = [3, 1, 2];

const sorted = nums.toSorted((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 2, 3]
const updated = nums.with(1, 99);              // [3, 99, 2]
const spliced = nums.toSpliced(1, 1, 8, 9);    // [3, 8, 9, 2]

console.log(nums);       // [3, 1, 2] (unchanged)
console.log(nums.at(-1)); // 2

interviewQuestions.title: Explicit Resource Management: using, await using & Symbol.dispose
interviewQuestions.content: The `using` and `await using` declarations bind resource lifetimes to lexical block scope, automatically invoking Symbol.dispose or Symbol.asyncDispose on exit.

blocks.text:
• Problem: Forgetting `try { ... } finally { cleanup(); }` leaks file handles, DB connections, locks, or subscriptions when early returns or exceptions occur.
• `using` / `await using`: Declares block-scoped resources that automatically invoke `[Symbol.dispose]()` (sync) or `[Symbol.asyncDispose]()` (async) in reverse declaration order (LIFO) when the block exits.
• SuppressedError: If both the block body and disposal throw, JavaScript throws a `SuppressedError` preserving both errors instead of losing the original exception.

interviewQuestions.title: Error Chaining ({ cause }), AggregateError & Custom Error Classes
interviewQuestions.content: Passing `{ cause }` when re-throwing preserves the original low-level stack trace while adding domain context; AggregateError bundles multiple failures.

blocks.text:
• Error `{ cause }` (ES2022): `new Error('High-level message', { cause: originalErr })` keeps the root exception inspectable without losing stack traces or stringifying errors.
• `AggregateError`: Represents multiple errors wrapped in one (thrown by `Promise.any()`), exposing an `.errors` array.
• Custom Errors: Subclass `Error`, pass `options` (`super(msg, options)`), and set `this.name = this.constructor.name` for clean `instanceof` and log filtering.

interviewQuestions.title: Modern Intl APIs & Why Date Is Flawed (Temporal Motivation)
interviewQuestions.content: Built-in Intl formatters replace heavy date/i18n libraries for localization, while Temporal addresses Date's mutability, zero-indexed months, and timezone flaws.

blocks.text:
• Intl Ecosystem: `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, `Intl.NumberFormat`, `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat`, `Intl.ListFormat`, and `Intl.Segmenter` (locale-aware word/grapheme splitting) are zero-bundle-size browser natives.
• Legacy `Date` Pitfalls: Mutable methods (`setDate`), 0-indexed months (`0 = Jan`), inconsistent string parsing, and poor DST/IANA timezone support.
• Temporal API: Introduces immutable, timezone-explicit types (`Temporal.PlainDate`, `Temporal.ZonedDateTime`, `Temporal.Instant`) with exact calendar arithmetic.

interviewQuestions.title: Map vs Object and Set vs Array: Performance & Trade-offs
interviewQuestions.content: Map and Set provide O(1) average lookup/deletion, arbitrary key types, and clean iteration without prototype key collisions.

blocks.text:
• Map vs Object: `Map` allows any value (objects, functions, primitives) as keys, preserves insertion order reliably, tracks `.size` in O(1), and has no prototype keys (`__proto__`, `toString`). Plain objects are faster for fixed static schemas and serialize natively to JSON.
• Set vs Array: `Set.has()` is O(1) average vs `Array.includes()` O(n), automatically enforces uniqueness via SameValueZero (`NaN === NaN`), and lacks index access.

interviewQuestions.title: WeakMap & WeakSet: Weak References and Garbage Collection
interviewQuestions.content: WeakMap and WeakSet hold weak references to object keys/values, allowing the garbage collector to reclaim them once no strong references remain.

blocks.text:
• Key Constraint: Keys in `WeakMap` and values in `WeakSet` must be objects (or non-registered Symbols in ES2023+).
• No Enumeration: They have no `.size`, `.keys()`, or `.clear()` because GC timing is non-deterministic—exposing keys would leak GC state.
• Best Use Cases: Associating private metadata or cached computations with DOM nodes or class instances without causing memory leaks.

interviewQuestions.title: WeakRef & FinalizationRegistry: Use Cases and Non-Deterministic Caveats
interviewQuestions.content: WeakRef lets you read an object via .deref() without keeping it alive; FinalizationRegistry runs a cleanup callback after an object is collected.

blocks.text:
• WeakRef: `ref.deref()` returns the target object or `undefined` if already collected.
• FinalizationRegistry: Registers a callback fired asynchronously *after* garbage collection reclaims a target.
• Critical Interview Warning: Never rely on `FinalizationRegistry` for essential resource cleanup (sockets, DB handles) or app logic—GC timing varies wildly across engines and may never fire before process exit. Use it only for optional cache eviction or diagnostics.

interviewQuestions.title: V8 Garbage Collection & Common Memory Leaks in SPAs
interviewQuestions.content: JS engines collect unreachable objects using generational mark-and-sweep; SPA memory leaks happen when detached DOM nodes, timers, or listeners remain reachable from roots.

blocks.text:
• How GC Works (V8): Uses reachability from roots (global scope, call stack) with a Generational collector: fast Scavenger for short-lived Young Generation objects and Mark-Sweep-Compact for Old Generation.
• Top SPA Memory Leaks:
  1. Forgotten `setInterval` / global `window` event listeners.
  2. Detached DOM nodes still referenced by JS variables or closures.
  3. Unbounded in-memory caches (`Map` without LRU eviction).
  4. Closures accidentally retaining large outer objects.
• Detection: Chrome DevTools Memory tab → compare two Heap Snapshots and filter by 'Detached'.

interviewQuestions.title: Proxy & Reflect: Why Use Reflect Inside Proxy Traps?
interviewQuestions.content: Proxy intercepts fundamental object operations via traps, while Reflect forwards those operations safely while preserving receiver binding (`this`) and return semantics.

blocks.text:
• Proxy: Wraps a target object to intercept `get`, `set`, `has`, `deleteProperty`, `apply`, and `construct` operations (used in Vue 3 reactivity, Immer, validation).
• Why `Reflect` Over `target[prop]`:
  1. Preserves `receiver`: Inside getters or inherited methods, `Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver)` ensures `this` points to the proxy so nested reads also trigger traps.
  2. Uniform Return Values: `Reflect.set()` and `Reflect.deleteProperty()` return booleans matching trap invariants.
  3. Respects internal proxy invariants (e.g., non-configurable properties).

interviewQuestions.title: Symbols, Global Symbol Registry & Well-Known Symbols
interviewQuestions.content: Symbols create guaranteed-unique property keys hidden from normal enumeration, while well-known symbols customize built-in language protocols.

blocks.text:
• Uniqueness: `Symbol('id') !== Symbol('id')`. Symbol properties are skipped by `for...in`, `Object.keys()`, and `JSON.stringify()`, avoiding key collisions.
• Global Registry: `Symbol.for('app.key')` creates/reuses a shared symbol across realms; `Symbol.keyFor(sym)` retrieves its key.
• Well-Known Symbols: Hook into JS internals—`Symbol.iterator` (`for...of`), `Symbol.asyncIterator` (`for await...of`), `Symbol.toPrimitive` (coercion), `Symbol.toStringTag`, and `Symbol.dispose`.

interviewQuestions.title: Property Descriptors & Object.freeze vs seal vs preventExtensions
interviewQuestions.content: Every property has metadata flags (writable, enumerable, configurable); preventExtensions, seal, and freeze progressively lock down object mutability.

blocks.text:
• Data Descriptor Flags: `value`, `writable` (can reassign), `enumerable` (visible in `Object.keys`/`for...in`), `configurable` (can delete or redefine flags).
• Accessor Descriptor Flags: `get`, `set`, `enumerable`, `configurable`.
• Lockdown Levels:
  - `Object.preventExtensions(obj)`: Blocks adding new properties.
  - `Object.seal(obj)`: Prevents adding/deleting properties (`configurable: false`), existing writable values can still change.
  - `Object.freeze(obj)`: Makes all own properties non-writable and non-configurable (shallow only).

interviewQuestions.title: ES2022 Private Class Fields (#), Static Blocks & Brand Checks (#x in obj)
interviewQuestions.content: True `#private` class fields enforce hard runtime encapsulation inaccessible outside the class body, unlike TypeScript-only `private` or `_underscore` conventions.

blocks.text:
• Hard Encapsulation: `#balance` cannot be accessed or reflected via `Object.keys()`, `Proxy`, or subclasses—outside access throws a `SyntaxError`.
• Brand Checks (`#field in obj`): Safely checks if an object is an authentic instance of the class without throwing a `TypeError`.
• Static Initialization Blocks (`static { ... }`): Run once at class definition time with privileged access to private static fields.
• Getters/Setters: Expose computed or validated properties cleanly without breaking caller syntax.

interviewQuestions.title: IEEE 754 Floating-Point Precision, Safe Integers & BigInt
interviewQuestions.content: JavaScript `number` uses 64-bit IEEE 754 floats (safe integers up to 2^53 - 1), causing binary rounding errors like 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3; BigInt handles arbitrary-precision integers.

blocks.text:
• Floating-Point Quirks: Decimal fractions like `0.1` have infinite binary representations, leading to rounding drift. Compare floats with `Number.EPSILON` or store money in integer cents.
• Safe Integers: `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is `2^53 - 1` (`9007199254740991`). Beyond this, integers lose precision.
• `BigInt`: Created with `123n` or `BigInt('123')` for arbitrary-precision integers (e.g., 64-bit DB IDs, cryptography). Cannot be mixed with `number` in arithmetic and throws on `JSON.stringify()` without a custom replacer.

interviewQuestions.title: ArrayBuffer, DataView, TypedArrays & ES2025 Float16Array
interviewQuestions.content: ArrayBuffer allocates raw binary memory, while TypedArrays and DataView interpret those bytes efficiently for files, WebGL, audio, and AI/ML workloads.

blocks.text:
• ArrayBuffer vs Views: `ArrayBuffer` is an opaque raw byte block—you read/write it through views.
• TypedArrays (`Uint8Array`, `Int32Array`, `Float64Array`, ES2025 `Float16Array`): Fast fixed-type views using platform endianness. `Float16Array` cuts memory bandwidth in half for WebGPU/ML tensors.
• `DataView`: Lets you read/write mixed binary types with explicit endianness (`littleEndian: true/false`), ideal for network protocols and file headers.
• `SharedArrayBuffer` + `Atomics`: Share binary memory across Web Workers without copying.

interviewQuestions.title: Prototype Pollution Attacks, Object.create(null) & Mitigation
