interviewQuestions.content: Prototype pollution occurs when untrusted input injects properties onto `Object.prototype` via `__proto__` or `constructor.prototype`, corrupting every object in the runtime.

blocks.text:
• Attack Vector: Recursive object merges or bracket assignments (`target[userKey] = val`) using `'__proto__'` or `'constructor'` from parsed JSON.
• Impact: Can bypass auth checks (`if (user.isAdmin)`), alter app config, or trigger XSS/RCE gadgets.
• Mitigations:
  1. Guard merges against `'__proto__'`, `'constructor'`, and `'prototype'`.
  2. Use `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` (ES2022) instead of `obj.hasOwnProperty(key)`.
  3. Use `Map` or `Object.create(null)` for untrusted key-value dictionaries, and prefer `Object.getPrototypeOf()` over `__proto__`.

interviewQuestions.title: ES Modules (ESM) vs CommonJS (CJS): Bindings, Loading & Tree-Shaking
interviewQuestions.content: ESM uses static, asynchronous loading with live read-only bindings enabling tree-shaking; CommonJS uses synchronous runtime require() with copied exports.

blocks.text:
• Static vs Dynamic: ESM `import`/`export` structure is analyzed statically before execution, allowing bundlers to eliminate dead code (tree-shaking). CJS `require()` executes dynamically at runtime.
• Live Bindings vs Copies: ESM exports live read-only references to module bindings; CJS copies exported primitive values at `require()` time.
• Environment Details: ESM runs in strict mode automatically, has `import.meta.url` instead of `__dirname`/`__filename`, and supports top-level `await`.

interviewQuestions.title: Optional Chaining (?.), Nullish Coalescing (??) & Logical Assignment
interviewQuestions.content: `?.` short-circuits on nullish values, `??` falls back only on null/undefined (preserving 0, '', false), and logical assignment operators combine checks with mutation.

blocks.text:
• `??` vs `||`: `||` falls back on *all* falsy values (`0`, `''`, `false`, `NaN`), often causing bugs with numeric counts or empty strings; `??` triggers strictly on `null` or `undefined`.
• Optional Chaining (`?.`): Works on properties (`obj?.a`), bracket lookups (`arr?.[0]`), and function calls (`cb?.()`), returning `undefined` if the left side is nullish.
• Logical Assignment (`??=`, `||=`, `&&=`): Short-circuit before assigning, avoiding unnecessary setter calls or DOM writes when the condition isn't met.

interviewQuestions.title: Destructuring Defaults, Rest Parameters vs arguments & Spread Pitfalls
interviewQuestions.content: Destructuring defaults apply only when a value is strictly `undefined`; rest parameters create true Arrays unlike the legacy array-like `arguments` object.

blocks.text:
• Default Value Rule: `const { x = 10 } = { x: null }` yields `x === null`—defaults trigger *only* for `undefined`.
• Rest (`...args`) vs `arguments`: Rest parameters produce a real `Array` (with `.map`/`.reduce`), work in arrow functions, and capture only trailing args; `arguments` is an array-like object absent in arrow functions.
• Spread Pitfalls: `{ ...a, ...b }` ignores non-enumerable and inherited properties, skips `undefined` spreads safely in objects (`{ ...maybeObj }`), and throws `TypeError` on non-iterables in array spread (`[...null]`).

interviewQuestions.title: Currying, Partial Application & Function Composition (pipe / compose)
interviewQuestions.content: Currying transforms an N-ary function into unary steps for reuse; pipe and compose chain small pure functions left-to-right or right-to-left.

blocks.text:
• Currying vs Partial Application: Currying converts `f(a, b, c)` into `f(a)(b)(c)` (one argument per call); partial application fixes some arguments upfront (`f.bind(null, a)` or `(b, c) => f(a, b, c)`).
• `pipe` vs `compose`: `pipe(...fns)` executes left-to-right via `reduce`; `compose(...fns)` executes right-to-left via `reduceRight`.
• Practical Benefit: Enables reusable configuration (e.g., `withLogger('AUTH')(handler)`) and readable data pipelines.

interviewQuestions.title: Recursion Limits, Tail Call Optimization (TCO) & the Trampoline Pattern
interviewQuestions.content: Because V8 and SpiderMonkey do not implement ES6 Tail Call Optimization, deep recursion risks RangeError stack overflows unless rewritten iteratively or trampolined.

blocks.text:
• Stack Overflow: Each recursive frame consumes call stack memory (~10k–15k frames in browsers before throwing `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`).
• TCO Reality in JS: Although ES6 specified Proper Tail Calls in strict mode, only Safari's JavaScriptCore implements it; V8 (Chrome/Node) and SpiderMonkey (Firefox) do not.
• Trampoline Pattern: Instead of recursing directly, return a thunk (`() => nextStep()`) and drive it inside a `while` loop, achieving O(1) stack space.

interviewQuestions.title: Tagged Template Literals: Raw Strings, XSS Escaping & DSLs
interviewQuestions.content: Tagged template functions receive literal string chunks separately from interpolated values, enabling safe HTML/SQL escaping and embedded DSLs.

blocks.text:
• Signature: `tag(strings, ...values)` receives an immutable array of static string parts (plus `strings.raw` for unescaped backslashes) and all dynamic expressions separately.
• Security & DSLs: Libraries like styled-components, GraphQL (`gql`), and SQL query builders (`sql` parameterized queries) rely on tagged templates to distinguish trusted syntax from untrusted inputs.
• `String.raw`: Built-in tag useful for regex patterns or Windows file paths without double-escaping.

interviewQuestions.title: Strict Mode ('use strict'): Silent Failures Turned Into Errors
interviewQuestions.content: Strict mode eliminates silent JS pitfalls by throwing on accidental globals, read-only mutations, duplicate parameter names, and defaulting unbound `this` to `undefined`.

blocks.text:
• Key Behavioral Changes:
  - Undeclared variable assignment throws `ReferenceError` instead of creating a global property.
  - Writing to non-writable/frozen properties or deleting undeletable properties throws `TypeError`.
  - Unbound `this` in regular functions is `undefined` rather than `globalThis`.
  - Disallows `with`, octal syntax (`010`), and duplicate function parameter names.
• Implicit Strict Mode: ES Modules (`import`/`export`) and `class` bodies are *always* strict automatically.

interviewQuestions.title: Iterable vs Iterator Protocols & Early Exit Cleanup (.return())
interviewQuestions.content: An Iterable implements `[Symbol.iterator]()` returning an Iterator with `.next()`; loops call `.return()` if exited early via `break` or `throw`.

blocks.text:
• Iterable Protocol: Any object with a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method (Arrays, Strings, Maps, Sets, NodeLists)—consumed by `for...of`, spread `[...]`, and destructuring.
• Iterator Protocol: Object with a `.next()` method returning `{ value, done }`.
• Early Termination: If `for...of` exits via `break`, `return`, or exception, JS invokes `iterator.return?.()` so iterators can release resources.
• Note: Plain `{}` objects are NOT iterable by default; use `Object.entries(obj)`.

interviewQuestions.title: eval() / new Function() Risks vs ShadowRealm Isolation
interviewQuestions.content: eval() and new Function() share the host's globals and intrinsics, risking XSS and prototype tampering; ShadowRealm creates an isolated realm without DOM overhead.

blocks.text:
• Why `eval` / `new Function` Are Dangerous: `eval` accesses local scope, both execute in the same realm (allowing `Object.prototype` pollution), hinder JIT optimization, and are blocked by strict CSP (`script-src` without `'unsafe-eval'`).
• `iframe` Sandboxes: Isolate globals/DOM, but carry heavy layout overhead and async `postMessage` serialization.
• `ShadowRealm`: Provides a lightweight isolated JS global environment with its own intrinsics (`Array`, `Object`) on the same thread; only primitives and wrapped callable functions cross the boundary, blocking object/prototype leakage.

interviewQuestions.title: IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver & MutationObserver
interviewQuestions.content: Modern browser Observer APIs replace expensive scroll/resize polling and layout thrashing with asynchronous, compositor-friendly callbacks.

blocks.text:
• IntersectionObserver: Detects when elements enter/exit the viewport or container asynchronously—ideal for lazy loading, infinite scroll, and ad/analytics impressions without `scroll` listeners or `getBoundingClientRect()`.
• ResizeObserver: Reacts to actual element box size changes (not just `window.resize`), powering responsive charts/canvases.
• MutationObserver: Batches and reports DOM tree changes (added nodes, attribute edits) as microtasks.
• Always disconnect observers (`.disconnect()`) on component unmount to prevent leaks.

interviewQuestions.title: Task Scheduling: queueMicrotask, requestIdleCallback & scheduler.yield()
interviewQuestions.content: Long synchronous tasks (>50ms) block user input and hurt INP; yielding via scheduler.yield() or task chunking returns control to the main thread.

blocks.text:
• `queueMicrotask(fn)`: Schedules `fn` before the next task AND before rendering—abusing it starves painting and input.
• `requestIdleCallback(fn)`: Runs low-priority background work during idle frame slices (not ideal for critical logic; check `deadline.timeRemaining()`).
• `scheduler.yield()` (Prioritized Task Scheduling API): Yields to pending user input/rendering and resumes your continuation with higher priority than `setTimeout(0)`—key for optimizing Interaction to Next Paint (INP).

interviewQuestions.title: Cross-Tab Communication: BroadcastChannel, storage Event & SharedWorker
interviewQuestions.content: Tabs on the same origin can sync state (like logout or theme changes) via BroadcastChannel, the window `storage` event, or a SharedWorker.

blocks.text:
• `BroadcastChannel`: Simple same-origin pub/sub across tabs, iframes, and workers; supports structured cloning without touching disk.
• `window` `'storage'` Event: Fires in *other* same-origin tabs whenever `localStorage` mutates (string-only, doesn't fire in the originating tab).
• `SharedWorker`: A single background worker shared across same-origin tabs via `MessagePort`, ideal for sharing one WebSocket connection or IndexedDB coordinator.
• `MessageChannel`: Point-to-point two-way ports between iframes, workers, or main thread.

interviewQuestions.title: WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events (SSE) & navigator.sendBeacon()
interviewQuestions.content: Use WebSockets for bidirectional low-latency messaging, SSE for simpler unidirectional HTTP streaming with auto-reconnect, and sendBeacon for reliable unload telemetry.

blocks.text:
• WebSockets (`ws://` / `wss://`): Full-duplex binary/text protocol over TCP; best for chat, multiplayer games, and collaborative cursors (requires manual heartbeat/reconnect logic).
• Server-Sent Events (`EventSource`): Unidirectional server-to-client text stream over standard HTTP with built-in automatic reconnection and `Last-Event-ID` resume (great for AI token streaming & live feeds).
• `navigator.sendBeacon()`: Queues small async `POST` payloads that survive tab close/navigation without blocking unload, unlike `fetch()` without `keepalive: true`.

interviewQuestions.title: Service Workers Lifecycle & Cache API Strategies
interviewQuestions.content: Service Workers act as programmable network proxies running off the main thread, enabling offline support and caching strategies like Stale-While-Revalidate.

blocks.text:
• Lifecycle: Register → `install` (precache static assets; `skipWaiting()` activates immediately) → `activate` (clean old caches; `clients.claim()`) → `fetch` / `push` / `sync`.
• Common Strategies:
  - Cache-First: Static hashed assets.
  - Network-First: Fresh API/HTML with offline fallback.
  - Stale-While-Revalidate: Return cached response instantly while updating cache in the background.
• Gotcha: Requires HTTPS (except `localhost`) and has no DOM access.

interviewQuestions.title: IndexedDB vs localStorage: Async Transactions, Indexing & Quotas
interviewQuestions.content: IndexedDB is an asynchronous, transactional NoSQL object store supporting large structured data, Blobs, and indexes—solving localStorage's synchronous 5MB string limits.

blocks.text:
• Why Not `localStorage` for Large Data: `localStorage` is synchronous (blocks main thread on read/write), capped at ~5–10MB, and stores only UTF-16 strings (requiring `JSON.parse/stringify`).
• `IndexedDB` Advantages: Asynchronous, accessible inside Web/Service Workers, stores structured JS objects, `Blob`/`File` binaries, and supports fast indexed range queries via `IDBIndex`.
• Transactions & Versioning: Schema upgrades happen inside `onupgradeneeded`; operations execute inside atomic transactions (`readonly` / `readwrite`).

interviewQuestions.title: Frontend Security: XSS, CSRF, Content Security Policy (CSP) & Trusted Types
interviewQuestions.content: Prevent XSS with safe DOM sinks (`textContent`), sanitization, and CSP nonces/Trusted Types; prevent CSRF with `SameSite` cookies and anti-CSRF tokens.

blocks.text:
• Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): Untrusted input executes as JS via `innerHTML`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, or `javascript:` URLs. Prefer `textContent`, sanitize HTML with DOMPurify, and enforce CSP (`script-src 'nonce-...'` without `'unsafe-inline'`).
• Trusted Types API: Enforces typed objects (`TrustedHTML`) at dangerous DOM sinks so raw strings cannot be assigned to `innerHTML`.
• Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF): Exploits automatic cookie sending on cross-origin requests. Mitigate with `SameSite=Lax`/`Strict` cookies, anti-CSRF tokens, and checking `Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site` headers.

interviewQuestions.title: Measuring & Profiling JS Performance: Long Tasks, INP & DevTools
interviewQuestions.content: Track real-user responsiveness via PerformanceObserver (Long Tasks, Long Animation Frames, INP) and diagnose bottlenecks with Chrome DevTools Flame Charts and Coverage.

blocks.text:
• Key JS Bottlenecks: Main-thread Long Tasks (>50ms), layout thrashing (interleaved DOM reads/writes), excessive hydration/bundle parse cost, and GC pauses.
• Browser Telemetry: `PerformanceObserver` measures `longtask`, `long-animation-frame` (LoAF), and `event` durations contributing to INP (Interaction to Next Paint, target <= 200ms).
• DevTools Workflow: Use Performance Flame Chart (CPU throttling 4x) to inspect self vs total time, Coverage tab to spot unused JS, and `performance.mark()`/`measure()` for custom timings.

languages.aboutDescription: JavaScript is a high-level, dynamic, single-threaded programming language used to build interactive and scalable web applications.

roadmap.title: Core Syntax, Types & Lexical Scope
roadmap.description: Master primitive vs. reference types, type coercion, block scoping (let/const), closures, hoisting, and strict mode behavior.

roadmap.title: Functions, Prototypes & Modern OOP
roadmap.description: Understand the `this` binding rules, prototype chain, ES6 classes with private `#` fields, iterators, and generator functions.

roadmap.title: Collections & Functional Array Pipelines
roadmap.description: Use Map, Set (with ES2025 set operations), WeakMap/WeakSet, immutable array methods (toSorted, toReversed, with), and lazy iterator helpers.

roadmap.title: Asynchronous JavaScript & Event Loop
roadmap.description: Deeply understand the call stack, microtask vs. macrotask queues, Promises, async/await, AbortController, and Promise combinators.

roadmap.title: DOM APIs, Browser Storage & Fetch
roadmap.description: Handle event delegation, MutationObserver/IntersectionObserver, Web Storage, IndexedDB, Fetch streaming, and CORS mechanics.

roadmap.title: ES Modules, Tooling & Runtime Internals
roadmap.description: Configure ESM vs. CJS interoperability, import attributes, V8 hidden classes/inline caching awareness, and memory leak profiling.

roadmap.title: Web Workers, SharedArrayBuffer & Metaprogramming
roadmap.description: Build off-main-thread concurrency with Web Workers, Atomics, Proxy/Reflect traps, Symbols, and structured performance benchmarking.

versions.title: ECMAScript 2025 (ES16)
changes: Iterator helper methods (.map(), .filter(), .take(), .drop(), .flatMap()) for lazy evaluation
Native mathematical Set methods: union(), intersection(), difference(), and isSubsetOf()
Import Attributes and native JSON module imports (with { type: 'json' })
RegExp.escape(), Promise.try(), Float16Array, and RegExp pattern modifiers

changes: Object.groupBy() and Map.groupBy() for grouping iterables by key
Promise.withResolvers() for ergonomic external promise resolution
Resizable ArrayBuffer and ArrayBuffer.prototype.transfer() methods
String.prototype.isWellFormed() and toWellFormed() for Unicode safety, plus Atomics.waitAsync()

versions.title: ECMAScript 2023 (ES14)
changes: Immutable change-by-copy Array methods: toReversed(), toSorted(), toSpliced(), and with()
Array.prototype.findLast() and findLastIndex() for reverse searching
Support for Symbols as WeakMap keys
Standardized Hashbang (#!) grammar for executable JavaScript files

Private class fields, methods (#private), static initialization blocks, and ergonomic #brand checks
Error.prototype.cause for chaining underlying error origins
Array/String .at() negative indexing, Object.hasOwn(), and RegExp match indices (/d flag)

BigInt primitive for arbitrary-precision integers
Promise.allSettled() to inspect all settled promises regardless of rejection
Dynamic import(), globalThis, and String.prototype.matchAll()

languages.title: TypeScript
languages.description: Strongly typed superset of JavaScript that improves scalability, maintainability, and developer productivity.

insights.title: 01. What TypeScript Is and Static Type Checking
insights.content: TypeScript adds structural static types on top of JavaScript that catch bugs at compile time and erase completely at runtime.

blocks.text: TypeScript is a typed superset of JavaScript. The compiler (`tsc`) checks types statically before code runs, catching typos, null dereferences, and mismatched APIs—then emits standard JavaScript with zero runtime type overhead.

insights.title: 02. Primitive Types (string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol)
insights.content: Annotate primitive values using lowercase types: string, number, boolean, bigint, and symbol.

blocks.text: Always use lowercase `string`, `number`, and `boolean` rather than wrapper constructors `String`, `Number`, `Boolean`. `symbol` and `unique symbol` model distinct keys, and `bigint` handles arbitrary-precision integers.

insights.title: 03. Type Inference vs Explicit Type Annotations
insights.content: Let TypeScript infer local variables automatically, and reserve explicit annotations for function boundaries and uninitialized variables.

blocks.text: TypeScript infers variable types from their initializers (`let count = 0` infers `number`; `const pi = 3.14` infers literal `3.14`). Annotating function parameters is required, and annotating return types catches accidental contract changes.

insights.title: 04. any vs unknown: Safe Top Types
insights.content: Avoid any because it disables type checking; prefer unknown for dynamic values and narrow before using them.

blocks.text: `any` turns off the type checker and spreads unsafety everywhere it touches. `unknown` also accepts any value, but TypeScript forbids calling methods or accessing properties on it until you narrow its type via `typeof`, `instanceof`, or type guards.

insights.title: 05. void, never, null, and undefined
insights.content: Use void for functions with no meaningful return, never for unreachable code/throws, and explicit null/undefined unions.

blocks.text: `void` indicates a function's return value should be ignored. `never` represents the empty bottom type—returned by functions that always `throw` or loop infinitely, and used for impossible branches in exhaustiveness checks.

insights.title: 06. strictNullChecks and Null Handling
insights.content: With strictNullChecks enabled, null and undefined are distinct types that must be checked before access.

blocks.text: Under `strictNullChecks` (part of `strict: true`), `string` cannot hold `null` or `undefined` unless explicitly typed as `string | null`. Combine narrowing (`if (val)`), optional chaining (`?.`), and nullish coalescing (`??`) to handle nullables cleanly.

insights.title: 07. Typed Arrays (T[], Array<T>) and readonly Arrays
insights.content: Type homogeneous lists with T[] or Array<T>, and prevent accidental mutations using readonly T[] or ReadonlyArray<T>.

blocks.text: `readonly string[]` removes mutating methods like `.push()`, `.pop()`, and `.sort()` at compile time. Note that `string[]` is assignable to `readonly string[]`, making `readonly` great for function parameters that shouldn't mutate inputs.

insights.title: 08. Tuples, Optional Elements, and Labeled Tuples
insights.content: Model fixed-length arrays with known per-index types using tuples, adding labels for readable IDE tooltips.

blocks.text: Tuples enforce exact element positions and types (like React's `[state, setState]`). They support optional trailing elements (`[string, number?]`), rest elements (`[string, ...number[]]`), `readonly` tuples, and descriptive labels (`[x: number, y: number]`).

insights.title: 09. Object Type Annotations and Optional Properties
insights.content: Describe object shapes inline or with named types and mark non-required keys with the ? modifier.

blocks.text: An optional property `subtitle?: string` allows the property to be omitted (effectively `string | undefined`). Note the difference with `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`: omitting a key vs explicitly assigning `undefined`.

insights.title: 10. readonly Properties and Compile-Time Immutability
insights.content: Prevent property reassignment with readonly, understanding that it is shallow and enforced at compile time.

blocks.text: Marking a property `readonly` stops code from reassigning it after creation. Keep in mind `readonly` is shallow—nested objects inside a `readonly` property remain mutable unless also marked `readonly` or `Readonly<T>`.

insights.title: 11. Union Types (|) and Type Narrowing Basics
insights.content: Combine multiple possible types with | and access shared members directly or narrow before accessing type-specific members.

blocks.text: A union `string | number` represents a value that may be either type. TypeScript only lets you perform operations valid for *all* members of the union until you narrow the value with a runtime check.

insights.title: 12. Intersection Types (&)
insights.content: Compose multiple object types into a single type containing all combined properties using &.

blocks.text: An intersection `A & B` produces a type that must satisfy both `A` and `B` simultaneously. Note that intersecting conflicting primitive types like `string & number` collapses to `never`.

insights.title: 13. Literal Types (String, Numeric, and Boolean Literals)
insights.content: Restrict values to exact strings, numbers, or booleans—typically paired with unions for finite state modeling.

blocks.text: Combining literal types into unions (`"GET" | "POST" | "DELETE"`) gives compile-time validation and autocomplete without needing runtime enum objects.

insights.title: 14. type Aliases
insights.content: Name any type—primitives, unions, tuples, functions, or objects—using type aliases for clarity and reuse.

blocks.text: `type` aliases create a reusable name for any TypeScript type expression without generating any runtime JavaScript code. Unlike `interface`, `type` can alias unions, primitives, tuples, and mapped types.

insights.title: 15. interface Declarations and Declaration Merging
insights.content: Define object contracts with interface, extend them with extends, and understand automatic declaration merging.

blocks.text: `interface` models object shapes and supports `extends` for clean inheritance. Two `interface` declarations with the same name in the same scope automatically merge—which enables extending global types like `Window` or library interfaces.

insights.title: 16. interface vs type Alias: Choosing Wisely
insights.content: Use interface for extendable object/class contracts and public library APIs; use type for unions, tuples, and type-level transformations.

blocks.text: Both `interface` and `type` describe objects well, and modern TS optimizes both. Prefer `type` for unions, intersections, mapped/conditional types, and tuples; prefer `interface` when you want `extends` performance or intentional declaration merging.

insights.title: 17. Function Parameter and Return Type Annotations
insights.content: Annotate function parameters explicitly and add return types to public functions to enforce stable contracts.

blocks.text: With `noImplicitAny` enabled (part of `strict`), function parameters require explicit types unless contextually typed. Adding an explicit return type prevents unintended return-type drift if implementation details change.

insights.title: 18. Optional, Default, and Rest Parameters in TypeScript
insights.content: Mark optional params with ?, infer types from default values, and type rest args as arrays or tuples.

blocks.text: Optional parameters (`tag?: string`) must follow required parameters and have type `T | undefined`. Default parameters (`tax = 0.14`) automatically infer their type and make the argument optional for callers.

insights.title: 19. Function Type Expressions and Call Signatures
insights.content: Type callbacks with arrow function type syntax and model callable objects with properties using call signatures.

blocks.text: Use `(a: number) => string` for standard callbacks. When a function itself carries attached properties (like middleware or validator functions), describe it with an object call signature `{ (val: string): boolean; ruleName: string }`.

insights.title: 20. enum vs String Literal Unions & as const Objects
insights.content: Understand numeric and string enums, and why modern TS codebases often prefer string literal unions or as const objects.

blocks.text: TypeScript `enum` generates runtime objects (and numeric enums even emit reverse mappings and permit any number assignment in older TS). Using an `as const` object plus a derived union type gives full runtime values with zero enum quirks.

insights.title: 21. Type Assertions (as) and Safety Rules
insights.content: Use `as` only when you know more than the compiler (such as DOM queries), remembering it performs no runtime check or conversion.

blocks.text: Type assertions (`value as HTMLInputElement`) tell the compiler to treat an expression as a more specific or general type without altering runtime JS. TypeScript prevents impossible assertions unless you go through `unknown` first (`x as unknown as T`).

insights.title: 22. Non-Null Assertion Operator (!) and Its Risks
insights.content: The postfix ! removes null and undefined from a type at compile time—use sparingly in favor of explicit guards.

blocks.text: `expr!` asserts to TypeScript that `expr` is neither `null` nor `undefined`. Because it emits zero runtime check, an incorrect `!` causes a runtime `TypeError`. Prefer `if (!val) throw ...` or `??` in production code.

insights.title: 23. as const Assertions for Deeply Readonly Literals
insights.content: Freeze literal types and tuple shapes at the type level using `as const` without widening strings to string or arrays to T[].

blocks.text: Appending `as const` to an expression infers the narrowest literal types, makes all object properties `readonly` recursively, and turns array literals into `readonly` tuples.

insights.title: 24. typeof Operator in Type Position
insights.content: Derive a TypeScript type directly from an existing runtime variable, config object, or function using typeof.

blocks.text: In runtime expressions, `typeof x` returns a string. In a type position (`type Config = typeof defaultConfig`), TypeScript extracts the static type of that value—keeping runtime objects and types in a single source of truth.

insights.title: 25. keyof Type Operator
insights.content: Extract a union of all property keys of an object type using keyof T.

blocks.text: `keyof T` produces a string or numeric literal union of `T`'s public keys. It is foundational for type-safe property lookups (`<T, K extends keyof T>`) and mapped types.

insights.title: 26. Indexed Access Types (T[K] and Arr[number])
insights.content: Look up the type of a nested property with T["prop"] or the element union of an array/tuple with T[number].

blocks.text: Indexed access types let you reuse sub-types directly from larger types without duplicating them. Using `[number]` on a `readonly` tuple extracts a union of all its element types.

insights.title: 27. Type Narrowing with typeof Guards
insights.content: Use runtime typeof checks so TypeScript narrows union types automatically inside each branch.

blocks.text: TypeScript's Control Flow Analysis tracks `typeof` checks (`"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"function"`, `"object"`). Remember that `typeof null === "object"`, so pair object checks with `val !== null`.

insights.title: 28. Truthiness and Equality Narrowing
insights.content: Filter out null and undefined with truthiness checks or === / !== comparisons to narrow unions cleanly.

blocks.text: Checking `if (val)` removes `null` and `undefined` (watch out for empty string `""` or `0` if those are valid!). Equality checks like `x === y` or `val != null` (which checks both `null` and `undefined`) also narrow both operands.

insights.title: 29. The in Operator and instanceof Narrowing
insights.content: Differentiate object union variants by checking for unique properties with `in` or class prototypes with `instanceof`.

blocks.text: `"fly" in pet` narrows an object union to variants containing `fly`, while `err instanceof Error` narrows class instances safely inside `catch (err: unknown)` blocks.

insights.title: 30. Discriminated Unions (Tagged Unions)
insights.content: Add a shared literal discriminant field (such as kind or status) so TypeScript narrows complex state variants reliably.

blocks.text: Discriminated unions are one of TypeScript's most powerful modeling patterns. By giving every variant a common literal property (`status: "loading" | "success" | "error"`), invalid combinations (like `loading: true` alongside `error`) become impossible.

insights.title: 31. Exhaustiveness Checking with never
insights.content: Ensure switch statements cover every union variant at compile time by passing the default branch to a never helper.

blocks.text: When a new variant is added to a union later, an `assertNever(x: never)` helper in the `default` branch immediately produces a compile error wherever you forgot to handle the new case.

insights.title: 32. Custom Type Predicates (arg is Type)
insights.content: Write reusable narrowing functions whose boolean return type informs TypeScript what type an argument has when true.

blocks.text: A type guard function returns `arg is TargetType`. Note that TypeScript trusts your predicate implementation—always write an accurate runtime check inside it. Great for filtering `null`/`undefined` or validating API objects.

insights.title: 33. Assertion Functions (asserts value is Type)
insights.content: Throw if an invariant fails and automatically narrow the checked variable for all lines following the call.

blocks.text: Assertion functions (`function assert(cond: unknown): asserts cond` or `asserts val is T`) throw an error when invalid and narrow control flow for the remainder of the scope when they return normally. Note: they must be declared with `function` or explicit type annotation.

insights.title: 34. Index Signatures ([key: string]: Value)
insights.content: Type dictionaries with arbitrary dynamic keys using index signatures, and pair with noUncheckedIndexedAccess for safety.

blocks.text: An index signature `{ [key: string]: number }` models objects with unknown key names. Because accessing an absent key yields `undefined` at runtime, either type values as `number | undefined` or enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` in `tsconfig.json`.

insights.title: 35. tsconfig.json Essentials (strict, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, moduleResolution)
insights.content: Configure strict mode, modern module resolution, and safe index access flags for rock-solid TypeScript projects.

blocks.text: Always enable `"strict": true` (activates `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `strictFunctionTypes`, etc.). Adding `"noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true` prevents out-of-bounds array/dictionary assumptions, and `"moduleResolution": "bundler"` matches Vite/Next/Bun.

insights.title: 36. Introduction to Generics (<T>)
insights.content: Write reusable functions and data structures that preserve exact input-to-output type relationships using type parameters.

blocks.text: Generics parameterize types just like functions parameterize values. Instead of losing type information with `any` or `unknown`, `<T>` captures the caller's exact type automatically via inference.

insights.title: 37. Multiple Type Parameters and Generic Defaults
insights.content: Relate multiple inputs and outputs with <T, U> and supply fallback types using <T = Default>.

blocks.text: Functions like `pair` or `mapObject` use multiple type parameters to connect independent types, while generic type defaults (`interface ApiResponse<T = unknown>`) make common usages concise while allowing overrides.

insights.title: 38. Generic Constraints with extends
insights.content: Constrain a generic type parameter with `T extends Shape` so your function can safely access required properties.

blocks.text: An unconstrained `<T>` allows any type—so you can't read `val.length`. Adding `<T extends { length: number }>` requires callers to pass a type with a numeric `length` while still preserving the caller's exact subtype on return.

insights.title: 39. Using keyof in Generic Constraints
insights.content: Tie a key parameter directly to an object's keys via `<T, K extends keyof T>` for typo-proof property access.

blocks.text: `function getProp<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]` guarantees that `key` actually exists on `obj` and returns the exact property type `T[K]` rather than a wide union.

insights.title: 40. Generic Interfaces and Generic Type Aliases
insights.content: Parameterize reusable wrappers like Result<T, E>, Paginated<T>, and Repository<T> using generic types and interfaces.

blocks.text: Generic types and interfaces form the backbone of typed application architecture—letting you define standard envelopes (`Result<T, E>`, `Page<T>`) once and instantiate them for every entity.

insights.title: 41. Generic Classes
insights.content: Build type-safe containers, queues, caches, and state stores using class-level type parameters.

blocks.text: A generic class `class Stack<T>` shares `T` across its constructor, instance properties, and instance methods. Note that `static` members cannot reference class-level `T` because static members belong to the constructor, not instances.

insights.title: 42. Utility Types: Partial<T>, Required<T>, and Readonly<T>
insights.content: Transform all properties of an object type to optional, required, or readonly in one line.

blocks.text: `Partial<T>` makes every key optional (great for patch/update payloads). `Required<T>` strips `?` from all keys. `Readonly<T>` adds `readonly` shallowly to every key.

insights.title: 43. Utility Types: Pick<T, K> and Omit<T, K>
insights.content: Derive focused DTO or form types by selecting specific keys with Pick or removing sensitive/auto-generated keys with Omit.

blocks.text: `Pick<T, K>` keeps only the keys in union `K`, whereas `Omit<T, K>` removes them. Because `Pick` checks `K extends keyof T`, it catches typos in key names—while `Omit` accepts any key union unless constrained.

insights.title: 44. Record<K, V> for Dictionaries and Exhaustive Maps
insights.content: Build typed key-value maps and enforce that every member of a string literal union has an entry.

blocks.text: `Record<Keys, Value>` creates an object type whose keys are `Keys` and values are `Value`. Using a finite union like `Record<Status, string>` guarantees at compile time that no status label is forgotten.

insights.title: 45. Exclude<T, U> and Extract<T, U>
insights.content: Filter union types by removing members assignable to U (Exclude) or keeping only assignable members (Extract).

blocks.text: Whereas `Pick`/`Omit` operate on object keys, `Exclude<T, U>` and `Extract<T, U>` distribute over union members directly—making it effortless to slice event unions or role unions.

insights.title: 46. NonNullable<T>
insights.content: Strip null and undefined from any union type cleanly using NonNullable<T>.

blocks.text: `NonNullable<T>` is defined as `T & {}` (in modern TS), which eliminates `null` and `undefined` from union types—very handy when deriving types from optional fields or nullable API responses.

insights.title: 47. ReturnType<T> and Parameters<T>
insights.content: Extract a function's return type and parameter tuple without duplicating or manually exporting separate types.

blocks.text: `ReturnType<typeof fn>` and `Parameters<typeof fn>` let you wrap, log, or memoize functions (especially third-party functions whose parameter/return types aren't exported separately).

insights.title: 48. ConstructorParameters<T> and InstanceType<T>
insights.content: Inspect class constructor arguments and instance types generically using ConstructorParameters and InstanceType.

blocks.text: When writing factories or dependency injection helpers that accept a class constructor (`typeof MyClass`), `ConstructorParameters<T>` yields the constructor argument tuple and `InstanceType<T>` yields the constructed instance type.

insights.title: 49. Awaited<T> for Unwrapping Promises
insights.content: Recursively unwrap Promise<T> and PromiseLike<T> types to get the resolved value type with Awaited<T>.

blocks.text: Introduced in TS 4.5, `Awaited<T>` mirrors runtime `await` behavior by recursively unwrapping nested Promises (`Promise<Promise<string>>` -> `string`). Pair it with `ReturnType<typeof asyncFn>` to extract async function outputs.

insights.title: 50. ThisParameterType<T> and OmitThisParameter<T>
insights.content: Annotate explicit `this` parameters on functions for strict call-site checking, and extract or strip `this` via utility types.

blocks.text: TypeScript allows a fake leading `this: Context` parameter (erased at compile time) to enforce what `this` must be at call sites. `ThisParameterType<F>` reads that type and `OmitThisParameter<F>` creates a `this`-free signature after `.bind()`.

insights.title: 51. Function Overloads: Overload vs Implementation Signatures
insights.content: Declare multiple public call signatures above a single compatible implementation signature that callers never see directly.

blocks.text: Function overloads let different input combinations map to distinct return types. Remember that the implementation signature is internal only—callers can only invoke one of the overload signatures listed above it.

insights.title: 52. Contextual Typing in Callbacks
insights.content: TypeScript infers callback parameter types automatically from the expected function position without explicit annotations.

blocks.text: When you pass an inline callback to `.map()`, `.filter()`, or an event listener, TypeScript flows type information backward from the signature into your callback parameters.

insights.title: 53. Class Access Modifiers (public, protected, private, #private)
insights.content: Contrast compile-time private/protected modifiers with ECMAScript #private fields that enforce hard privacy at runtime.

blocks.text: TS `private` and `protected` exist only at compile time (and disappear in emitted JS). ECMAScript `#field` private fields enforce true runtime encapsulation and cannot be bypassed via `as any` or bracket access.

insights.title: 54. Parameter Properties and readonly Class Fields
insights.content: Declare and initialize class fields concisely directly inside constructor parameters using visibility or readonly modifiers.

blocks.text: Prefixing a constructor parameter with `public`, `protected`, `private`, or `readonly` automatically declares the class property and assigns it—note that `erasableSyntaxOnly` (TS 5.8+) prefers explicit fields when stripping types.

insights.title: 55. Abstract Classes and implements
insights.content: Share base implementation alongside required abstract methods via abstract class, and verify contracts with implements.

blocks.text: An `abstract class` cannot be instantiated directly; subclasses must implement its `abstract` methods while inheriting concrete shared helpers. Unlike `extends`, a class can `implements` multiple interfaces.

insights.title: 56. The override Keyword and noImplicitOverride
insights.content: Mark subclass overrides explicitly with `override` so base class renames or removals trigger immediate compile errors.

blocks.text: Without `override`, renaming a method on a base class leaves an orphaned method on the subclass silently. Enabling `noImplicitOverride` forces every overriding method to declare `override` explicitly.

insights.title: 57. Polymorphic this Return Types for Fluent Chaining
insights.content: Return `this` from fluent builder methods so subclasses inherit method chaining typed to the subclass itself.

blocks.text: If a base class method returns `BaseBuilder`, calling it on a `SubBuilder` loses subclass methods in the chain. Returning `this` (polymorphic `this` type) dynamically resolves to whichever subclass invoked the method.

insights.title: 58. Structural Typing and Excess Property Checks
insights.content: TypeScript compares types by shape compatibility, while fresh object literals receive extra excess-property checks.

blocks.text: In structural (duck) typing, `{ name, age, extra }` is assignable to `{ name }` via an intermediate variable—but passing a fresh object literal directly flags unknown properties to catch typos.

insights.title: 59. Parameter Contravariance and strictFunctionTypes
insights.content: Understand why function parameters are contravariant under strictFunctionTypes while method shorthand stays bivariant.

blocks.text: With `strictFunctionTypes`, a callback accepting a narrower subtype (`(dog: Dog) => void`) cannot be assigned where `(animal: Animal) => void` is expected, preventing runtime errors when a `Cat` is passed. Note that method syntax `handle(a: Animal): void` remains bivariant by design for `Array<T>` compatibility.

insights.title: 60. Basic Conditional Types (T extends U ? X : Y)
insights.content: Branch at the type level using ternary `T extends U ? X : Y` logic to compute output types dynamically.

blocks.text: Conditional types behave like ternary expressions for types: if `T` is assignable to `U`, evaluate to `X`, otherwise `Y`. They are essential for building generic type utilities and overload-free polymorphic APIs.

insights.title: 61. Distributive Conditional Types Over Unions
insights.content: Naked type parameters in `T extends U ? X : Y` distribute across each union member; wrap in `[T]` to disable distribution.

blocks.text: When `T` is a naked type parameter and a union (`string | number`), `T extends string ? A : B` evaluates each union member separately and unions the results. Wrapping `[T] extends [U]` disables distribution when you want to test the union as a whole.

insights.title: 62. Mapped Types ({ [K in keyof T]: ... })
insights.content: Iterate over a union of keys to construct new object types systematically from existing shapes.

blocks.text: Mapped types loop over keys `[K in keyof T]` to transform property value types—for example wrapping every field in a validation rule, getter, or nullable wrapper while keeping autocomplete and JSDoc intact.

insights.title: 63. Mapping Modifiers (+readonly, -readonly, +?, -?)
insights.content: Add or strip `readonly` and optional `?` modifiers across all keys of an object type using + and - prefixes.

blocks.text: In mapped types, `-?` removes optionality (how `Required<T>` is implemented) and `-readonly` creates a mutable copy of a `Readonly` or `as const` type.

insights.title: 64. Key Remapping with `as` in Mapped Types
insights.content: Rename keys dynamically or filter keys out (by returning never) using `as` clauses inside mapped types.

blocks.text: Adding `as NewKey` after `[K in keyof T]` lets you transform property names (like `getName`, `onClick`) or filter out unwanted properties by mapping them to `never`.

insights.title: 65. Template Literal Types
insights.content: Compose combinatorial string unions and enforce structured string formats (events, CSS units, routes) at compile time.

blocks.text: Template literal types use backtick interpolation in type position: `` `${A}-${B}` `` produces the Cartesian product of all union members in `A` and `B`, and validates patterns like `` `${number}px` ``.

insights.title: 66. Intrinsic String Manipulation Types
insights.content: Transform string literal types using Uppercase, Lowercase, Capitalize, and Uncapitalize.

blocks.text: TypeScript includes four compiler-intrinsic string type transformers (`Uppercase<S>`, `Lowercase<S>`, `Capitalize<S>`, `Uncapitalize<S>`) that distribute over unions and pair cleanly with template literal types.

insights.title: 67. import type and verbatimModuleSyntax
insights.content: Use `import type` / `export type` for type-only imports so bundlers and runtimes cleanly erase them without runtime side effects.

blocks.text: TypeScript's `verbatimModuleSyntax` enforces explicit `import type` for anything used solely as a type. This guarantees tools like Babel, Vite, esbuild, and Bun never emit broken runtime imports for erased types.

insights.title: 68. Typing Promises, async/await, and Typed fetch Wrappers
insights.content: Annotate async functions with Promise<T> and wrap fetch with generics (plus runtime validation) instead of blind `any`.

blocks.text: `res.json()` in DOM lib types returns `Promise<any>`. Writing a typed generic wrapper `fetchJson<T>()` (ideally paired with a validator/type guard) keeps API boundaries type-safe.

insights.title: 69. Typing DOM Elements and Event Handlers
insights.content: Use specific HTMLElement subtypes with querySelector<T> and differentiate event.target from event.currentTarget.

blocks.text: `document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("#email")` returns `HTMLInputElement | null`. Inside event listeners, `event.currentTarget` is typed to the attached element, whereas `event.target` is only `EventTarget | null` and must be narrowed.

insights.title: 70. Typing Map, Set, and Custom Iterables
insights.content: Parameterize Map<K, V> and Set<T>, and type custom iterators with Iterable<T> and IterableIterator<T>.

blocks.text: Built-in collections accept type arguments (`new Map<string, User>()`, `new Set<number>()`). Note that `map.get(key)` always returns `V | undefined` because the key may be absent.

insights.title: 71. Type Inference in Conditional Types with infer
insights.content: Capture and name an embedded sub-type inside a conditional `extends` clause using the `infer` keyword.

blocks.text: `infer R` declares a pattern-matched type variable inside `T extends ... ? R : ...`. It lets you unwrap array elements, function return types, Promise values, or tuple heads declaratively.

insights.title: 72. Recursive infer Patterns (Flatten, Trim, DeepUnwrap)
insights.content: Combine `infer` with recursion and template literals to transform nested arrays or strings at the type level.

blocks.text: Recursive conditional types invoke themselves on sub-parts captured by `infer`—for example recursively trimming whitespace from string literal types or unwrapping arbitrarily nested arrays.

insights.title: 73. infer with extends Constraints (TS 4.7+)
insights.content: Constrain an inferred type variable directly with `infer X extends Constraint` so TypeScript preserves the narrowed literal/specific type.

blocks.text: Before TS 4.7, `infer` required nested conditional types to check a constraint on `X`. Writing `infer X extends string` or `infer N extends number` validates and narrows in a single clean clause.

insights.title: 74. Recursive Mapped Types: DeepReadonly<T> and DeepPartial<T>
insights.content: Apply readonly or optional modifiers across arbitrarily nested objects and arrays while skipping primitives and functions.

blocks.text: Built-in `Readonly<T>` and `Partial<T>` are shallow. A recursive mapped type checks if each property is a function or primitive first so functions aren't turned into empty `{}` mapped objects.

insights.title: 75. Tail-Recursion Elimination in Conditional Types
insights.content: Write accumulator-based tail-recursive type aliases so TypeScript supports up to 1,000+ iterations without hitting depth limits.

blocks.text: Non-tail-recursive types hit TypeScript's ~50-level instantiation depth cap. Placing the recursive call directly in the return branch with an accumulator (`Acc extends unknown[] = []`) triggers TS tail-recursion optimization (up to ~1000 steps).

insights.title: 76. Variadic Tuple Types ([...T, ...U])
insights.content: Spread generic tuple parameters inside tuple types to concatenate, prepend, or type curry/partial functions cleanly.

blocks.text: Variadic tuple types allow spreading generic `T extends readonly unknown[]` anywhere inside `[...T, ...U]`, enabling exact return types for array concatenation, middleware pipelines, and partial application.

insights.title: 77. Tuple Manipulation (Head, Tail, Last, Zip)
insights.content: Slice, inspect, and recombine tuple types using pattern matching with rest elements and infer.

blocks.text: Tuple types support rest patterns at the start, middle, or end (`[...infer Init, infer Last]`). This powers type-level list utilities like `Head`, `Tail`, `Last`, and `DropFirst`.

insights.title: 78. satisfies Operator vs as vs Type Annotations (TS 4.9+)
insights.content: Validate that an expression matches a contract with `satisfies` while preserving its narrow inferred literal properties.

blocks.text: A type annotation `const palette: Record<string, string | number[]> = ...` widens values so you lose knowledge of which keys hold arrays vs strings. `satisfies` checks conformance *without* widening the inferred type.

insights.title: 79. const Type Parameters (<const T>) (TS 5.0+)
insights.content: Infer literal and readonly types from function arguments automatically without forcing callers to write `as const`.

blocks.text: Adding `const` before a type parameter (`function defineRoutes<const T>(routes: T)`) tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest literal types directly at the call site, making DSLs and route configs ergonomic.

insights.title: 80. NoInfer<T> Utility Type (TS 5.4+)
insights.content: Block a parameter position from contributing to generic type inference so typos in secondary arguments get caught.

blocks.text: In `createState<T>(options: T[], defaultOption: T)`, passing an invalid `defaultOption` would normally widen `T` instead of flagging an error! Wrapping `defaultOption: NoInfer<T>` forces `T` to be inferred strictly from `options`.

insights.title: 81. Covariance, Contravariance, and in / out Annotations
insights.content: Document and speed up variance checking on generic types using explicit `out` (covariant) and `in` (contravariant) modifiers.

blocks.text: A producer (`() => T`) is covariant (`out T`: `Producer<Dog>` is a `Producer<Animal>`). A consumer (`(val: T) => void`) is contravariant (`in T`: `Consumer<Animal>` is a `Consumer<Dog>`). Explicit `in`/`out` catches accidental position violations and accelerates `tsc`.

insights.title: 82. Branded (Nominal) Types for Domain Safety
insights.content: Simulate nominal typing over primitives so UserId and OrderId cannot be swapped accidentally even though both are strings.

blocks.text: Because TypeScript is structurally typed, two `type UserId = string` and `type OrderId = string` aliases are interchangeable. Intersecting with a compile-time `unique symbol` brand prevents mix-ups with zero runtime overhead.

insights.title: 83. Phantom Types and Compile-Time State Machines
insights.content: Encode workflow states into unused generic type parameters so invalid transitions (e.g., submitting unvalidated data) won't compile.

blocks.text: A phantom type parameter appears in a type signature without needing a runtime property—allowing you to enforce state transitions like `Draft -> Validated -> Published` strictly at compile time.

insights.title: 84. Builder Pattern with Progressive Generic Accumulators
insights.content: Track which configuration steps have been called in a generic type parameter, enabling .build() only once required fields are set.

blocks.text: By intersecting or updating a phantom state generic `TState` on each chained method, `.build()` can require `this: RequestBuilder<{ url: true; method: true }>` and fail to compile if any mandatory step was skipped.

insights.title: 85. Type-Safe Event Emitter with Mapped Event Maps
insights.content: Bind event names to their exact payload types using `<K extends keyof Events>` so listeners and emitters stay synchronized.

blocks.text: Defining an `Events` interface mapping event names to payload types ensures `.on("login", fn)` infers `fn`'s payload automatically and `.emit("login", payload)` rejects malformed data.

insights.title: 86. Nested Dot-Path Keys and PathValue<T, P>
insights.content: Compute valid `"user.address.city"` dot-separated paths and resolve the target leaf type at compile time.

blocks.text: Combining recursive mapped types, template literals, and conditional recursion lets libraries like React Hook Form or i18n typed helpers autocomplete nested translation or form keys.

insights.title: 87. Type-Safe Exhaustive Pattern Matching Helper
insights.content: Implement an expression-oriented `match(union, handlers)` helper backed by mapped types over discriminated unions.

blocks.text: Using `Extract<T, { kind: K }>` inside a mapped handler object guarantees every variant has a matching handler with its exact narrowed variant passed as the argument.

insights.title: 88. Mutually Exclusive Object Types (XOR<A, B>)
insights.content: Prevent mixing properties from two mutually exclusive option shapes using `never` optional keys.

blocks.text: A standard union `A | B` still allows an object containing properties of *both* `A` and `B`! Marking keys unique to the other branch as `?: never` builds a strict `XOR<T, U>` constraint.

insights.title: 89. Modeling Recursive JSON Values and Containing `any`
insights.content: Represent valid JSON payloads with a recursive JsonValue type and isolate untyped external boundaries behind unknown.

blocks.text: Writing a recursive `JsonValue` type prevents accidentally passing functions, `Map`, or `undefined` to JSON serializers. At untyped boundaries, convert `any` immediately to `unknown` and parse/validate before returning.

insights.title: 90. Declaration Files (.d.ts) and the declare Keyword
insights.content: Provide static type shapes for JavaScript libraries or build outputs without emitting runtime code using .d.ts files.

blocks.text: `.d.ts` files contain only type declarations (`declare function`, `declare const`, `export interface`) and zero implementation. Enabling `"declaration": true` in `tsconfig.json` generates them automatically for libraries.

insights.title: 91. Ambient Modules and Global Augmentation (declare global)
insights.content: Type non-code imports like `.svg` or `.css` with `declare module` and extend Window or Array inside modules with `declare global`.

blocks.text: When importing assets in Vite/Next (`import logo from './logo.svg'`), wildcard ambient modules (`declare module "*.svg"`) tell TypeScript their export type. Inside an ES module file, use `declare global { interface Window { ... } }` to augment globals.

insights.title: 92. Module Augmentation for Extending Third-Party Types
insights.content: Add custom properties or theme tokens to third-party library interfaces cleanly via `declare module "pkg"`.

blocks.text: Libraries like Express, Fastify, React Router, or MUI expose extensible interfaces. Writing `declare module "library-name"` inside a module merges your custom fields into their existing interfaces.

insights.title: 93. TypeScript 5.0 Standard ECMAScript Decorators
insights.content: Instrument classes, methods, and fields using standard Stage 3 decorators without legacy experimentalDecorators.

blocks.text: TypeScript 5.0 implemented the standard ECMAScript decorator proposal. Each decorator receives `(target, context)` where `context` carries `{ kind, name, addInitializer, access, metadata }` with full generic type safety.

insights.title: 94. using, await using, and Disposable Types (TS 5.2+)
insights.content: Type deterministic resource cleanup with Disposable, AsyncDisposable, and DisposableStack in TypeScript 5.2+.

blocks.text: TypeScript 5.2 introduced type support for `using` and `await using`, plus global `Disposable` and `AsyncDisposable` interfaces and `DisposableStack` for composing multiple cleanups in LIFO order.

insights.title: 95. Inferred Type Predicates in .filter() (TS 5.5+)
insights.content: TypeScript 5.5 automatically infers type predicates from simple filter callbacks, narrowing `(string | null)[]` to `string[]`.

blocks.text: Previously, `[1, null, 2].filter((x) => x !== null)` stayed `(number | null)[]` unless you wrote a manual type predicate. Since TS 5.5, functions returning a single narrowing boolean automatically infer `x is NonNullable<...>`.

insights.title: 96. Isolated Declarations for Fast .d.ts Emit (TS 5.5+)
insights.content: Annotate exported function returns explicitly so external tools (oxc, swc, Bun) can emit .d.ts files in parallel without full tsc.

blocks.text: With `isolatedDeclarations: true`, TypeScript requires explicit type annotations on exported functions and variables whose types can't be trivially inferred per-file—unlocking 10x+ faster monorepo `.d.ts` builds.

insights.title: 97. Type-Level Arithmetic via Tuple Lengths
insights.content: Perform compile-time counting, addition, and bounds checks by building and measuring tuple lengths.

blocks.text: TypeScript has no built-in `+` operator in type expressions, so type-level math constructs tuples of length `N` and accesses `T["length"]`—useful for fixed-size vector types or depth counters.

insights.title: 98. Parsing String Patterns at the Type Level (Route Params)
insights.content: Extract `:param` placeholders from URL route strings using template literal `infer` to type route handlers automatically.

blocks.text: Combining template literal pattern matching with recursion allows Express/Next-style route helpers to derive `{ userId: string; postId: string }` directly from `"/users/:userId/posts/:postId"`.

insights.title: 99. Control Flow Analysis in Closures and Aliased Conditions (TS 5.4+)
insights.content: Understand when TypeScript preserves narrowing inside callbacks (TS 5.4+ for non-reassigned variables) and when reassignment resets narrowing.

blocks.text: Historically, checking `if (url)` didn't preserve narrowing inside a `setTimeout` or `.map()` closure even for `const` or non-reassigned `let` variables. TS 5.4 preserves narrowing inside closures created *after* the last reassignment.

insights.title: 100. TypeScript Compiler Performance & Scalability Patterns
insights.content: Keep IDE autocomplete snappy and builds fast using interface extends, project references, explicit return types, and tsc --diagnostics.

blocks.text: Large intersections (`A & B & C`) force TypeScript to recompute combined properties repeatedly, whereas `interface C extends A, B` caches flat member tables. Also avoid massive combinatorial template-literal unions and enable `incremental: true` + `skipLibCheck: true`.

interviewQuestions.title: Structural Typing (Duck Typing) vs Nominal Typing
interviewQuestions.content: TypeScript checks type compatibility by shape (members) rather than explicit declaration names, unlike nominal systems like Java or C#.

blocks.text:
• Structural Compatibility: Type `A` is assignable to `B` if `A` has at least all required properties of `B` with compatible types.
• Classes Included: Even instances of different classes are interchangeable if their public shapes match (unless they contain `private`/`protected` members).
• Caveat: Two distinct concepts with identical primitives (e.g., `UserId` vs `OrderId` both as `string`) are interchangeable unless you simulate nominal typing via Branded Types.

interviewQuestions.title: type Aliases vs interface: Key Differences & When to Use Which
interviewQuestions.content: Both describe object shapes, but interfaces support declaration merging and faster error messages while type aliases handle unions, tuples, and mapped/conditional types.

blocks.text:
• `interface` Only: Declaration merging (re-opening interfaces across modules, useful for library augmentation) and `class implements` ergonomics.
• `type` Only: Unions (`A | B`), primitives, tuples, conditional types, and mapped types.
• Performance & Safety: Interfaces cache structural relationships well in large codebases and produce cleaner error messages; `type` does not accidentally merge across files.
• Rule of Thumb: Use `interface` for extensible public object/API contracts and `type` for unions, intersections, and utility transformations.

interviewQuestions.title: any vs unknown vs never vs void
interviewQuestions.content: `any` disables type checking; `unknown` is the type-safe top type requiring narrowing; `never` represents impossible values; `void` marks ignored function returns.

blocks.text:
• `any`: Opts out of type checking completely—propagates unsafety.
• `unknown`: Accepts any value, but forbids property access or calls until narrowed via `typeof`, `instanceof`, or type guards.
• `never`: Bottom type with zero values—returned by functions that always throw or infinite-loop, and used in exhaustiveness checks.
• `void`: Indicates a function's return value shouldn't be relied upon (callbacks returning `void` can still accept functions returning a value, e.g. `() => void`).

interviewQuestions.title: Union (|) vs Intersection (&) Types & Conflicting Property Intersections
interviewQuestions.content: Unions represent a value matching at least one member; intersections combine all members into one type—reducing conflicting primitives to `never`.

blocks.text:
• Union (`A | B`): Value can be `A` or `B`. Before narrowing, TypeScript only allows properties guaranteed on *every* member.
• Intersection (`A & B`): Value must satisfy *both* `A` and `B` simultaneously.
• Pitfall: Intersecting incompatible primitive types (`string & number`) produces `never`. Extending interfaces with conflicting property types fails immediately at declaration time instead of silently collapsing to `never`.

interviewQuestions.title: The `satisfies` Operator vs Type Annotations (:) and Assertions (as)
interviewQuestions.content: `satisfies` validates that an expression matches a target type without widening or discarding its narrow inferred literal properties.

blocks.text:
• Type Annotation (`const x: T = ...`): Enforces `T` on the variable, widening away specific keys/literal types (e.g., `colors.green` becomes `string | number[]`).
• Type Assertion (`as T`): Overrides the compiler and can hide missing or invalid properties.
• `satisfies T`: Best of both worlds—catches typos/missing keys against `T` at compile time while retaining exact inferred literal and property types on the variable.

interviewQuestions.title: `const` Type Parameters (<const T>) in TypeScript 5.0+
interviewQuestions.content: Prefixing a generic type parameter with `const` instructs TypeScript to infer deeply readonly literal types automatically without requiring `as const` at call sites.

blocks.text:
• Problem Before TS 5.0: Passing `['/home', '/about']` to a generic function inferred `string[]` unless the caller remembered to write `as const`.
• `<const T>` Solution: Library authors put `const` directly on the type parameter so arguments infer as exact readonly tuples/literals.
• Caveat: `const` inference only applies to inline literal arguments passed directly to the call—if a caller passes an already-widened variable, it remains widened.

interviewQuestions.title: Type Widening vs Literal Narrowing & `as const` Assertions
interviewQuestions.content: `let` widens literals (`'hi'` -> `string`) while `const` preserves primitives; `as const` recursively freezes objects and arrays into deeply readonly literal types.

blocks.text:
• Type Widening: Object properties inside `const obj = { mode: 'dark' }` still widen `mode` to `string` because object properties are mutable.
• `as const`: Marks every nested property `readonly`, turns arrays into `readonly` tuples, and narrows all primitives to exact literals.
• Common Pattern: Derive union types directly from runtime lookup tables (`const ROLES = ['admin', 'user'] as const; type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number]`).

interviewQuestions.title: Discriminated Unions & Exhaustiveness Checking with `never`
interviewQuestions.content: Discriminated unions share a literal tag field for safe narrowing, and assigning the `default` branch to `never` forces a compile error if a new variant goes unhandled.

blocks.text:
• Discriminant Property: A shared literal property (e.g., `status`, `kind`, `type`) across all union members.
• Advantages Over Optional Bags: Eliminates impossible states like `{ loading: true, error: 'fail', data: [...] }`.
• Exhaustiveness Check: Assigning the leftover variable in `default` to `never` (or calling `assertNever(res)`) guarantees future union additions fail at compile time.

interviewQuestions.title: Custom Type Predicates (`is`), Assertion Functions (`asserts`) & TS 5.5 Inference
interviewQuestions.content: Type predicates narrow values on boolean returns, `asserts` narrows for the remainder of the scope by throwing, and TypeScript 5.5 auto-infers predicates in `.filter()`.

blocks.text:
• `val is T`: Tells the compiler that returning `true` guarantees `val` has type `T`. Caution: TS trusts your boolean logic—wrong checks cause runtime bugs.
• `asserts val is T`: Throws on failure; narrows `val` for all subsequent lines in the calling block.
• TS 5.5 Inferred Type Predicates: Simple callbacks like `.filter(x => x !== undefined)` now automatically narrow `(T | undefined)[]` to `T[]` without writing manual `is` predicates.

interviewQuestions.title: Generics, `extends` Constraints & Default Type Parameters
interviewQuestions.content: Generics parameterize types across reusable functions and classes; `extends` constrains valid inputs while `= Default` provides fallback types.

blocks.text:
• Purpose: Preserve exact input-to-output type relationships instead of erasing types to `any` or wide unions.
• Constraints (`T extends U`): Restrict `T` so you can safely access guaranteed properties (e.g., `T extends { length: number }`) or keys (`K extends keyof T`).
• Defaults (`<T = string>`): Allow callers to omit explicit type arguments when not inferred from parameters.

interviewQuestions.title: `keyof`, Type-Level `typeof`, and Indexed Access Types (`T[K]`)
interviewQuestions.content: `typeof` lifts a runtime value into type space, `keyof` extracts its property keys as a union, and `T[K]` looks up property or array element types.

blocks.text:
• `typeof value` (type position): Captures the TypeScript type of a runtime variable or function (distinct from JS runtime `typeof`).
• `keyof T`: Produces a union of all public keys (`string | number | symbol` subsets) of `T`.
• Indexed Access (`T[K]`): Extracts the type of property `K` (e.g., `User['address']['city']`) or array element type (`Users[number]`).

interviewQuestions.title: Conditional Types & Distributive Conditional Types Over Unions
interviewQuestions.content: Conditional types (`T extends U ? X : Y`) distribute automatically over naked union type parameters; wrapping in tuples (`[T] extends [U]`) disables distribution.

blocks.text:
• Syntax: `T extends U ? X : Y` evaluates type-level branching.
• Distributivity Rule: When `T` is a *naked* (unwrapped) generic parameter receiving a union `A | B`, TS evaluates `(A extends U ? X : Y) | (B extends U ? X : Y)`—this is how `Exclude<T, U>` and `Extract<T, U>` work.
• Opting Out: Wrap both sides in a tuple `[T] extends [U]` when you want to test the union as a single whole type.

interviewQuestions.title: Pattern Matching with the `infer` Keyword
interviewQuestions.content: `infer` declares a temporary type variable inside the `extends` clause of a conditional type to extract return types, parameters, array elements, or Promise payloads.

blocks.text:
• Where Valid: Strictly inside the `extends` clause of a conditional type (`T extends ... infer R ? R : ...`).
• Common Extractions: Function return types (`ReturnType`), parameters (`Parameters`), constructor instances (`InstanceType`), recursive promise unwrapping (`Awaited`), and string substrings.
• Multiple `infer` Positions: If the same `infer U` appears in multiple covariant positions, TS creates a union; in contravariant positions (parameters), it creates an intersection.

interviewQuestions.title: Mapped Types, +/- Modifiers & `as` Key Remapping
interviewQuestions.content: Mapped types iterate over property keys to transform object types, using `+`/`-` prefixes to add/strip `readonly` or `?`, and `as` to rename or filter keys.

blocks.text:
• Modifiers: `+readonly`/`-readonly` and `+?`/`-?` explicitly add or remove optionality and immutability (e.g., `Required<T>` uses `-?`).
• Key Remapping (`as`): Rename keys dynamically with template literals or filter keys out by mapping unwanted keys to `never` (`[K in keyof T as T[K] extends Function ? K : never]`).
• Note: Filter `symbol`/`number` keys with `string & K` before passing keys to string template literals.

interviewQuestions.title: Template Literal Types & Intrinsic String Manipulation Types
interviewQuestions.content: Template literal types interpolate string/number unions into Cartesian-product string literal unions, paired with Uppercase, Lowercase, Capitalize, and Uncapitalize.

blocks.text:
• Cartesian Expansion: Interpolating two unions (`${A}-${B}`) generates every combination automatically.
• Intrinsic Helpers: `Uppercase<S>`, `Lowercase<S>`, `Capitalize<S>`, and `Uncapitalize<S>` are compiler-intrinsic transforms.
• Real-World Uses: Typed event names (`onClick`), CSS design tokens, i18n translation keys, and REST/router path parameter extraction.

interviewQuestions.title: Core Built-In Utility Types: Pick vs Omit, Extract vs Exclude & Record
interviewQuestions.content: Built-in utility types transform object properties (`Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `Record`) or filter unions (`Extract`, `Exclude`, `NonNullable`).

blocks.text:
• Object vs Union Confusion (Classic Trap): `Pick`/`Omit` operate on *object property keys*; `Extract`/`Exclude` operate on *union members*.
• `Partial<T>` / `Required<T>` / `Readonly<T>`: Shallowly toggle optionality or readonly.
• `Record<K, V>`: Creates an object type mapping keys `K` to values `V`.
• `NonNullable<T>`: Strips `null` and `undefined` from a union (`T & {}` under the hood).

interviewQuestions.title: Controlling Generic Inference with `NoInfer<T>` (TypeScript 5.4+)
interviewQuestions.content: `NoInfer<T>` blocks TypeScript from using a parameter position as an inference candidate, forcing `T` to be inferred strictly from other arguments.

blocks.text:
• The Inference Bug: Without `NoInfer`, passing a wrong second argument like `'typo'` to `createFSM(['idle', 'loading'], 'typo')` widens `S` to `'idle' | 'loading' | 'typo'` instead of catching the typo!
• `NoInfer<T>` Fix: Marks `initial` as a consumer of `S` rather than an inference source, so `'typo'` fails immediately.
• Previous Workaround: Developers used to write `S & {}` or extra type parameters `<S, D extends S>`.

interviewQuestions.title: Variance in TypeScript: Covariance, Contravariance, Invariance & `in`/`out`
interviewQuestions.content: Outputs are covariant (narrower can replace broader), inputs/function parameters are contravariant under `strictFunctionTypes`, and mutable read-write slots are invariant.

blocks.text:
• Covariance (`out T`): If `Dog extends Animal`, `Producer<Dog>` is assignable to `Producer<Animal>` (safe for return values).
• Contravariance (`in T`): `Consumer<Animal>` is assignable to `Consumer<Dog>`—a handler accepting *any* Animal safely handles a Dog (enforced on function types under `strictFunctionTypes: true`; methods remain bivariant!).
• Invariance (`in out T`): Mutable structures require exact type match.
• Explicit `in`/`out` Annotations (TS 4.7+): Improve type-checking speed and catch accidental variance mismatches.

blocks.code:
// Explicit variance annotations (TS 4.7+)
interface Producer<out T> { get(): T }      // Covariant
interface Consumer<in T> { accept(v: T): void } // Contravariant
interface Box<in out T> { value: T }         // Invariant

interviewQuestions.title: Function Overloads vs Union Parameters vs Conditional Return Types
interviewQuestions.content: Use union parameters when return types don't depend on input types; use overloads or conditional return types when input and output types are coupled.

blocks.text:
• Prefer Union Parameters First: Simpler, cleaner errors, and accepts union-typed arguments directly.
• Overload Caveat: Callers passing a union `string | number` cannot match separate `string` / `number` overloads unless a combined overload exists; also implementation signatures are hidden from callers.
• Conditional Return Types (`T extends string ? number : string`): Handle union inputs naturally via distribution, though they sometimes require internal assertions inside the function body.

interviewQuestions.title: Tuples, Labeled Elements, Optional Slots & Variadic Tuple Types
interviewQuestions.content: Tuples model fixed-position arrays with per-index types, optional trailing elements, labeled IDE hints, and generic spread compositions (`[...T, ...U]`).

blocks.text:
• Tuples vs Arrays: `string[]` is variable-length homogeneous; `[string, number]` enforces length and exact index types.
• Labeled Tuples: `[x: number, y: number]` improves IDE autocomplete without changing runtime behavior.
• Variadic Tuples (`[...T, string]`): Let generic functions spread and preserve exact tuple structures (e.g., typing `promisify` or `curry`).
• Trap: Calling `.push()` on a mutable tuple is allowed at compile time—use `readonly [...]`.

interviewQuestions.title: Recursive Type Aliases (JSONValue, DeepReadonly) & Recursion Limits
interviewQuestions.content: TypeScript supports self-referential type aliases for trees, JSON schemas, and deep transformations like `DeepReadonly<T>`, subject to instantiation depth limits.

blocks.text:
• Practical Recursive Types: `JSONValue`, nested menu trees, `DeepPartial<T>`, `DeepReadonly<T>`, and dot-path string generators.
• Function Guard: Always check `T extends Function` before `T extends object` in `DeepReadonly` so function call signatures aren't turned into empty `{}` objects!
• Tail-Recursion Optimization: TS 4.5+ supports tail-recursive conditional types up to ~1,000 iterations (vs ~50 for non-tail recursion) before throwing `Type instantiation is excessively deep`.

blocks.code:
type JSONValue =
  | string
  | number
  | boolean
  | null
  | JSONValue[]
  | { [key: string]: JSONValue };

type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => any
  ? T
  : T extends object
    ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }
    : T;

interviewQuestions.title: `enum` vs `const enum` vs `as const` Objects
interviewQuestions.content: Standard enums emit runtime IIFE code and numeric enums lack type safety against arbitrary numbers; `as const` objects with derived unions are usually preferred in modern TS.

blocks.text:
• Numeric `enum` Hazard: By default, numeric enums generate reverse mappings and allow assigning arbitrary numbers (`const r: NumEnum = 999` in older TS, or subtle indexing bugs).
• `const enum` Pitfalls: Inlines numbers at compile time, breaking `isolatedModules`, Babel/esbuild/SWC transpilers, and `--erasableSyntaxOnly`.
• `as const` Object Pattern: Zero custom runtime syntax, fully erasable, tree-shakeable, and works seamlessly with Node/Bun type stripping.

interviewQuestions.title: TypeScript 5.8 `--erasableSyntaxOnly` for Native Type-Stripping Runtimes
interviewQuestions.content: `--erasableSyntaxOnly` bans non-erasable TS constructs (enums, namespaces, parameter properties) so files run directly in Node.js `--experimental-strip-types`, Bun, or Deno.

blocks.text:
• Why It Exists: Modern runtimes like Node.js (native type stripping), Deno, and lightweight transpilers erase type annotations without performing AST transformations.
• What Gets Flagged: `enum`, `namespace` containing runtime code, class constructor parameter properties (`constructor(public x: number)`), and `import =` / `export =`.
• Pair With `verbatimModuleSyntax`: Guarantees every `import type` and type syntax can be stripped cleanly line-for-line.

interviewQuestions.title: TypeScript 5.5+ `isolatedDeclarations` for Fast `.d.ts` Generation
interviewQuestions.content: `isolatedDeclarations` requires explicit type annotations on exported APIs so external tools (oxc, swc) can emit `.d.ts` files per-file in parallel without full type-checking.

blocks.text:
• The Monorepo Bottleneck: Traditionally, only `tsc` could emit `.d.ts` files because inferred export types required resolving types across the entire dependency graph.
• How `isolatedDeclarations` Helps: Enforces explicit return/property types on module exports, allowing Rust/Go tools (`oxc`, `rolldown`, `tsdown`) to emit `.d.ts` files 10x+ faster in parallel.
• Trade-off: Slightly more explicit annotations on public exports, zero overhead inside private/local functions.

interviewQuestions.title: TypeScript 5.9 `import defer` (Deferred Module Evaluation)
interviewQuestions.content: `import defer * as ns from '...'` loads a module synchronously without executing its top-level body or side effects until one of its exports is first accessed.

blocks.text:
• Problem Solved: Dynamic `import()` forces code to become `async`, while eager `import` runs expensive initialization at startup even for rarely used branches.
• Semantics: Only namespace imports (`import defer * as ns`) are allowed; loading/parsing still happens upfront, but evaluation waits until `ns.prop` is read.
• Ideal Use Case: Heavy SDKs, feature-flagged tools, and CLI subcommands needing fast cold-start times.

interviewQuestions.title: Standard ECMAScript Decorators (TS 5.0+) vs `experimentalDecorators`
interviewQuestions.content: TypeScript 5.0+ supports Stage 3 standard decorators using `(value, context)` without `experimentalDecorators` or `reflect-metadata`.

blocks.text:
• Standard Decorators (TS 5.0+): Receive `(value, context)` where `context` provides `kind`, `name`, `static`, `private`, and `addInitializer()`. Supported natively by browsers/TC39.
• Legacy `experimentalDecorators`: Older TS-specific API passing `(target, propertyKey, descriptor)` and relying on `emitDecoratorMetadata` (still required by NestJS/TypeORM DI).
• Key Difference: Standard decorators do NOT support parameter decorators.

interviewQuestions.title: TypeScript 5.2+ `using` / `await using` & `Disposable` Interfaces
