interviewQuestions.content: TypeScript provides built-in `Disposable` and `AsyncDisposable` types plus `DisposableStack` for deterministic cleanup via `using` and `await using`.

blocks.text:
• Built-in Types: `Disposable` requires `[Symbol.dispose](): void`; `AsyncDisposable` requires `[Symbol.asyncDispose](): Promise<void>`.
• `DisposableStack` / `AsyncDisposableStack`: Aggregate multiple cleanup callbacks (`stack.defer(() => ...)`) under one `using` variable.
• Compilation Target: Requires `lib: ['esnext.disposable']` (or ES2025+) and downlevels cleanly to `try/finally` when targeting older ES versions.

interviewQuestions.title: Control Flow Analysis & Narrowing Mechanisms
interviewQuestions.content: TypeScript narrows union types dynamically across branches using `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, equality checks, truthiness, and control-flow exits.

blocks.text:
• Narrowing Constructs: `typeof` (primitives), `instanceof` (class prototypes), `'prop' in obj` (property existence), `Array.isArray()`, and literal equality (`===`).
• Assignment Narrowing: Assigning a specific type to a union variable narrows it until reassigned.
• TS 5.5 Improvement: Control flow analysis now narrows indexed accesses like `obj[key]` when both `obj` and `key` are effectively constant.

interviewQuestions.title: Excess Property Checking vs Structural Typing on Variables
interviewQuestions.content: TypeScript rejects unknown properties when passing fresh object literals directly, but permits extra properties through intermediate variables due to structural typing.

blocks.text:
• Why Both Rules Exist: Fresh object literals with unknown keys almost always indicate a typo (e.g., `colour` vs `color`), so TS enforces strict key checks on literals.
• Intermediate Variables: Assigning through a variable falls back to pure structural subtyping (extra properties are safe).
• Empty Weak-Type Rule: An object literal passed to an optional-only interface (`{ a?: number }`) fails if it shares *zero* properties with the target.

interviewQuestions.title: Declaration Merging & Module Augmentation (`declare module` / `declare global`)
interviewQuestions.content: Declaration merging combines identically named interfaces or namespaces, enabling safe module augmentation of third-party libraries and global objects.

blocks.text:
• What Merges: `interface` + `interface`, `namespace` + `namespace`, and `namespace` + `class`/`function`/`enum` (type aliases do NOT merge).
• Module Augmentation: Inside a module file (must have an `import`/`export`), `declare module 'pkg' { interface ... }` extends library types without editing `node_modules`.
• `declare global`: Adds properties to `Window`, `ProcessEnv`, or `Array.prototype` from inside a module.

interviewQuestions.title: Ambient Declarations (`.d.ts`), `declare`, and `@types/*` Packages
interviewQuestions.content: `.d.ts` files describe runtime shapes of JavaScript libraries, CSS/asset imports, or build-time globals without emitting JavaScript code.

blocks.text:
• Purpose: Provide compile-time types for untyped JS libraries, bundler asset imports (`*.svg`, `*.css`), and injected globals (`__DEV__`).
• Script vs Module `.d.ts`: A `.d.ts` without top-level `import`/`export` puts declarations in global scope; adding `export {}` scopes it as a module.
• Library Publishing: `declaration: true` generates `.d.ts` files alongside `.js` output, paired with `types` or `exports['.'].types` in `package.json`.

interviewQuestions.title: `moduleResolution`: `node` vs `nodenext` vs `bundler`
interviewQuestions.content: Choose `nodenext` for Node.js ESM/CJS libraries (requiring explicit file extensions) and `bundler` for Vite/Next.js/Webpack apps supporting extensionless imports and `package.json` `exports`.

blocks.text:
• `node` (Legacy Node10): Ignores `package.json` `exports` / `imports` fields and conditional entrypoints—avoid in modern projects.
• `nodenext` / `node16`: Enforces Node's real ESM/CJS rules, `exports` field resolution, and explicit `.js` extensions on relative ESM imports.
• `bundler` (TS 5.0+): Respects `package.json` `exports` and subpath imports like `nodenext`, while permitting extensionless relative imports and `.ts` extensions when `noEmit` / `allowImportingTsExtensions` is enabled.

interviewQuestions.title: Essential Strict Compiler Flags Beyond `strict: true`
interviewQuestions.content: `strict: true` enables `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, and `strictFunctionTypes`, while `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` catch subtle runtime crashes.

blocks.text:
• Included in `strict: true`: `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables`.
• `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`: Adds `| undefined` to array indexing (`arr[0]`) and index signatures (`dict[key]`), preventing silent `Cannot read properties of undefined` crashes.
• `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`: Distinguishes `{ x?: number }` (omitted or `number`) from `{ x?: number | undefined }` (explicitly passing `undefined`).

interviewQuestions.title: `isolatedModules` vs `verbatimModuleSyntax` (`import type`)
interviewQuestions.content: `verbatimModuleSyntax` enforces explicit `import type` / `export type` annotations so single-file transpilers (esbuild, SWC, Babel, Node) never emit broken runtime imports.

blocks.text:
• Why Single-File Transpilers Need It: Tools like Babel, SWC, and `esbuild` compile one file at a time without whole-program type info, so they cannot tell if `import { Foo } from './bar'` is a class or a type-only interface.
• `verbatimModuleSyntax` (TS 5.0+): Replaces `importsNotUsedAsValues` and `preserveValueImports` with one simple rule—any import without `type` stays in JS output; anything with `import type` is dropped.

interviewQuestions.title: `abstract class` vs `interface` & TS `private` vs JS `#private`
interviewQuestions.content: Interfaces are purely compile-time contracts supporting multiple implementation; abstract classes emit runtime base classes with shared concrete methods and constructors.

blocks.text:
• `abstract class` vs `interface`: A class can `implement` multiple interfaces (zero runtime cost), but can `extend` only one abstract class (which can hold shared state and implemented helper methods).
• `private` vs `#private`: TS `private` is erased at runtime (accessible via `obj['secret']` or in plain JS); `#field` is enforced by the JS engine itself and cannot be accessed outside the class.

interviewQuestions.title: Typing `this` Parameters, `ThisParameterType` & Polymorphic `this`
interviewQuestions.content: Adding a fake first `this: Type` parameter constrains a function's calling context, while returning `this` enables fluent method chaining across subclasses.

blocks.text:
• Explicit `this` Parameter: `function fn(this: Context, arg: string)` is erased in emitted JS and ensures callers bind the expected `this`.
• Utility Types: `ThisParameterType<Fn>`, `OmitThisParameter<Fn>`, and `ThisType<T>` (marker for object literal methods).
• Polymorphic `this`: Returning `this` instead of `BaseClass` lets subclass instances keep their narrower subclass type during chained calls.

interviewQuestions.title: Constructor Signatures, `InstanceType<T>` & Typed Class Mixins
interviewQuestions.content: Represent constructable classes with `new (...args: any[]) => T`, extract their instance type with `InstanceType<typeof Class>`, and compose behaviors via Mixin factories.

blocks.text:
• Class Value vs Instance Type: `class Foo {}` introduces both a value (the constructor `typeof Foo`) and a type (an instance `Foo`).
• `InstanceType<typeof Foo>`: Extracts `Foo` from its constructor type; `ConstructorParameters<typeof Foo>` extracts constructor args.
• Mixins: Functions taking a `Constructor<T>` base class and returning an anonymous subclass extending `Base`, enabling reusable composable behaviors.

interviewQuestions.title: Branded (Opaque / Nominal) Types in TypeScript
interviewQuestions.content: Branded types intersect a primitive with a phantom `unique symbol` property to simulate nominal typing and prevent mixing semantically distinct IDs or units.

blocks.text:
• Why Use Them: Prevent swapping `UserId` and `OrderId`, `USD` and `EUR`, or `SanitizedHTML` and raw `string` with zero runtime overhead.
• `unique symbol` Advantage: Using `declare const brand: unique symbol` hides the phantom field from autocomplete and stops accidental `{ __brand: ... }` object tampering.
• Pair With Type Guards / Factories: Validate or construct branded values at system boundaries (`parseUserId(raw)`).

interviewQuestions.title: Index Signatures (`[key: string]: T`) vs `Record<K, V>` vs `Map<K, V>`
interviewQuestions.content: `Record<K, V>` supports finite literal union keys, index signatures allow open-ended keys, and `Map<K, V>` safely handles arbitrary runtime keys without prototype pitfalls.

blocks.text:
• Index Signatures (`[key: string]: T`): Accept any `string` key; cannot directly restrict keys to a finite union.
• `Record<K, V>`: Works with both `string` and literal unions (`Record<'en' | 'ar', string>`), requiring every union key.
• Safety Tip: Enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` or use `Map<K, V>` for dynamic lookups because plain index access assumes keys always exist unless typed `| undefined`.

interviewQuestions.title: `readonly` Modifiers, `ReadonlyArray<T>` & Shallow Immutability Pitfalls
interviewQuestions.content: `readonly` prevents reassignment at compile time only, is shallow on nested objects, and allows mutable arrays to be assigned to `readonly` parameters.

blocks.text:
• Shallow Only: `Readonly<User>` prevents `user.address = ...` but still allows `user.address.city = ...` unless nested types are also `Readonly`.
• Asymmetric Assignability: `number[]` is assignable to `readonly number[]` (good for function params that promise not to mutate), but `readonly number[]` is NOT assignable to `number[]`.
• Interface Mutability Aliasing: A `readonly` property in one reference does not stop mutation via another non-readonly alias to the same object.

interviewQuestions.title: Schema Type Inference Patterns (How `z.infer<typeof schema>` Works)
interviewQuestions.content: Schema libraries attach phantom or conditional type parameters to runtime validator objects and extract the validated static type using conditional `infer` helpers.

blocks.text:
• Core Mechanism: A validator object carries a type parameter `Schema<Output>` (either in method return types or a phantom `_output?: Output` field).
• `Infer<S>` Helper: `S extends Schema<infer T> ? T : never` extracts `Output` so runtime validation and compile-time types share a single source of truth.
• Benefit: Eliminates drift between manual TypeScript interfaces and runtime API validation.

interviewQuestions.title: Designing a Strongly Typed EventEmitter / Pub-Sub in TypeScript
interviewQuestions.content: Parameterizing an EventEmitter with an event-map type and constraining methods with `K extends keyof Events` couples each event name to its exact payload type.

blocks.text:
• Pattern: Define `interface AppEvents { login: { userId: string }; logout: void }` and pass it to `TypedEmitter<AppEvents>`.
• Indexed Coupling: `on<K extends keyof Events>(event: K, cb: (data: Events[K]) => void)` ensures `cb` receives `{ userId: string }` when `event` is `'login'`.
• Bonus Refinement: Make `payload` optional when `Events[K]` is `void` or `undefined` using conditional rest parameters (`...args: Events[K] extends void ? [] : [payload: Events[K]]`).

interviewQuestions.title: Why `Object.keys(obj)` Returns `string[]` Instead of `(keyof T)[]`
interviewQuestions.content: Because TypeScript uses structural subtyping, an object typed as `T` may contain extra runtime properties beyond `keyof T`, making `(keyof T)[]` unsound.

blocks.text:
• Soundness Reason: If `const full = { a: 1, b: 2 }; const partial: { a: number } = full;`, `Object.keys(partial)` returns `['a', 'b']` at runtime—so assuming `'b'` cannot exist would break `partial[k]` lookups.
• Safe Alternatives:
  1. Iterate `Object.entries(obj)` or `Object.values(obj)` when possible.
  2. For closed `as const` objects you control, write a small typed helper `typedKeys<T extends object>(o: T)` with `Object.keys(o) as (keyof T)[]` and document the assumption.

interviewQuestions.title: Practical Uses of `never` in Type Algebra and Unreachable Code
interviewQuestions.content: `never` acts as the identity element for unions (`T | never` === `T`), enabling union filtering, exhaustive switch guards, and impossible state elimination.

blocks.text:
• Union Identity: `A | never` simplifies to `A`, which is how conditional types drop non-matching union members.
• Intersection Absorber: `A & never` collapses to `never`, catching conflicting types.
• Mutually Exclusive Props: `{ a: string; b?: never } | { a?: never; b: string }` prevents passing both `a` and `b` together.

blocks.code:
type OnlyStrings<T> = T extends string ? T : never;
type Result = OnlyStrings<"a" | 42 | "b">; // "a" | "b" (never disappears in unions!)

interviewQuestions.title: Typing Async Functions, `Awaited<T>` & `catch (err: unknown)`
interviewQuestions.content: `async` functions always return `Promise<T>`; `Awaited<T>` recursively unwraps nested Promises, and strict TS types caught errors as `unknown`.

blocks.text:
• `Awaited<T>`: Built-in recursive utility type matching runtime `await` behavior (`Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>` → `number`).
• `ReturnType<typeof asyncFn>`: Returns `Promise<T>`, so combine `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fn>>` to extract the resolved payload.
• Catch Clauses: With `useUnknownInCatchVariables` (part of `strict: true`), `err` is `unknown` instead of `any`, forcing `err instanceof Error` checks.

interviewQuestions.title: Typing React/TSX Components: `ReactNode`, `ComponentProps` & Generic Components
interviewQuestions.content: Prefer `React.ReactNode` for `children`, extend native HTML attributes via `ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'tag'>`, and constrain generic TSX arrow components (`<T,>`).

blocks.text:
• `ReactNode` vs `JSX.Element` (`ReactElement`): `ReactNode` covers strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays, and elements—ideal for `children` props.
• Extending HTML Elements: `React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>` inherits all native button props cleanly (use `ComponentPropsWithRef` if forwarding refs).
• TSX Parsing Quirk: In `.tsx` files, `<T>` looks like a JSX tag—write `<T,>` or `<T extends object>` in arrow functions.

interviewQuestions.title: TypeScript Project References (`composite`, `tsc -b`) in Monorepos
interviewQuestions.content: Project References split massive codebases into independently built sub-projects using `composite: true` and `tsc --build`, enabling incremental `.tsbuildinfo` caching.

blocks.text:
• How It Works: Each workspace package sets `composite: true` (enforcing `declaration: true` and explicit `include`/`rootDir`), while consumers list `references: [{ path }]`.
• Build Mode (`tsc -b`): Builds dependencies in topological order and skips unchanged packages using `.tsbuildinfo`.
• Editor Benefit: VS Code Go-to-Definition jumps directly to `.ts` source files instead of compiled `.d.ts` files when `declarationMap: true` is enabled.

interviewQuestions.title: Type-Level String Parsing (Typed Route Parameters & Dot-Paths)
interviewQuestions.content: Combining template literal types, `infer`, and recursion lets TypeScript parse URL parameters or nested object paths entirely at compile time.

blocks.text:
• How It Works: Template literal pattern matching splits on delimiters like `:` or `/` (`${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`) and recurses on `Rest`.
• Real-World Frameworks: Powers typed routing in TanStack Router, Next.js typed routes, Express route params, and deep i18n/form paths (`user.address.city`).
• Non-Greedy Matching: The leading `${string}` matches lazily up to the first literal delimiter.

blocks.code:
type ExtractParams<Path extends string> =
  Path extends `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}`
    ? Param | ExtractParams<Rest>
    : Path extends `${string}:${infer Param}`
      ? Param
      : never;

type Params = ExtractParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">; // "userId" | "postId"

interviewQuestions.title: Compile-Time Type Erasure vs Runtime Validation at Trust Boundaries
interviewQuestions.content: TypeScript performs zero runtime checks—all interfaces and assertions vanish after compilation, so external APIs, JSON, and URL params must be validated at runtime.

blocks.text:
• Type Erasure: `res.json() as User` does NOT verify that `res.json()` actually matches `User`—it just silences the compiler.
• Trust Boundaries: Validate `fetch` responses, `JSON.parse`, `localStorage`, query params, and `process.env` using Zod, Valibot, ArkType, or explicit type guards.
• Best Practice: Infer TS types from the runtime schema (`z.infer<typeof UserSchema>`) instead of duplicating definitions.

interviewQuestions.title: Debugging Type Errors, `@ts-expect-error` vs `@ts-ignore` & Compiler Performance
interviewQuestions.content: Prefer `@ts-expect-error` over `@ts-ignore` so stale suppressions fail the build; diagnose slow type-checking with `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` and `--generateTrace`.

blocks.text:
• `@ts-expect-error` vs `@ts-ignore`: `@ts-ignore` silently stays forever even after the bug is fixed; `@ts-expect-error` throws an error if the next line becomes valid (ideal for type tests).
• Type-Check Speed Tips: Prefer interfaces over huge deeply intersecting unions, annotate return types on complex exported functions, and use `skipLibCheck: true`.
• Profiling: Run `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` or `tsc --generateTrace` to locate expensive recursive types.

languages.title: Python
languages.description: Versatile language used for backend development, automation, and building scalable web applications.

insights.title: 01. Variables & Dynamic Typing
insights.content: Python variables are name bindings to objects in memory, and their type is determined at runtime.

blocks.text: Unlike statically typed languages, you do not declare a variable's type before assigning it. Reassigning a name simply binds it to a different object, while type() lets you inspect the object's class at runtime.

blocks.code:
user_name = "Ahmed"
age = 28
print(type(user_name), type(age))

# Rebinding the same name to another type
age = "twenty-eight"
print(age, type(age))

insights.title: 02. Core Scalar Types: int, float, bool & None
insights.content: Python provides arbitrary-precision integers, IEEE-754 floats, booleans, and None for representing absence of a value.

blocks.text: Integers in Python never overflow fixed bit widths, while floats follow 64-bit precision (use Decimal when exact base-10 arithmetic is required). Booleans are a subclass of int, and None is a singleton checked with 'is None'.

blocks.code:
big_num = 10 ** 30
price = 19.99
is_active = True
middle_name = None

print(big_num + 1)
print(isinstance(True, int))
print(middle_name is None)

insights.title: 03. Strings, Indexing & Slicing
insights.content: Strings are immutable Unicode sequences supporting zero-based indexing, negative indices, and slice notation.

blocks.text: Use s[start:stop:step] to extract substrings without mutating the original string. Negative indices count backward from the end, and s[::-1] reverses a sequence cleanly.

blocks.code:
text = "Python 3.12"
print(text[0], text[-1])
print(text[0:6])
print(text[::-1])

insights.title: 04. String Methods & f-string Formatting
insights.content: f-strings embed expressions directly inside string literals with concise formatting specifiers.

blocks.text: Common string methods like strip(), split(), join(), and replace() return new strings because strings are immutable. f-strings evaluate expressions at runtime and support alignment, decimals, and debug output with {var=}.

blocks.code:
raw = "  ahmed,python,django  "
parts = raw.strip().split(",")
score = 0.9467

print(" | ".join(parts).upper())
print(f"User: {parts[0].title()} | Score: {score:.1%}")
print(f"{score=:.2f}")

insights.title: 05. Arithmetic, Comparison & Logical Operators
insights.content: Python distinguishes true division (/), floor division (//), exponentiation (**), and short-circuiting logical operators.

blocks.text: Comparison operators can be chained naturally like 0 <= x <= 10. Logical operators and, or, and not short-circuit and return the deciding operand rather than forcing a strict boolean when using and/or.

blocks.code:
a, b = 7, 2
print(a / b, a // b, a % b, a ** b)

x = 5
print(1 <= x <= 10)
display_name = "" or "Guest"
print(display_name)

insights.title: 06. Conditional Statements: if, elif, else
insights.content: Control execution flow using indentation-scoped if, elif, and else branches.

blocks.text: Python uses 4-space indentation instead of braces to delimit blocks. Conditions are evaluated top-to-bottom, and only the first matching branch executes.

insights.title: 07. Truthiness, Falsiness & Ternary Expressions
insights.content: Empty containers, zero, and None evaluate to False in boolean contexts, enabling concise checks and inline conditionals.

blocks.text: Instead of checking len(items) > 0, Pythonic code uses 'if items:'. Conditional expressions (a if cond else b) assign values inline without verbose multi-line if blocks.

blocks.code:
items = []
message = "Has items" if items else "Empty cart"
print(message)

for val in [0, "", [], None, "ok", [1]]:
    print(f"{val!r:6} -> {bool(val)}")

insights.title: 08. Lists: Creation, Indexing & Mutability
insights.content: Lists are ordered, mutable sequences capable of holding heterogeneous elements and supporting slice assignment.

blocks.text: Unlike strings or tuples, lists can be modified in place after creation. Be mindful that assigning list_b = list_a creates an alias to the same list, not a copy.

blocks.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits[1] = "mango"
copy_fruits = fruits.copy()
copy_fruits.append("orange")

print(fruits)
print(copy_fruits)

insights.title: 09. List Methods: append, extend, pop & sort
insights.content: Master in-place list operations and understand the difference between list.sort() and sorted().

blocks.text: append() adds one element (even if it is a list), whereas extend() unpacks another iterable into the list. list.sort() mutates the list and returns None, while sorted() returns a new sorted list.

blocks.code:
nums = [3, 1, 4]
nums.append(1)
nums.extend([5, 9])
last = nums.pop()

ordered = sorted(nums)
nums.sort(reverse=True)
print(f"popped={last}, ordered={ordered}, desc={nums}")

insights.title: 10. Tuples & Extended Unpacking
insights.content: Tuples are immutable ordered records ideal for fixed structures, multiple return values, and star unpacking.

blocks.text: Tuples consume less memory than lists and can serve as dictionary keys if their elements are hashable. Extended unpacking with *rest captures arbitrary middle or trailing items.

blocks.code:
point = (10, 20)
x, y = point

first, *middle, last = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
print(f"{x=}, {y=}, {first=}, {middle=}, {last=}")

insights.title: 11. Dictionaries: Key-Value Mapping & Safe Access
insights.content: Dictionaries map hashable keys to values with average O(1) lookup time and preserve insertion order.

blocks.text: Direct indexing d[key] raises KeyError when the key is missing, while d.get(key, default) returns a fallback value safely. Keys must be immutable/hashable types like str, int, or tuple.

blocks.code:
user = {"name": "Ahmed", "role": "backend"}
user["active"] = True

print(user["name"])
print(user.get("email", "not-provided"))
print("role" in user)

insights.title: 12. Dictionary Methods: items, setdefault & Merge (|)
insights.content: Iterate cleanly over keys and values with .items() and merge dictionaries using the | operator.

blocks.text: Since Python 3.9, d1 | d2 creates a merged dictionary and d1 |= d2 updates in place. Use setdefault() when initializing a missing key with a mutable default like a list.

insights.title: 13. Sets & Mathematical Set Operations
insights.content: Sets store unique hashable elements and support O(1) membership checks plus union, intersection, and difference.

blocks.text: Use {} only for dicts; an empty set must be created with set(). Sets excel at deduplicating collections and comparing permissions or tag lists cleanly.

insights.title: 14. for Loops, range() & enumerate()
insights.content: Iterate directly over iterables with for loops and track item indices cleanly using enumerate().

blocks.text: Avoid manual index counters like range(len(items)); iterate over items directly or use enumerate(items, start=1) when you need both the index and the element.

blocks.code:
steps = ["Parse", "Validate", "Save"]
for idx, step in enumerate(steps, start=1):
    print(f"Step {idx}: {step}")

squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 5)]
print(squares)

insights.title: 15. while Loops, break, continue & loop-else
insights.content: Control loop execution with break and continue, and use the optional else clause for search completion.

blocks.text: The else block on a for or while loop runs only if the loop finished normally without hitting a break statement—making search-or-fallback logic cleaner without flag variables.

insights.title: 16. Parallel Iteration with zip()
insights.content: Pair elements from multiple iterables lazily using zip(), and use strict=True to catch length mismatches.

blocks.text: zip() stops at the shortest iterable by default. Passing strict=True (Python 3.10+) raises a ValueError if the inputs do not have identical lengths, preventing silent data truncation.

blocks.code:
names = ["Ali", "Sara", "Omar"]
scores = [92, 88, 95]

for name, score in zip(names, scores, strict=True):
    print(f"{name}: {score}")

score_map = dict(zip(names, scores))
print(score_map)

insights.title: 17. Defining Functions, Docstrings & Return Values
insights.content: Functions encapsulate reusable logic with def, optional docstrings, and explicit return values.

blocks.text: If a function exits without a return statement, it implicitly returns None. Returning a tuple allows returning multiple values cleanly.

insights.title: 18. Default, Keyword, *args & **kwargs Parameters
insights.content: Python supports flexible function signatures combining positional, keyword, variadic *args, and **kwargs parameters.

blocks.text: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, while **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. Use * in a signature to enforce keyword-only parameters for clarity.

insights.title: 19. Avoiding the Mutable Default Argument Pitfall
insights.content: Default argument values are evaluated once at function definition time, never per call.

blocks.text: Using a list or dict as a default parameter causes all calls to share the exact same object. Always default to None and create a fresh container inside the function body.

blocks.code:
def add_item(item: str, bucket: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add_item("a"))
print(add_item("b"))

insights.title: 20. Variable Scope & the LEGB Resolution Rule
insights.content: Python resolves names in four ordered scopes: Local, Enclosing, Global, and Built-in (LEGB).

blocks.text: Assigning to a variable inside a function creates a local variable unless declared global or nonlocal. Prefer passing arguments and returning values over mutating global state.

blocks.code:
rate = 0.15  # Global

def compute_tax(amount: float) -> float:
    local_rate = rate  # Reads Global
    return amount * local_rate

print(compute_tax(200))

insights.title: 21. Lambda Expressions & Custom Key Sorting
insights.content: Lambda functions create concise single-expression anonymous functions, commonly used as sort keys.

blocks.text: While def is preferred for named reusable logic, lambda shines inside sorted(..., key=...), min(), and max() for inline attribute or dictionary lookups.

blocks.code:
tasks = [
    {"title": "Deploy", "priority": 2},
    {"title": "Fix bug", "priority": 1},
    {"title": "Docs", "priority": 3},
]
ordered = sorted(tasks, key=lambda t: t["priority"])
print([t["title"] for t in ordered])

insights.title: 22. Functional Built-ins: any(), all(), sum(), map(), filter()
insights.content: Python's built-in higher-order and predicate functions express data checks and aggregations declaratively.

blocks.text: any() and all() short-circuit on generator expressions, making them fast and memory-friendly. While comprehensions often replace map/filter, passing an existing function to map() remains concise.

blocks.code:
scores = [78, 85, 92, 64]
print("All passed:", all(s >= 60 for s in scores))
print("Any top:", any(s >= 90 for s in scores))
print("Total:", sum(scores))
print("Strings:", list(map(str, scores)))

insights.title: 23. List Comprehensions & Filtering
insights.content: List comprehensions transform and filter iterables in a single readable expression.

blocks.text: They run faster than equivalent for-append loops and keep transformation logic close together. Avoid deeply nested comprehensions when a standard loop is clearer.

blocks.code:
numbers = range(1, 11)
even_squares = [n ** 2 for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]
labels = ["even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd" for n in range(1, 5)]

print(even_squares)
print(labels)

insights.title: 24. Dictionary & Set Comprehensions
insights.content: Build lookup tables and deduplicated sets directly from iterables using {} comprehension syntax.

blocks.text: Dict comprehensions {k: v for ...} make inverting mappings or indexing objects by ID effortless, while set comprehensions {expr for ...} collect unique transformed values.

insights.title: 25. Exception Handling: try, except, else & finally
insights.content: Handle runtime errors gracefully by catching specific exceptions and isolating the happy path with else.

blocks.text: Always catch specific exception types (never bare except:) so bugs are not silently swallowed. Code in else runs only when try succeeds, while finally always executes for cleanup.

insights.title: 26. Raising Exceptions & Custom Exception Classes
insights.content: Signal domain-specific failures clearly by raising built-in or custom subclasses of Exception.

blocks.text: Inherit from Exception (never BaseException) and use 'raise NewError(...) from original_exc' when wrapping lower-level exceptions so the full traceback cause is preserved.

insights.title: 27. File I/O with open() and Context Managers
insights.content: Always open files using a with statement and explicit UTF-8 encoding so handles close deterministically.

blocks.text: The with block guarantees the file descriptor is flushed and closed even if an exception occurs. Specify encoding='utf-8' to avoid OS-dependent default encodings.

blocks.code:
from pathlib import Path

sample = Path("/tmp/py_note.txt")
with open(sample, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("Line 1\nLine 2\n")

with open(sample, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    lines = [line.strip() for line in f]
print(lines)

insights.title: 28. Serializing & Parsing JSON Data
insights.content: Use the built-in json module to convert between Python dicts/lists and JSON strings or files.

blocks.text: dumps()/loads() operate on strings, while dump()/load() read and write file objects. Pass ensure_ascii=False when writing non-Latin text such as Arabic so characters remain readable.

blocks.code:
import json

payload = {"name": "أحمد", "skills": ["Python", "Django"]}
encoded = json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
decoded = json.loads(encoded)

print(encoded)
print(decoded["skills"])

insights.title: 29. Reading & Writing CSV Files with DictReader/DictWriter
insights.content: Prefer csv.DictReader and csv.DictWriter over manual string splitting so quoted commas and headers work reliably.

blocks.text: Always pass newline='' when opening CSV files for writing or reading so the csv module manages line endings cleanly across platforms.

blocks.code:
import csv
import io

buf = io.StringIO()
writer = csv.DictWriter(buf, fieldnames=["name", "role"])
writer.writeheader()
writer.writerow({"name": "Ahmed", "role": "Engineer"})

buf.seek(0)
rows = list(csv.DictReader(buf))
print(rows)

insights.title: 30. Modules, Packages & __name__ == '__main__'
insights.content: Organize code into modules and packages, and guard script entry points with if __name__ == '__main__':.

blocks.text: When a module is imported, __name__ equals the module's name; when executed directly, __name__ is '__main__'. Guarding execution prevents side effects during imports or tests.

insights.title: 31. Virtual Environments (venv) & Dependency Isolation
insights.content: Isolate project dependencies per workspace using Python's built-in venv module so packages never conflict globally.

blocks.text: Each virtual environment gets its own python interpreter and site-packages folder. You can inspect active environment paths directly from sys.prefix and sys.executable.

blocks.code:
import sys
import venv
from pathlib import Path

# Creating a venv programmatically:
# venv.create(Path(".venv"), with_pip=True)
in_venv = sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix
print(f"Executable: {sys.executable}")
print(f"Inside virtualenv: {in_venv}")

insights.title: 32. Identity (is) vs Equality (==)
insights.content: == compares object values, whereas 'is' compares memory identity (whether two names reference the exact same object).

blocks.text: Never use 'is' to compare strings or numbers because small-integer/string interning can hide bugs. Reserve 'is' strictly for singletons like None, True, False, or sentinel objects.

blocks.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
c = a

print("a == b:", a == b)
print("a is b:", a is b)
print("a is c:", a is c)
print("None check:", None is None)

insights.title: 33. Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy
insights.content: A shallow copy duplicates only the outer container, while copy.deepcopy() recursively clones nested mutable objects.

blocks.text: List slicing [:] and .copy() create shallow copies, meaning inner lists or dicts are still shared between the original and the copy. Use copy.deepcopy() for nested structures.

blocks.code:
import copy

original = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = original.copy()
deep = copy.deepcopy(original)

original[0].append(99)
print("shallow:", shallow)
print("deep:", deep)

insights.title: 34. Modern Filesystem Paths with pathlib
insights.content: Use pathlib.Path for object-oriented, cross-platform path joining, file reading, and globbing.

blocks.text: The / operator joins path segments cleanly regardless of OS separators. Path also provides .read_text(), .write_text(), .mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True), and .rglob().

blocks.code:
from pathlib import Path

base = Path("/tmp/demo_pkg")
base.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
cfg = base / "config.txt"
cfg.write_text("debug=true\n", encoding="utf-8")

print(cfg.name, cfg.suffix, cfg.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip())

insights.title: 35. Timezone-Aware Dates with datetime & zoneinfo
insights.content: Always store and compute timestamps as timezone-aware datetimes using UTC and zoneinfo.

blocks.text: Naive datetimes lack timezone context and cause subtle DST and API bugs. Python 3.9+ includes zoneinfo.ZoneInfo in the standard library for IANA timezones.

blocks.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

now_utc = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
cairo_now = now_utc.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Africa/Cairo"))
print("UTC:", now_utc.isoformat())
print("Cairo:", cairo_now.isoformat())

insights.title: 36. Iterators & the Iterator Protocol (__iter__, __next__)
insights.content: Any object implementing __iter__ and __next__ can be traversed lazily one element at a time.

blocks.text: An iterable returns an iterator from __iter__(), while an iterator produces items via __next__() and raises StopIteration when exhausted. Iterators are single-pass.

insights.title: 37. Generators & the yield Keyword
insights.content: Generator functions suspend execution at each yield, preserving local state with minimal memory overhead.

blocks.text: Calling a generator function returns a generator iterator without running its body immediately. Each next() resumes execution right after the previous yield.

insights.title: 38. Generator Expressions & Memory Efficiency
insights.content: Generator expressions produce values on demand using parenthesis syntax, avoiding full list allocation.

blocks.text: Unlike list comprehensions [x for x in ...], (x for x in ...) computes one item at a time. Pass them directly into sum(), max(), any(), or streaming pipelines.

blocks.code:
import sys

list_comp = [x * 2 for x in range(10_000)]
gen_expr = (x * 2 for x in range(10_000))

print("List bytes:", sys.getsizeof(list_comp))
print("Gen bytes:", sys.getsizeof(gen_expr))
print("Sum:", sum(gen_expr))

insights.title: 39. yield from & Composable Generator Pipelines
insights.content: Delegate iteration cleanly to sub-generators with yield from and chain streaming stages without intermediate lists.

blocks.text: yield from sub_iterable forwards yielded values directly and reduces boilerplate nested loops, making recursive tree traversals and streaming ETL pipelines clean.

insights.title: 40. Closures & the nonlocal Keyword
insights.content: A closure retains access to variables from an enclosing function scope even after the outer function returns.

blocks.text: Use nonlocal when an inner function needs to rebind (mutate) a variable defined in the enclosing function rather than creating a new local variable.

blocks.code:
def make_counter(start: int = 0):
    count = start
    def increment(step: int = 1) -> int:
        nonlocal count
        count += step
        return count
    return increment

counter = make_counter(10)
print(counter(), counter(5))

insights.title: 41. Function Decorators & functools.wraps
insights.content: Decorators wrap functions to add cross-cutting behavior like timing, caching, or auth checks without altering their core logic.

blocks.text: Always decorate the inner wrapper with @functools.wraps(func) so the original function's __name__, __doc__, and annotations are preserved for debugging and introspection.

insights.title: 42. Parameterized Decorators (Decorator Factories)
insights.content: Accept configuration arguments in a decorator by adding an outer factory function that returns the actual decorator.

blocks.text: A decorator factory is a three-level function: factory(options) -> decorator(func) -> wrapper(*args, **kwargs). This pattern powers retry, rate-limit, and permission decorators.

insights.title: 43. Stacking Decorators & Class Decorators
insights.content: Stacked decorators apply bottom-up at definition time, and decorators can also transform entire classes.

blocks.text: With @dec_a above @dec_b above def f, Python executes dec_a(dec_b(f)). Class decorators receive a class object and return a modified or wrapped class.

insights.title: 44. Context Managers with __enter__ & __exit__
insights.content: Implement the context manager protocol to guarantee resource setup and teardown around a with block.

blocks.text: __enter__ returns the bound resource (as ...), while __exit__(exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) runs on block exit. Returning True from __exit__ suppresses the raised exception.

blocks.code:
class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        import time
        self.start = time.perf_counter()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        import time
        self.elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start
        return False  # Do not suppress exceptions

with Timer() as t:
    sum(range(50_000))
print(f"Elapsed: {t.elapsed:.6f}s")

insights.title: 45. contextlib.contextmanager & ExitStack
insights.content: Write lightweight context managers as generator functions with @contextmanager and manage dynamic contexts with ExitStack.

blocks.text: In a @contextmanager generator, code before yield acts as __enter__, and code in a finally block after yield acts as __exit__. ExitStack cleanly enters a variable number of resources.

blocks.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager, ExitStack

@contextmanager
def managed_tag(name: str):
    print(f"<{name}>")
    try:
        yield name
    finally:
        print(f"</{name}>")

with ExitStack() as stack:
    stack.enter_context(managed_tag("body"))
    stack.enter_context(managed_tag("p"))
    print("Hello")

insights.title: 46. Classes, __init__ & Class vs Instance Attributes
insights.content: Class attributes are shared across all instances, whereas instance attributes belong to each object's own __dict__.

blocks.text: Assigning to self.attr creates an instance attribute, while mutating a mutable class attribute (like a list) affects every instance. Keep per-instance state inside __init__.

blocks.code:
class User:
    role = "member"  # Class attribute

    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name  # Instance attribute

u1 = User("Ahmed")
u2 = User("Sara")
u1.role = "admin"  # Shadows only on u1
print(u1.role, u2.role, User.role)

insights.title: 47. @classmethod vs @staticmethod
insights.content: @classmethod receives the class (cls) for alternative constructors, while @staticmethod is a namespaced utility function.

blocks.text: Because @classmethod binds cls dynamically, subclasses inherit factory constructors cleanly. @staticmethod receives neither self nor cls and behaves like a plain function grouped on the class.

insights.title: 48. Managed Attributes with @property
insights.content: Use @property to expose computed or validated attributes with clean attribute-access syntax.

blocks.text: You can start with a public attribute and later refactor it into a @property with a @attr.setter without breaking callers who access obj.attr directly.

insights.title: 49. Inheritance, super() & Method Resolution Order (MRO)
insights.content: super() delegates method calls cooperatively along the class's C3 linearized Method Resolution Order (__mro__).

blocks.text: Always call super() rather than hardcoding ParentClass.method(self) so cooperative multiple inheritance and mixins resolve each ancestor once in the exact MRO order.

insights.title: 50. Multiple Inheritance & Mixin Design
insights.content: Mixins are small, focused classes that inject reusable capabilities into other classes via cooperative inheritance.

blocks.text: A good mixin is stateless (or relies on super().__init__), implements a narrow behavior like JSON serialization or timestamps, and is placed before the base class in the inheritance list.

insights.title: 51. Dunder Methods: __repr__, __str__ & Comparisons
insights.content: Implement __repr__ for unambiguous developer representations, __str__ for display, and __eq__/__lt__ for comparisons.

blocks.text: __repr__ should ideally look like a valid constructor call and acts as a fallback if __str__ is missing. Combining @functools.total_ordering with __eq__ and __lt__ auto-generates <=, >, >=.

insights.title: 52. Container Dunder Methods: __len__, __getitem__, __contains__
insights.content: Make custom objects behave like native Python sequences by implementing container dunder methods.

blocks.text: Implementing __len__ and __getitem__ (including slice handling) gives your class indexing, len(), iteration, and 'in' support automatically—and __contains__ lets you optimize membership checks.

insights.title: 53. Callable Objects with __call__
insights.content: Defining __call__ allows class instances to be invoked like functions while keeping stateful attributes.

blocks.text: Callable instances are ideal for stateful callbacks, strategy objects, or class-based decorators where configuration and history need to live on self.

insights.title: 54. Dataclasses, field(default_factory) & frozen=True
insights.content: @dataclass eliminates boilerplate __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ methods for data-holding classes.

blocks.text: Use field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults, frozen=True for immutable hashable value objects, and slots=True (Python 3.10+) to save memory.

blocks.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class OrderItem:
    sku: str
    qty: int = 1
    tags: tuple[str, ...] = field(default_factory=tuple)

item = OrderItem("BOOK-1", 2, ("tech",))
print(item)

insights.title: 55. Enumerations with Enum, IntEnum & StrEnum
insights.content: Replace magic strings and numbers with Enum subclasses for self-documenting, type-safe constants.

blocks.text: StrEnum (Python 3.11+) combines string interoperability with strict enum membership, making it great for status fields, API choices, and Django/JSON serialization.

blocks.code:
from enum import StrEnum, auto

class JobStatus(StrEnum):
    PENDING = auto()
    RUNNING = auto()
    DONE = auto()

status = JobStatus.RUNNING
print(status, status == "running", list(JobStatus))

insights.title: 56. NamedTuple & TypedDict for Structured Records
insights.content: Use typing.NamedTuple for lightweight immutable tuples with field names, and TypedDict for typed JSON-like dicts.

blocks.text: TypedDict carries zero runtime overhead—at runtime it is a normal dict—while letting static type checkers (mypy/pyright) verify dictionary keys and value types.

insights.title: 57. Type Hints, Union (|) & Callable Annotations
insights.content: Modern Python uses built-in generic syntax (list[str], dict[str, int]) and X | Y unions for static safety.

blocks.text: Type annotations are not enforced at runtime by Python itself, but tools like mypy, pyright, and IDEs catch type mismatches early and improve code readability.

insights.title: 58. Regular Expressions with the re Module
insights.content: Use raw strings (r'...') and compiled patterns with re for validating, extracting, and substituting text.

blocks.text: Named capture groups (?P<name>...) make complex regex matches self-documenting, and re.compile() avoids re-parsing the pattern in hot loops.

blocks.code:
import re

PATTERN = re.compile(r"^(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<month>\d{2})-(?P<day>\d{2})$")
match = PATTERN.match("2026-11-19")
if match:
    print(match.groupdict())

insights.title: 59. collections: Counter, defaultdict & deque
insights.content: Leverage Counter for frequency counting, defaultdict for auto-initialized buckets, and deque for O(1) ends.

blocks.text: Unlike list.pop(0) which is O(n), collections.deque supports O(1) appendleft and popleft, making it ideal for queues and sliding windows.

blocks.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque

counts = Counter("mississippi")
grouped = defaultdict(list)
for k, v in [("a", 1), ("a", 2), ("b", 3)]:
    grouped[k].append(v)

q = deque(["t1", "t2"], maxlen=3)
q.appendleft("t0")
print(counts.most_common(2), dict(grouped), list(q))

insights.title: 60. Priority Queues & Top-K Selection with heapq
insights.content: heapq turns a regular Python list into a min-heap in O(n) with O(log n) push and pop.

blocks.text: Use heapq.heappush/heappop for priority scheduling and heapq.nlargest/nsmallest for top-K queries without sorting the entire dataset.

blocks.code:
import heapq

jobs = [(3, "email"), (1, "backup"), (2, "index")]
heapq.heapify(jobs)

while jobs:
    priority, task = heapq.heappop(jobs)
    print(priority, task)

insights.title: 61. Binary Search & Sorted Insertion with bisect
insights.content: Search and maintain sorted sequences in O(log n) time using the standard library bisect module.

blocks.text: bisect_left returns the first insertion index keeping sort order, and insort inserts directly. Great for score brackets, rate-limit windows, and time-series lookups.

blocks.code:
import bisect

breakpoints = [60, 70, 80, 90]
grades = ["F", "D", "C", "B", "A"]

def grade(score: int) -> str:
    return grades[bisect.bisect_right(breakpoints, score)]

print([grade(s) for s in (55, 70, 89, 95)])

insights.title: 62. functools: partial, lru_cache & singledispatch
insights.content: functools provides memoization (@lru_cache/@cache), partial function application, and type-based dispatch.

blocks.text: @lru_cache caches pure function results by arguments, partial freezes leading arguments, and @singledispatch enables clean function overloading by the first argument's type.

insights.title: 63. Lazy Iteration Combinators with itertools
insights.content: itertools offers fast C-implemented building blocks like chain, islice, batched, groupby, and product.

blocks.text: Use itertools.islice to slice generators without converting them to lists, and remember itertools.groupby requires the input to be pre-sorted by the grouping key.

blocks.code:
import itertools

merged = list(itertools.chain([1, 2], [3, 4]))
first_three = list(itertools.islice(itertools.count(10, 5), 3))
pairs = list(itertools.product(["A", "B"], [1, 2]))

print(merged, first_three, pairs)

insights.title: 64. Structured Application Logging with logging
insights.content: Replace print() debugging with the logging module for configurable severity levels, formatters, and handlers.

blocks.text: Create module-level loggers via logging.getLogger(__name__) and use lazy %-formatting (logger.info('User %s', uid)) so string formatting is skipped if the log level is disabled.

blocks.code:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s",
)
logger = logging.getLogger("app.billing")
logger.info("Processed invoice %s for $%.2f", "INV-101", 49.5)

insights.title: 65. Unit Testing with unittest & unittest.mock
insights.content: Write automated tests with unittest.TestCase and isolate external dependencies using patch and MagicMock.

blocks.text: Mocking replaces slow or non-deterministic boundaries (HTTP APIs, clocks, email senders) so unit tests stay fast, deterministic, and isolated.

insights.title: 66. Building CLI Tools with argparse
insights.content: argparse parses positional arguments, flags, types, defaults, and generates --help documentation automatically.

blocks.text: Support subcommands via add_subparsers() and pass argv explicitly to parse_args(argv) when writing testable CLI entry points.

blocks.code:
import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Export records")
parser.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=10)
parser.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")

args = parser.parse_args(["--limit", "25", "--dry-run"])
print(args.limit, args.dry_run)

insights.title: 67. Running External Commands Safely with subprocess
insights.content: Execute external processes using subprocess.run() with an argument list and check=True rather than shell=True.

blocks.text: Passing an explicit list of arguments avoids shell injection vulnerabilities. Set capture_output=True, text=True, and timeout=... to handle output and hung commands safely.

blocks.code:
import subprocess
import sys

res = subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "-c", "print('hello from child')"],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
    check=True,
    timeout=5,
)
print(res.stdout.strip())

insights.title: 68. Cryptographic Hashing & Tokens with hashlib & secrets
insights.content: Use hashlib for SHA-256 digests and secrets (never random) for API keys, CSRF tokens, and password reset links.

blocks.text: The random module uses a predictable Mersenne Twister PRNG and is unsafe for security. secrets uses the OS CSPRNG, and secrets.compare_digest prevents timing attacks.

blocks.code:
import hashlib
import secrets

token = secrets.token_urlsafe(24)
digest = hashlib.sha256(token.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
print("Token:", token)
print("SHA-256:", digest)
print("Equal:", secrets.compare_digest(digest, digest))

insights.title: 69. Binary Protocols with struct & memoryview
insights.content: Pack and unpack fixed-width binary frames with struct, and slice byte buffers without copying via memoryview.

blocks.text: Network headers and binary file formats require explicit endianness (like '!IH' for network big-endian unsigned int + short). memoryview avoids allocating new bytes objects on slices.

blocks.code:
import struct

packet = struct.pack("!IH", 1024, 200)
view = memoryview(packet)
msg_id, status = struct.unpack("!IH", view)
print(packet.hex(), msg_id, status)

insights.title: 70. Modern Python Packaging with pyproject.toml
insights.content: pyproject.toml (PEP 517/518/621) is the single declarative standard for build metadata, dependencies, and tool config.

blocks.text: It replaces legacy setup.py scripts with static metadata for package name, version, dependencies, console_scripts entry points, and linter/formatter settings.

blocks.code:
import tomllib

pyproject_sample = """
[project]
name = "my-service"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["django>=5.0"]
"""
data = tomllib.loads(pyproject_sample)
print(data["project"]["name"], data["project"]["dependencies"])

insights.title: 71. Structural Pattern Matching (match / case)
insights.content: Introduced in Python 3.10, match/case destructures sequences, mappings, and class attributes with optional guard clauses.

blocks.text: Unlike a simple C-style switch, structural pattern matching binds variables from nested shapes, checks type structure, and evaluates 'if' guards before matching a branch.

blocks.code:
def handle_event(event: dict) -> str:
    match event:
        case {"type": "click", "x": x, "y": y} if x >= 0 and y >= 0:
            return f"Click at ({x}, {y})"
        case {"type": "key", "code": code}:
            return f"Key pressed: {code}"
        case _:
            return "Unknown event"

print(handle_event({"type": "click", "x": 12, "y": 40}))

insights.title: 72. Structural Subtyping (Static Duck Typing) with Protocol
insights.content: typing.Protocol defines interfaces by behavior rather than inheritance, enabling decoupled architecture.

blocks.text: Any class implementing the required methods/attributes satisfies the Protocol automatically without inheriting from it. Add @runtime_checkable only if isinstance() checks are needed.

insights.title: 73. Generic Classes & PEP 695 Type Parameter Syntax
insights.content: Write type-safe reusable containers and repositories using PEP 695 generic brackets [T] (or TypeVar).

blocks.text: Python 3.12 introduced concise generic syntax like class Repository[T]: and def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T, removing verbose TypeVar boilerplate.

insights.title: 74. Typing Decorators Accurately with ParamSpec
insights.content: ParamSpec preserves the exact parameter types and return type of wrapped functions in typed decorators.

blocks.text: Without ParamSpec, typing a decorator with Callable[..., Any] loses IDE autocomplete and argument validation for the decorated function.

insights.title: 75. Descriptors: __get__, __set__ & __set_name__
insights.content: Descriptors power Python's @property, methods, and Django's model fields by intercepting attribute access.

blocks.text: A data descriptor implements both __get__ and __set__, taking precedence over instance __dict__. __set_name__ automatically captures the attribute name on class creation.

insights.title: 76. Memory & Attribute Optimization with __slots__
insights.content: Declaring __slots__ replaces per-instance __dict__ hash tables with fixed compact attribute slots.

blocks.text: For classes instantiated millions of times, __slots__ dramatically cuts memory usage and speeds up attribute lookups, at the cost of disallowing arbitrary dynamic attributes.

blocks.code:
class CompactPoint:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")

    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p = CompactPoint(1.5, 2.5)
print(p.x, p.y, hasattr(p, "__dict__"))

insights.title: 77. Dynamic Attributes: __getattr__ vs __getattribute__
insights.content: __getattr__ runs only when normal attribute lookup fails, whereas __getattribute__ intercepts every lookup.

blocks.text: Always delegate via super().__getattribute__(name) inside __getattribute__ to avoid infinite recursion. Prefer __getattr__ for lazy proxies or dynamic attribute forwarding.

insights.title: 78. Customizing Class Creation with __init_subclass__
insights.content: __init_subclass__ provides a clean, lightweight hook to validate or register subclasses without a metaclass.

blocks.text: Introduced in PEP 487, __init_subclass__ runs automatically whenever a class inherits from your base class—ideal for plugin registries and enforcing class attributes.

insights.title: 79. Metaclasses & Dynamic Class Creation with type()
insights.content: A metaclass is a class whose instances are classes themselves, controlling class construction via __new__ and __init__.

blocks.text: Django's ORM ModelBase uses a metaclass to convert declarative Field attributes into _meta columns. Use metaclasses only when __init_subclass__ or class decorators are insufficient.

insights.title: 80. Abstract Base Classes with abc.ABC
insights.content: Enforce explicit interface contracts at instantiation time using abc.ABC and @abstractmethod.

blocks.text: Unlike Protocol (which is structural and checked statically), inheriting from ABC prevents instantiating subclasses that forget to implement abstract methods.

insights.title: 81. Weak References & WeakValueDictionary with weakref
insights.content: weakref lets caches and observer registries reference objects without preventing garbage collection.

blocks.text: A strong reference keeps an object alive in memory. WeakValueDictionary automatically drops entries once no strong references to the value remain.

blocks.code:
import weakref

class Session:
    def __init__(self, sid: str):
        self.sid = sid

cache: weakref.WeakValueDictionary[str, Session] = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
s = Session("abc")
cache["abc"] = s
print("Cached:", "abc" in cache)

del s
print("After del:", "abc" in cache)

insights.title: 82. Reference Counting & Cyclic Garbage Collection
insights.content: CPython reclaims memory immediately via reference counting and uses the cyclic gc module to break reference cycles.

blocks.text: When two objects reference each other, their refcounts never drop to zero on their own; CPython's generational garbage collector periodically detects and collects unreachable cycles.

blocks.code:
import gc
import sys

obj = []
print("Initial refcount:", sys.getrefcount(obj) - 1)

a, b = [], []
a.append(b)
b.append(a)
del a, b
collected = gc.collect()
print("Cycle objects collected:", collected)

insights.title: 83. The GIL: Choosing Threads vs Processes vs Asyncio
insights.content: CPython's Global Interpreter Lock serializes Python bytecode execution per process, guiding concurrency choices.

blocks.text: Use asyncio or ThreadPoolExecutor for I/O-bound workloads (network, DB, files, where the GIL is released during I/O), and ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU-bound work.

blocks.code:
import os

def concurrency_advisor(workload: str) -> str:
    match workload:
        case "high-concurrency-io":
            return "asyncio"
        case "blocking-io":
            return "ThreadPoolExecutor"
        case "cpu-heavy":
            return f"ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers={os.cpu_count()})"
        case _:
            return "sequential"

print(concurrency_advisor("cpu-heavy"))

insights.title: 84. ThreadPoolExecutor & Thread Synchronization with Lock
insights.content: Run blocking I/O tasks concurrently with ThreadPoolExecutor and protect shared mutable state using threading.Lock.

blocks.text: Even with the GIL, compound operations like counter += 1 are not atomic across bytecode instructions. Always wrap shared mutations in 'with lock:'.

blocks.code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import threading

lock = threading.Lock()
total = 0

def add_chunk(n: int) -> None:
    global total
    with lock:
        total += n

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    pool.map(add_chunk, [10, 20, 30, 40])

print("Total:", total)

insights.title: 85. True CPU Parallelism with ProcessPoolExecutor
insights.content: Bypass the GIL for CPU-bound computations by distributing work across OS processes with ProcessPoolExecutor.

blocks.text: Worker functions and arguments must be picklable, and entry points must sit behind if __name__ == '__main__': to avoid recursive process spawning on spawn-based platforms.

insights.title: 86. Inter-Process Communication with Queue & SharedMemory
insights.content: Coordinate producer-consumer pipelines across processes with multiprocessing.Queue or zero-copy SharedMemory.

blocks.text: Queues serialize messages safely across process boundaries, while multiprocessing.shared_memory exposes a raw memory block for large numeric buffers without pickling overhead.

blocks.code:
from multiprocessing import shared_memory

shm = shared_memory.SharedMemory(create=True, size=16)
try:
    shm.buf[:5] = b"hello"
    print(bytes(shm.buf[:5]).decode())
finally:
    shm.close()
    shm.unlink()

insights.title: 87. asyncio Basics: Coroutines, await & Event Loop
insights.content: Asyncio achieves high-concurrency single-threaded I/O by yielding control to an event loop at await points.

blocks.text: Calling an async def function creates a coroutine object; awaiting it suspends only the current task while the event loop runs other ready tasks.

blocks.code:
import asyncio

async def fetch_item(item_id: int) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return f"item-{item_id}"

async def main():
    result = await fetch_item(7)
    print(result)

asyncio.run(main())

insights.title: 88. Concurrent Tasks: create_task, gather & wait_for
insights.content: Schedule coroutines concurrently on the event loop using create_task/gather and enforce deadlines with asyncio.timeout.

blocks.text: Sequentially awaiting coroutines runs them one by one; scheduling them as tasks or passing them to gather() overlaps their I/O wait time.

blocks.code:
import asyncio

async def fetch(name: str, delay: float) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return name

async def main():
    async with asyncio.timeout(1.0):
        results = await asyncio.gather(fetch("users", 0.02), fetch("orders", 0.01))
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())

insights.title: 89. Structured Concurrency with asyncio.TaskGroup
insights.content: asyncio.TaskGroup (Python 3.11+) guarantees all child tasks finish or are cancelled cleanly if one fails.

blocks.text: Unlike fire-and-forget tasks or gather(), TaskGroup scopes task lifetimes to an async with block and raises an ExceptionGroup if any task fails.

blocks.code:
import asyncio

async def job(n: int) -> int:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return n * 10

async def main():
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        t1 = tg.create_task(job(1))
        t2 = tg.create_task(job(2))
    print(t1.result(), t2.result())

asyncio.run(main())

insights.title: 90. Async Generators, Async Context Managers & Semaphores
insights.content: Stream asynchronous data with async for, manage async resources with async with, and bound concurrency via Semaphore.

blocks.text: Unbounded asyncio.gather over thousands of URLs can exhaust sockets; wrapping calls with an asyncio.Semaphore caps simultaneous in-flight requests cleanly.

blocks.code:
import asyncio

async def stream_ids(n: int):
    for i in range(n):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.005)
        yield i

async def main():
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(2)
    async def bounded(i: int):
        async with sem:
            return i * 2

    items = [i async for i in stream_ids(4)]
    out = await asyncio.gather(*(bounded(i) for i in items))
    print(out)

asyncio.run(main())

insights.title: 91. Task-Safe Context State with contextvars
insights.content: contextvars provides per-task and per-thread isolated context variables—the async replacement for threading.local.

blocks.text: Essential in async web frameworks like Django ASGI and FastAPI for propagating request IDs, current users, or trace spans across await boundaries without leaking between requests.

blocks.code:
import asyncio
import contextvars

request_id: contextvars.ContextVar[str] = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id", default="-")

async def handle(rid: str):
    token = request_id.set(rid)
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        print("Handled:", request_id.get())
    finally:
        request_id.reset(token)

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(handle("req-1"), handle("req-2"))

asyncio.run(main())

insights.title: 92. Dynamic Imports & Plugin Loading with importlib
insights.content: Load modules dynamically from dotted string paths at runtime using importlib.import_module().

blocks.text: Django uses this exact mechanism to resolve middleware, storage backends, and settings strings like 'myapp.backends.CustomAuth'.

blocks.code:
import importlib

def load_symbol(dotted_path: str):
    module_path, attr_name = dotted_path.rsplit(".", 1)
    module = importlib.import_module(module_path)
    return getattr(module, attr_name)

sqrt_fn = load_symbol("math.sqrt")
print(sqrt_fn(81))

insights.title: 93. Safe Expression Parsing & Code Analysis with ast
insights.content: Parse Python source into an Abstract Syntax Tree using ast, and evaluate literal expressions safely with ast.literal_eval().

blocks.text: Never run eval() on untrusted strings. ast.literal_eval() parses only literals (strings, numbers, tuples, lists, dicts, booleans, None), while ast.walk() powers linters and static analyzers.

blocks.code:
import ast

safe_data = ast.literal_eval("{'env': 'prod', 'workers': 4}")
tree = ast.parse("def add(x, y): return x + y")
funcs = [n.name for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef)]

print(safe_data, funcs)

insights.title: 94. Inspecting CPython Bytecode with dis
insights.content: Use the dis module to disassemble Python functions into CPython virtual machine instructions.

blocks.text: Inspecting bytecode reveals why local variable lookups (LOAD_FAST) beat globals (LOAD_GLOBAL), why list comprehensions avoid repeated method lookups, and how operators compile.

blocks.code:
import dis

def square_sum(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a * a + b * b

dis.dis(square_sum)

insights.title: 95. Profiling & Micro-Benchmarking with cProfile & timeit
insights.content: Measure execution hotspots accurately with cProfile/pstats and benchmark small snippets with timeit.

blocks.text: Never optimize by guessing—profile realistic workloads first to locate the few functions consuming most cumulative time.

blocks.code:
import cProfile
import pstats
import timeit

duration = timeit.timeit("sum(range(1000))", number=1000)
print(f"timeit: {duration:.4f}s")

profiler = cProfile.Profile()
profiler.enable()
_ = sorted(range(5000, 0, -1))
profiler.disable()
pstats.Stats(profiler).sort_stats("tottime").print_stats(3)

insights.title: 96. Tracking Memory Allocations & Leaks with tracemalloc
insights.content: Use tracemalloc to capture heap snapshots and pinpoint exact file/line locations allocating the most memory.

blocks.text: Comparing two snapshots with snapshot2.compare_to(snapshot1, 'lineno') reveals growing allocations across requests or batch iterations.

blocks.code:
import tracemalloc

tracemalloc.start()
snap1 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
data = [list(range(100)) for _ in range(500)]
snap2 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()

for stat in snap2.compare_to(snap1, "lineno")[:2]:
    print(stat)
tracemalloc.stop()

insights.title: 97. Metaclasses vs __init_subclass__ vs Class Decorators
insights.content: Choose the simplest class-customization hook: class decorators or __init_subclass__ before reaching for metaclasses.

blocks.text: Class decorators mutate or wrap a single class; __init_subclass__ propagates automatically to subclasses; metaclasses are reserved for altering class creation namespaces or type-level behavior.

insights.title: 98. Operator Overloading & Returning NotImplemented
insights.content: Implement arithmetic dunder methods like __add__ and __radd__, returning NotImplemented for unsupported operand types.

blocks.text: Returning NotImplemented (never raising TypeError directly) tells Python to try the other operand's reflected method (__radd__) before failing cleanly.

insights.title: 99. Walrus Operator (:=) & Positional-Only (/) Parameters
insights.content: Bind intermediate values inline with := and separate positional-only (/) from keyword-only (*) parameters.

blocks.text: The assignment expression (:=) prevents calling expensive functions twice in if/while/comprehension filters. Using '/' prevents callers from coupling to internal parameter names.

insights.title: 100. Designing Pythonic, Fail-Safe & Type-Checked APIs
insights.content: Combine small protocols, immutable dataclasses, keyword-only options, and explicit domain exceptions for resilient APIs.

blocks.text: Great Python libraries accept broad input types (Iterable, Mapping, PathLike), return predictable immutable structures, validate invariants early, and stay friendly to both runtime and static type checkers.

interviewQuestions.title: What is the GIL in CPython, and does it make Python code thread-safe?
interviewQuestions.content: The GIL is a mutex allowing only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time per interpreter; it protects CPython internals, not user-level compound operations.

blocks.text:
• What the GIL is: A global mutex in CPython that serializes execution of Python bytecode so reference counting and internal C structures remain consistent.
• Why it does NOT guarantee thread safety: Even a single Python line like `x += 1` compiles to multiple bytecodes (`LOAD_FAST`, `LOAD_CONST`, `BINARY_OP`, `STORE_FAST`). CPython can switch threads between bytecode instructions (every ~5ms via `sys.getswitchinterval()`).
• Fix: Always protect shared mutable state with `threading.Lock` or `RLock`.

blocks.code:
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def safe_increment():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        with lock:  # Without this lock, race conditions corrupt counter
            counter += 1

interviewQuestions.title: How does the GIL affect I/O-bound vs CPU-bound workloads?
interviewQuestions.content: Threads speed up I/O-bound tasks because the GIL is released during blocking I/O, whereas CPU-bound tasks suffer lock contention and need multiprocessing or C extensions.

blocks.text:
• I/O-bound tasks (HTTP calls, DB queries, disk I/O): CPython releases the GIL while waiting on OS syscalls, so `threading` or `asyncio` achieves high concurrency.
• CPU-bound tasks (image processing, crypto, heavy loops): Threads contend for the GIL on a single core and can be slower than single-threaded code due to context-switching overhead.
• Solution for CPU-bound work: Use `multiprocessing` / `ProcessPoolExecutor`, C/Rust extensions (NumPy releases the GIL), or Python 3.12+ subinterpreters.

blocks.code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor

# I/O-bound: threads release GIL during network wait
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as pool:
    responses = list(pool.map(fetch_url, urls))

# CPU-bound: separate processes bypass the GIL
with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
    hashes = list(pool.map(compute_heavy_hash, payloads))

interviewQuestions.title: Explain Per-Interpreter GIL (PEP 684) and Free-Threaded Python (PEP 703) in Python 3.12+
interviewQuestions.content: Python 3.12 introduced a per-interpreter GIL allowing multi-core subinterpreters in one process, while Python 3.13 introduced an experimental no-GIL free-threaded build.

blocks.text:
• PEP 684 (Python 3.12): Moves GIL state from a global process variable to each subinterpreter (`PyInterpreterState`). Multiple isolated interpreters in a single process can execute Python bytecode truly in parallel across CPU cores.
• PEP 734 (Python 3.13): Exposes `concurrent.interpreters` / `interpreters` in stdlib for lightweight isolated concurrency without full OS process cloning.
• PEP 703 (Python 3.13+): Experimental `--disable-gil` (`python3.13t`) free-threaded build using biased reference counting, mimalloc, and critical sections so standard `threading` scales across cores.

blocks.code:
import sys

# Check if running on a free-threaded build (Python 3.13+)
if hasattr(sys, '_is_gil_enabled'):
    print('GIL enabled:', sys._is_gil_enabled())

interviewQuestions.title: How does CPython memory management work? (Reference Counting + Cyclic GC)
interviewQuestions.content: CPython combines immediate reference counting for deterministic deallocation with a generational cyclic garbage collector to reclaim reference cycles.

blocks.text:
• Primary mechanism — Reference Counting: Every `PyObject` holds `ob_refcnt`. When references drop to 0, memory is freed immediately (deterministic destruction).
• Limitation: Reference cycles (e.g., `a.ref = b; b.ref = a`) never reach refcount 0 on their own.
• Secondary mechanism — Cyclic GC (`gc` module): Tracks container objects (`list`, `dict`, `tuple`, user instances) across 3 generations (0, 1, 2). Periodically runs mark-and-sweep reachability checks to collect unreachable cycles.
• Allocation layer: CPython uses `pymalloc` (arenas -> pools -> blocks) for small objects <= 512 bytes to reduce OS `malloc` overhead.

blocks.code:
import gc, sys

a = []
b = [a]
a.append(b)  # Reference cycle
print(sys.getrefcount(a))  # Includes temporary arg reference

del a, b
collected = gc.collect()  # Cyclic GC breaks and frees the cycle
print('Collected objects:', collected)

interviewQuestions.title: How can memory leaks happen in Python, and when do you use `weakref`?
interviewQuestions.content: Memory leaks in Python occur from unintended lingering references (global caches, closures, unclosed resources); `weakref` references objects without incrementing refcount.

blocks.text:
• Common leak sources: Unbounded global dicts/caches, class-level lists, closures capturing large objects, registered callbacks/observers never unregistered, and C extensions leaking `Py_INCREF`.
• `weakref` solution: Creates a weak reference that does NOT increase `ob_refcnt`. When all strong references disappear, the object is garbage collected even if weakrefs remain.
• Built-in helpers: `weakref.WeakValueDictionary`, `WeakKeyDictionary`, and `WeakSet` are ideal for caches and observer registries.

blocks.code:
import weakref

class HeavyResource:
    pass

cache = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
res = HeavyResource()
cache['item'] = res
print('In cache:', 'item' in cache)  # True

del res  # Last strong reference gone -> entry auto-evicted
print('In cache:', 'item' in cache)  # False

interviewQuestions.title: What does `__slots__` do, and what are its trade-offs?
interviewQuestions.content: `__slots__` replaces each instance's dynamic `__dict__` with a fixed C-level descriptor array, saving memory and speeding up attribute lookup.

blocks.text:
• Default behavior: Every Python object gets a per-instance `__dict__` hash table, consuming significant RAM when instantiating millions of objects.
• With `__slots__`: CPython reserves fixed pointer slots directly in the object struct—no `__dict__` or `__weakref__` unless explicitly included.
• Trade-offs: Cannot dynamically attach unlisted attributes (`AttributeError`), `weakref` fails unless `'__weakref__'` is in `__slots__`, and subclassing without redefining `__slots__` re-introduces `__dict__`.

blocks.code:
class Point:
    __slots__ = ('x', 'y')
    def __init__(self, x: float, y: float):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p = Point(1.0, 2.0)
# p.z = 3.0  # AttributeError: 'Point' object has no attribute 'z'
# Python 3.10+: @dataclass(slots=True) automates this

interviewQuestions.title: Difference between `is` and `==`, and how does object interning work?
interviewQuestions.content: `==` checks value equality via `__eq__`, whereas `is` checks object identity (`id(a) == id(b)`); CPython caches small ints and certain strings.

blocks.text:
• `==`: Invokes `__eq__` to compare values (e.g., two separate lists `[1, 2] == [1, 2]` is `True`).
• `is`: Compares memory addresses (`id(a) == id(b)`). Always use `is None` / `is not None` for singletons.
• CPython Interning Gotcha: Small integers `[-5, 256]` and compile-time identifier strings are interned (reused), so `a = 256; b = 256; a is b` is `True`, whereas `a = 257; b = 257; a is b` can be `False` at runtime.

blocks.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
print(a == b)  # True (equal values)
print(a is b)  # False (distinct objects in memory)

x = None
if x is None:  # Idiomatic identity check
    pass

interviewQuestions.title: Why are mutable default arguments dangerous in Python, and how do you fix them?
interviewQuestions.content: Default argument expressions are evaluated once when the `def` statement runs, so a mutable default like `[]` or `{}` is shared across all calls.

blocks.text:
• Root cause: Python evaluates default parameter values once at function definition time (`func.__defaults__`), NOT on each invocation.
• Bug: Mutating a default list/dict persists across subsequent calls.
• Fix: Use `None` (or a unique `object()` sentinel if `None` is a valid input) and instantiate a fresh object inside the function body.

interviewQuestions.title: Explain Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy in Python
interviewQuestions.content: A shallow copy duplicates only the outer container (sharing nested mutable references), while `copy.deepcopy` recursively clones all nested objects.

blocks.text:
• Assignment (`b = a`): Creates a new alias pointing to the exact same object.
• Shallow Copy (`a.copy()`, `list(a)`, `a[:]`, `copy.copy(a)`): Allocates a new outer container, but inserts references to the same inner objects. Mutating nested lists/dicts affects both.
• Deep Copy (`copy.deepcopy(a)`): Recursively copies all nested objects and maintains a `memo` dict to handle circular references without infinite recursion.

blocks.code:
import copy

orig = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = copy.copy(orig)
deep = copy.deepcopy(orig)

shallow[0].append(99)
print(orig[0])  # [1, 2, 99] — affected!
print(deep[0])  # [1, 2] — isolated

interviewQuestions.title: How do decorators work, and how do you write a decorator that accepts arguments?
interviewQuestions.content: A decorator wraps a callable to extend behavior; adding arguments requires a 3-layer function factory and `@functools.wraps` to preserve metadata.

blocks.text:
• Mechanism: `@dec` above `def f():` is syntactic sugar for `f = dec(f)` executed at definition time.
• Parameterized decorator: Needs 3 nested functions — (1) outer factory takes decorator arguments, (2) middle decorator takes `func`, (3) inner `wrapper(*args, **kwargs)` runs around `func`.
• `@functools.wraps(func)`: Copies `__name__`, `__doc__`, `__annotations__`, and sets `__wrapped__` so `inspect.signature` and frameworks still see the original function.

interviewQuestions.title: In what order do stacked decorators execute, and how do class-based decorators work?
interviewQuestions.content: Stacked decorators apply bottom-up at definition time and execute top-down at call time; class-based decorators implement `__init__` and `__call__`.

blocks.text:
• Stacking order: `@dec_a` on top of `@dec_b` evaluates as `fn = dec_a(dec_b(fn))`. `dec_b` wraps first, then `dec_a` wraps the result. At call time, `dec_a`'s wrapper runs first, calling into `dec_b`'s wrapper.
• Class-based decorator: Implements `__init__(self, func)` and `__call__(self, *args, **kwargs)`. Note: if decorating instance methods, a class without `__get__` (descriptor protocol) will break `self` binding.

interviewQuestions.title: Explain Closures, `nonlocal`, and the Late Binding Bug in Python Loops
