'Soundness' means that if static analysis determines a variable is non-nullable, it is mathematically guaranteed to never evaluate to `null` at runtime (unlike languages with unsound nullability). Because of this guarantee, the Dart AOT compiler eliminates defensive null checks, reduces generated binary size, and improves runtime performance.

interviewQuestions.title: What is the difference between a nullable type (`?`) and the `late` modifier?
interviewQuestions.content: A nullable type explicitly permits null values, whereas `late` declares a non-nullable variable whose initialization is deferred until before its first read.

blocks.text: Use `?` (e.g., `String?`) when `null` is a valid, expected state that callers must handle. Use `late` when a variable is logically non-nullable, cannot be initialized in the constructor (such as fields initialized in Flutter's `initState` or lazy expensive values), and is guaranteed to be assigned before being read. Reading an uninitialized `late` variable throws a `LateInitializationError` at runtime.

interviewQuestions.title: Explain Dart's null-aware operators (`?.`, `??`, `??=`, `!`, and `...?`).
interviewQuestions.content: Dart provides concise null-aware operators to safely access members, supply fallback values, conditionally assign, assert non-nullability, and spread nullable collections.

blocks.text: `?.` short-circuits member access to `null` if the receiver is `null`. `??` returns the right-hand fallback when the left expression is `null`. `??=` assigns a value only if the variable is currently `null`. `!` (null assertion) casts a nullable expression to non-nullable, throwing a runtime error if `null`. `...?` safely spreads a nullable list or map into a collection literal without throwing.

interviewQuestions.title: Why doesn't Dart automatically promote nullable instance fields after a null check?
interviewQuestions.content: Dart cannot guarantee that an instance getter or mutable field won't return a different value between the null check and its usage, so flow analysis only promotes local variables and private final fields.

blocks.text: In Dart, a class property could be overridden by a custom getter in a subclass or mutated concurrently/via side effects between the `if (obj.prop != null)` check and the subsequent read. Since Dart 3.2, **private `final` fields** (e.g., `_name`) can be promoted if they aren't overridden, because the compiler can verify immutability within the library. For public or mutable fields, assign the value to a local `final` variable first.

interviewQuestions.title: What is the difference between `const` and `final` in Dart?
interviewQuestions.content: `final` variables are assigned once at runtime, while `const` variables must be known at compile time and produce deeply immutable, canonicalized values.

blocks.text: Both `final` and `const` prevent variable reassignment. However, `final` is evaluated at runtime (e.g., `DateTime.now()` or an API response), and if it holds a mutable collection like a `List`, the list's elements can still be modified. `const` requires a compile-time constant expression, makes the entire object graph deeply immutable, and canonicalizes identical instances in memory.

blocks.code:
const pi = 3.14159; // Compile-time constant
final now = DateTime.now(); // Runtime constant

const list1 = [1, 2]; // Deeply immutable
final list2 = [1, 2]; // Reference is final, contents can mutate: list2.add(3)

interviewQuestions.title: How does `const` canonicalization work in Dart and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.content: Dart stores only one canonical instance in memory for identical `const` expressions, making `identical()` comparisons O(1) and avoiding repeated allocations.

blocks.text: When you instantiate a class with a `const` constructor in a constant context, Dart deduplicates identical configurations into a single shared instance in memory (canonicalization). Consequently, `identical(a, b)` evaluates to `true`. In frameworks like Flutter, this enables rapid widget diffing because unchanged `const` subtrees refer to the exact same object identity.

interviewQuestions.title: Compare `var`, `dynamic`, and `Object?` in Dart.
interviewQuestions.content: `var` infers a fixed static type at compile time, `dynamic` disables static type checking entirely, and `Object?` is the statically checked top type of Dart's hierarchy.

blocks.text: `var` is not a type—it asks the compiler to infer the static type from the initial assignment, and that type cannot change later. `dynamic` opts out of static type checking: you can call any method on it without compile errors, risking `NoSuchMethodError` at runtime. `Object?` can hold any value (including `null`), but the compiler only allows calling `Object` methods (`toString`, `hashCode`, `==`) until you type-check or cast it.

blocks.code:
var a = 'hello';     // Inferred statically as String
dynamic b = 'hello'; // Static type checking disabled
Object? c = 'hello'; // Top type; static checks still enforced

interviewQuestions.title: What is a `factory` constructor and when should you use it?
interviewQuestions.content: A `factory` constructor does not always allocate a new instance of its class; it can return a cached instance, a singleton, or a subtype.

blocks.text: Unlike generative constructors, a `factory` constructor has no access to `this` and must explicitly return an object matching the class type. Common use cases include returning cached instances (flyweight/singleton patterns), deserializing JSON (`factory User.fromJson`), or returning a concrete subclass from an abstract base class based on input parameters.

interviewQuestions.title: What is a constructor initializer list in Dart and when is it required?
interviewQuestions.content: An initializer list runs before the constructor body executes, allowing you to initialize `final` fields, assert invariants, and call `super(...)`.

blocks.text: Placed after a colon `:` in a generative constructor, the initializer list executes before the constructor body and before `this` is available. It is required when computing values for `final` fields from constructor parameters, forwarding arguments to `super(...)`, or validating inputs with `assert(...)` in `const` constructors (which cannot have a body).

interviewQuestions.title: How do named constructors and redirecting constructors work in Dart?
interviewQuestions.content: Dart does not support constructor overloading by signature, so it uses named constructors for multiple construction paths and redirecting constructors (`: this(...)`) to delegate between them.

blocks.text: Because Dart lacks traditional constructor overloading, classes define named constructors like `Point.fromJson` to clarify intent. A redirecting constructor delegates its work to another constructor in the same class using `: this(...)` in the initializer list and cannot have a body of its own, avoiding duplicate initialization logic.

interviewQuestions.title: Explain Dart's event loop model and the execution priority of its queues.
interviewQuestions.content: Each Dart isolate runs a single-threaded event loop that drains synchronous code first, then empties the entire Microtask Queue before taking one item from the Event Queue.

blocks.text: A Dart isolate executes on one thread using two FIFO queues: the **Microtask Queue** and the **Event Queue**. After synchronous code finishes on the call stack, the loop drains **all** pending microtasks (including newly scheduled ones) before dequeuing a single task from the Event Queue (I/O, timers, UI events, `Future(...)`). Then it drains microtasks again, repeating until both queues are empty.

interviewQuestions.title: What is the difference between the Microtask Queue and Event Queue, and how can microtasks starve the event loop?
interviewQuestions.content: Microtasks run before the next event-loop tick for short internal continuations; recursively scheduling microtasks starves timers, I/O, and UI frame rendering.

blocks.text: The Microtask Queue (`scheduleMicrotask`, `Future.microtask`, `.then` continuations on completed futures) has strict priority over the Event Queue (`Future()`, `Timer`, network I/O, gestures). Because the event loop must completely empty the Microtask Queue before processing the next event or drawing a Flutter frame, an infinite chain of microtasks starves the Event Queue and freezes the application.

interviewQuestions.title: Does marking a function `async` move execution to a background thread?
interviewQuestions.content: No. An `async` function runs synchronously on the current isolate until its first `await`, where it suspends and schedules the continuation on the event loop.

blocks.text: `async` and `await` provide cooperative concurrency on the same thread—not parallelism. Everything before the first `await` executes immediately and synchronously. At `await`, the function returns an incomplete `Future` to its caller and registers the remainder of the function as a callback once the awaited `Future` completes. Heavy CPU loops inside an `async` function still block the UI thread.

interviewQuestions.title: What is the difference between a `Future` and a `Stream` in Dart?
interviewQuestions.content: A `Future` delivers a single asynchronous result (or error), whereas a `Stream` delivers zero or more asynchronous events over time.

blocks.text: A `Future<T>` models a one-shot asynchronous operation—such as an HTTP request or reading a file—that completes once with either a value of type `T` or an error. A `Stream<T>` models an ongoing sequence of asynchronous values—such as WebSocket messages, sensor updates, or user input—consumed via `await for` or `.listen()`.

interviewQuestions.title: Compare single-subscription streams and broadcast streams in Dart.
interviewQuestions.content: Single-subscription streams allow one listener and buffer events until subscribed; broadcast streams allow multiple concurrent listeners and drop events when no one is listening.

blocks.text: A **single-subscription stream** (the default for `async*` and file I/O) supports only one listener over its lifetime, starts producing data upon subscription, and supports pause/resume. Calling `.listen()` twice throws a `StateError`. A **broadcast stream** (`.asBroadcastStream()` or `StreamController.broadcast()`) allows multiple independent listeners simultaneously, ideal for event buses or state streams, though events emitted before a listener subscribes are not buffered.

interviewQuestions.title: How do `sync*` and `async*` generator functions work with `yield` and `yield*`?
interviewQuestions.content: `sync*` lazily generates a synchronous `Iterable`, `async*` generates an asynchronous `Stream`, `yield` emits one item, and `yield*` delegates to another iterable or stream.

blocks.text: Generator functions suspend execution on every `yield` until the consumer requests the next value (lazy evaluation). `sync*` returns an `Iterable<T>` evaluated synchronously on iteration. `async*` returns a `Stream<T>` capable of `await`ing internally before `yield`ing. `yield*` efficiently flattens and forwards all elements from a nested `Iterable` or `Stream` (great for recursive generators).

interviewQuestions.title: What is `Completer<T>` and when is it appropriate to use it?
interviewQuestions.content: `Completer<T>` lets you create a `Future` manually and resolve or reject it later from external callbacks.

blocks.text: A `Completer<T>` separates creating a `Future` (`completer.future`) from completing it (`completer.complete(value)` or `completer.completeError(error)`). You should primarily use it to bridge legacy callback-based APIs, event listeners, or isolate port responses into `Future`-based async/await code. Avoid using `Completer` when a simple `async` function suffices, as forgetting `completeError` can leave futures hanging forever.

interviewQuestions.title: Compare `Future.wait` and Dart 3's `Record.wait` for running futures concurrently.
interviewQuestions.content: `Future.wait` takes a homogeneous list of futures, while `(f1, f2).wait` preserves distinct static return types for each concurrent future and aggregates errors cleanly.

blocks.text: Both run futures concurrently rather than sequentially. `Future.wait<T>(Iterable<Future<T>>)` loses heterogenous typing (falling back to `List<Object?>` if types differ) and defaults `eagerError` to `false`. Dart 3's `Record.wait` extension on `Future` tuples like `(fetchUser(), fetchPosts()).wait` preserves exact strong types for each position and throws a `ParallelWaitError` containing both successful results and failures if any future rejects.

interviewQuestions.title: How do `StreamTransformer` and `StreamSubscription` backpressure (`pause`/`resume`) work?
interviewQuestions.content: `StreamTransformer` cleanly encapsulates reusable stream-to-stream conversions, while `StreamSubscription.pause()` signals upstream producers to stop emitting events.

blocks.text: `StreamTransformer<S, T>` transforms an incoming `Stream<S>` into a `Stream<T>` while preserving pause, resume, and cancel propagation. When a downstream consumer calls `subscription.pause()`, `StreamController`'s `onPause` callback fires so the producer can throttle work or pause an underlying socket—preventing memory bloat (backpressure). Calling `cancel()` triggers `onCancel` for resource cleanup.

interviewQuestions.title: What are Isolates in Dart and why do they not share mutable memory?
interviewQuestions.content: Isolates are independent actors with private memory heaps and event loops that communicate strictly via message passing, eliminating data races and locks.

blocks.text: Instead of OS threads sharing a heap (which require mutexes, locks, and risk deadlocks), Dart uses the Actor model via Isolates. Every Isolate owns an isolated memory heap, garbage collector, and event loop. Because memory is never mutated concurrently by two threads, Dart needs no synchronization locks and garbage collection stays fast per isolate.

blocks.code:
// Each isolate has its own memory heap and event loop
// No shared mutable state -> no mutexes or deadlocks

interviewQuestions.title: Compare `Isolate.run()` with `Isolate.spawn()` and `SendPort`/`ReceivePort`.
interviewQuestions.content: `Isolate.run()` handles one-shot background computations with zero boilerplate, whereas `Isolate.spawn()` is best for long-lived worker isolates exchanging multiple messages.

blocks.text: Introduced in Dart 2.19, `Isolate.run()` spawns an isolate, executes a closure, sends the result back (using `Isolate.exit` internally), and automatically terminates the isolate—ideal for single heavy tasks like JSON parsing or image compression. `Isolate.spawn()` combined with `ReceivePort`/`SendPort` establishes a persistent two-way channel suited for continuous streaming or stateful background workers.

interviewQuestions.title: How do `Isolate.exit()` and `TransferableTypedData` avoid copying overhead across isolates?
interviewQuestions.content: `Isolate.exit()` transfers ownership of the terminating isolate's result heap without deep copying, and `TransferableTypedData` moves byte buffers across live isolates in O(1).

blocks.text: Standard `SendPort.send()` copies immutable/mutable objects across isolate boundaries, though modern Dart optimizes immutable graphs. `Isolate.exit(sendPort, result)` immediately terminates the worker isolate and hands its memory chunk directly to the receiver in constant time. For ongoing isolates passing large binary buffers (`Uint8List`), `TransferableTypedData` transfers underlying buffer ownership without copying bytes.

interviewQuestions.title: What are mixins in Dart and how do they differ from inheritance and interfaces?
interviewQuestions.content: Mixins allow reusing concrete implementation code across unrelated class hierarchies without requiring a parent-child (`extends`) relationship.

blocks.text: Dart supports single class inheritance (`extends`), meaning a class can only have one superclass. `implements` forces you to re-implement every method of an interface. **Mixins** (`mixin` + `with`) let you inject reusable fields and concrete methods horizontally into any compatible class. Unlike classes, a `mixin` cannot declare generative constructors.

interviewQuestions.title: How does the `on` clause work in mixins, and how does Dart resolve method conflicts when applying multiple mixins?
interviewQuestions.content: The `on` clause restricts a mixin to subclasses of a specific superclass so it can call `super`, and Dart linearizes `with A, B` left-to-right so `B` overrides `A`.

blocks.text: Adding `on SomeClass` declares a superclass constraint, allowing the mixin to safely invoke `SomeClass` methods via `super`. When a class writes `class C extends S with A, B`, Dart creates a linear chain `S -> S+A -> S+A+B -> C`. Therefore, the rightmost mixin (`B`) wins on method collisions, and `super` inside `B` delegates to `A`.

interviewQuestions.title: What is `mixin class` in Dart 3 and why was it introduced?
interviewQuestions.content: In Dart 3, regular `class` declarations can no longer be used as mixins; `mixin class` explicitly declares a type usable as both an extended class and a mixin.

blocks.text: Before Dart 3, any constructorless class without an explicit `extends` could accidentally be used with `with`. Dart 3 tightened this by separating `class` and `mixin` semantics. Declaring `mixin class` opts a type into being used both via `extends`/`implements` and via `with`, provided it declares no generative constructors and only extends `Object`.

interviewQuestions.title: What are extension methods and why don't they work on `dynamic` variables?
interviewQuestions.content: Extension methods add static helper APIs to existing types without subclassing, and because they are resolved statically at compile time, they fail on `dynamic` receivers.

blocks.text: Extensions let you add getters, methods, and operators to third-party or core types (like `String` or `BuildContext`). Under the hood, the compiler translates `str.isBlank` into a static function call based on the expression's **static type**. Because `dynamic` bypasses static resolution, calling an extension method on a `dynamic` value throws a `NoSuchMethodError` at runtime.

interviewQuestions.title: What are `extension type` wrappers in Dart 3.3 and how do they achieve zero-cost abstraction?
interviewQuestions.content: Extension types provide compile-time wrapper types over an underlying representation type that are erased at runtime, incurring zero allocation overhead.

blocks.text: Unlike a wrapper class (`class UserId { final int value; }`), which allocates a new heap object for every instance, an `extension type` exists only during static analysis. At runtime, a `UserId` is simply the underlying `int`. This prevents primitive obsession bugs (e.g., swapping `UserId` and `OrderId` arguments) with zero memory or CPU cost.

interviewQuestions.title: How do generics work in Dart and what does it mean that Dart generics are reified?
interviewQuestions.content: Reified generics preserve their type arguments at runtime, meaning `list is List<String>` works accurately unlike type-erased languages such as Java.

blocks.text: Generics parameterize classes and functions over types (`Box<T>`) for compile-time type safety and code reuse. In languages with type erasure (like Java), `List<String>` becomes raw `List` at runtime. In Dart, generic type arguments are **reified**—stored on the runtime object—so `is List<String>` checks, `runtimeType`, and typed `Map<String, int>` serialization behave reliably at runtime.

interviewQuestions.title: Explain bounded generics (`extends`) and why Dart's covariant collections can throw runtime errors.
interviewQuestions.content: Bounded generics restrict `T` to subtypes of a bound, while Dart's covariant `List<T>` allows assigning `List<Sub>` to `List<Super>`, enforcing element types at runtime.

blocks.text: Using `<T extends SomeBase>` constrains type arguments so you can safely invoke `SomeBase` methods on `T` (note: default unbound `<T>` means `<T extends Object?>`). Additionally, Dart generics are **covariant** by design: `List<int>` is a subtype of `List<num>`. While convenient, mutating a `List<int>` through a `List<num>` reference by adding a `double` passes static checks and throws a `TypeError` at runtime.

interviewQuestions.title: What does the `covariant` keyword do on a method parameter and what is the trade-off?
interviewQuestions.content: `covariant` lets a subclass narrow a method parameter type when overriding, shifting type safety enforcement from compile time to a runtime check.

blocks.text: Normally, overriding a method only allows widening parameter types (contravariance) to satisfy the Liskov Substitution Principle. Putting `covariant` on a parameter (in the superclass or subclass) permits narrowing it in overrides—for example, `State<T>.didUpdateWidget(covariant T oldWidget)` in Flutter. The trade-off is that calling the method through a superclass reference with an incompatible argument fails at runtime.

interviewQuestions.title: What are Records in Dart 3 and how do positional and named fields work?
interviewQuestions.content: Records are anonymous, immutable, fixed-size aggregate types introduced in Dart 3 that let functions return multiple strongly typed values without creating helper classes.

blocks.text: Records group multiple values (positional like `(int, String)` accessed via `.$1`, `.$2`, and/or named like `({int id, String name})` accessed via `.id`) into a single value type. Records automatically implement structural equality (`==`) and `hashCode` based on their field values and shape, and pair naturally with destructuring assignments.

interviewQuestions.title: How does pattern matching and destructuring work in Dart 3?
interviewQuestions.content: Dart 3 patterns match values against structural shapes (records, lists, maps, objects) with optional `when` guards and bind inner fields into local variables in one step.

blocks.text: Patterns can appear in `switch` expressions/statements, `if-case` statements, `for-in` loops, and variable declarations. You can match constants, relational conditions (`>= 18`), list/map shapes (including rest elements `...`), and object properties (`User(age: var a)`), optionally refined with `when` guard clauses—dramatically reducing boilerplate casting and `if-else` chains.

interviewQuestions.title: How does exhaustiveness checking work in Dart 3 `switch` expressions?
interviewQuestions.content: The Dart 3 compiler statically verifies that `switch` expressions (and switches over `enum`, `bool`, or `sealed` types) cover every possible case, catching missing branches at compile time.

blocks.text: In a `switch` expression (which returns a value), all possible inputs must be handled. For closed type hierarchies—such as `bool`, `enum`, `Null`, or a `sealed` class family—the compiler tracks every subtype/value. If you add a new enum value or sealed subclass later and forget to handle it, compilation fails immediately unless a wildcard `_` is present (so omitting `_` is recommended for sealed hierarchies).

interviewQuestions.title: What is a `sealed` class in Dart 3 and how does it enable algebraic data types?
interviewQuestions.content: A `sealed` class cannot be extended or implemented outside its own library, forming a closed set of subtypes that enables exhaustive `switch` matching.

blocks.text: `sealed` classes are implicitly `abstract` (cannot be instantiated directly) and restrict direct subtyping to the same file/library. Because the compiler knows the complete, finite set of direct subclasses, `sealed` classes cleanly model state machines, network results (`Success` / `Failure` / `Loading`), and Bloc states with full compile-time exhaustiveness checking.

interviewQuestions.title: Explain Dart 3 class modifiers: `base`, `interface`, `final`, and `abstract interface`.
interviewQuestions.content: Dart 3 class modifiers control whether classes outside the defining library can extend, implement, or mix in a type, preventing fragile base-class bugs in public APIs.

blocks.text: `base` enforces inheritance (`extends`), blocking external `implements` so adding concrete methods won't break consumers (subtypes must also be `base`, `final`, or `sealed`). `interface` allows external `implements` while blocking `extends` (preventing subclassing of implementation details). `final` closes the hierarchy completely externally (neither `extends` nor `implements`). `abstract interface` is Dart's idiomatic pure interface.

blocks.code:
base class Vehicle { void move() {} } // Must be extended (not implemented) outside library
interface class ApiClient { void get() {} } // Can be implemented, not extended outside
final class Token {} // Cannot be extended or implemented outside
abstract interface class Repository { Future<void> save(); } // Pure interface

interviewQuestions.title: How do cascade (`..`, `?..`) and spread (`...`, `...?`) operators improve Dart ergonomics?
interviewQuestions.content: Cascade operators chain multiple operations on the same receiver object, while spread operators unpack collections inline (with null-aware variants for safety).

blocks.text: The cascade operator `..` invokes a method or sets a property on the receiver and evaluates to the receiver itself rather than the method's return value (ideal for builder patterns); `?..` short-circuits if the receiver is `null`. The spread operator `...` expands an iterable/map inside another collection literal, while `...?` safely skips expansion when the source is `null`.

interviewQuestions.title: Explain `==`, `hashCode`, and `identical()`, and why overriding `==` requires overriding `hashCode`.
interviewQuestions.content: `identical()` checks memory reference identity, `==` checks logical equality (defaulting to identity), and `hashCode` must remain consistent with `==` for `Set` and `Map` lookups.

blocks.text: By default, `Object.==` behaves like `identical()`. When you override `==` for value equality (or use `Equatable`/Freezed), you MUST override `hashCode` (using `Object.hash` or `Object.hashAll`) so equal objects always produce the same hash code. Otherwise, `HashMap` and `HashSet` will place logically equal objects into different hash buckets and fail lookups.

interviewQuestions.title: What are callable classes (`call()`) and function/constructor tear-offs in Dart?
interviewQuestions.content: Implementing `call()` lets an object instance be invoked like a function, while tear-offs pass a reference to an existing method or constructor without a wrapper closure.

blocks.text: Any class defining a `call(...)` method can be invoked directly as `instance(...)`, commonly used for use-case/interactor classes in Clean Architecture. A **tear-off** (`items.forEach(print)` or `list.map(User.fromJson)`) passes a method or constructor as a first-class function value without writing `(x) => print(x)`. Dart even supports constructor tear-offs like `Text.new`.

interviewQuestions.title: What capabilities do enhanced enums in Dart provide?
interviewQuestions.content: Enhanced enums can declare `final` fields, `const` constructors, methods, getters, and even implement interfaces or apply mixins.

blocks.text: Introduced in Dart 2.17, enhanced enums go far beyond simple integer constants. Every enum value can hold typed properties initialized via a private `const` constructor, expose computed getters and methods, override `toString()`, and `implement` interfaces or use `with` mixins—while retaining exhaustiveness checking in `switch` statements.

interviewQuestions.title: What is a `Zone` in Dart and how is `runZonedGuarded` used for async error tracking?
interviewQuestions.content: A `Zone` represents an execution context that persists across asynchronous callbacks, letting `runZonedGuarded` intercept uncaught asynchronous errors globally.

blocks.text: In async Dart, a standard `try-catch` block cannot catch exceptions thrown later in an unawaited `Future` or timer callback because the original call stack is gone. A `Zone` binds an execution environment across async gaps (`Future`, `Timer`, `Stream`), allowing `runZonedGuarded` to act as a global safety net for crash reporting tools (and in modern Flutter, pairing with `PlatformDispatcher.instance.onError`).

interviewQuestions.title: What is the semantic difference between `Error` and `Exception` in Dart?
interviewQuestions.content: `Exception` represents recoverable conditions that callers should catch and handle, while `Error` indicates programmer mistakes or violated invariants that should crash during development.

blocks.text: Classes implementing `Exception` (like `FormatException` or custom `ApiException`) represent expected failure modes—network timeouts, invalid user input—that application code should catch and recover from. Classes extending `Error` (like `RangeError`, `StateError`, `AssertionError`) signal bugs in code logic; you should fix the root bug rather than swallowing `Error`s in production.

interviewQuestions.title: Compare `on`, `catch`, and `rethrow` vs `throw e` in Dart exception handling.
interviewQuestions.content: `on` filters by exception type, `catch` binds the exception and stack trace, and `rethrow` propagates the original exception while preserving its stack trace.

blocks.text: Use `on SpecificException` when you only want to match a specific type without needing the exception object, or combine `on Type catch (e, stackTrace)` to inspect both. When propagating an error upward after logging, always use `rethrow` instead of `throw e;`—because `throw e;` resets the stack trace to the `catch` line, hiding the true origin of the failure.

interviewQuestions.title: Compare Dart's JIT and AOT compilation modes, and explain why Flutter uses both.
interviewQuestions.content: Dart uses Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation during development for stateful Hot Reload and Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) compilation in release builds for fast startup and predictable native speed.

blocks.text: Dart is rare in supporting both JIT and AOT compilers. In **JIT mode** (debug), the Dart VM compiles code dynamically and injects updated functions into memory, enabling sub-second Hot Reload. In **AOT mode** (release), all Dart code is precompiled to native ARM/x64 machine code (with tree shaking), yielding instant startup and smooth 60–120fps execution without runtime compilation warm-up.

blocks.code:
// Development: dart run / flutter run -> JIT (Hot Reload, fast iteration)
// Release: dart compile exe / flutter build -> AOT (native ARM/x64 machine code)

interviewQuestions.title: What is tree shaking in Dart AOT builds and what patterns can defeat it?
interviewQuestions.content: Tree shaking statically traces reachable code from `main()` and strips unused classes, functions, and assets; dynamic runtime reflection or large lookup maps can prevent it.

blocks.text: During AOT compilation (and `dart compile js`), Dart builds a call graph starting at `main()` and removes dead code, reducing binary size dramatically. Patterns that defeat tree shaking include runtime reflection (`dart:mirrors`, which is disabled in Flutter) and giant static maps registering every icon or class unconditionally—which is why Flutter enforces `--tree-shake-icons` compatibility with constant `IconData`.

blocks.code:
// Avoid reflection (dart:mirrors) so tree shaking works:
// Unused classes, methods, and icons are stripped in AOT builds.

interviewQuestions.title: What are `WeakReference` and `Finalizer` in Dart and when should you use them?
interviewQuestions.content: `WeakReference` holds an object without preventing garbage collection, and `Finalizer` runs a cleanup callback after an observed object is garbage collected.

blocks.text: A `WeakReference<T>` lets caches or observers reference an object while allowing the GC to reclaim it when no strong references remain (`weakRef.target` becomes `null`). A `Finalizer<T>` registers a callback to release external/native resources (like `dart:ffi` pointers or file handles) when a Dart wrapper object is GC'd—though `Finalizer` timing is non-deterministic and shouldn't replace explicit `dispose()`.

interviewQuestions.title: How do `typedef` aliases work in modern Dart?
interviewQuestions.content: Modern Dart `typedef` creates concise aliases for both function signatures and any generic or record type, improving readability without creating a new runtime type.

blocks.text: Originally limited to function types, `typedef` in modern Dart (2.13+) works for any type—including parameterized maps (`JsonMap`), callbacks (`ValueChanged<T>`), and Dart 3 `Record` shapes. A `typedef` is purely a compile-time alias, so `JsonMap` and `Map<String, dynamic>` remain 100% interchangeable everywhere.

interviewQuestions.title: Compare `const []`, `List.unmodifiable()`, and `UnmodifiableListView`.
interviewQuestions.content: `const []` is a compile-time constant, `List.unmodifiable()` allocates a defensive immutable copy, and `UnmodifiableListView` wraps an existing list in O(1) while reflecting its future mutations.

blocks.text: `const [...]` can only contain compile-time constants. `List.unmodifiable(source)` copies elements into a new list whose mutating methods throw `UnsupportedError`, making it safe even if `source` later changes. `UnmodifiableListView(source)` (from `dart:collection`) avoids the O(n) copy, making it great for exposing private internal lists read-only, though mutations to `source` remain visible through the view.

interviewQuestions.title: How does Dart's underscore (`_`) privacy differ from Java or C++ class privacy?
interviewQuestions.content: Dart privacy is library-scoped rather than class-scoped: identifiers starting with `_` are accessible anywhere within the same Dart library file (including `part` files).

blocks.text: Dart has no `private`, `protected`, or `public` keywords. Prefixing an identifier (`_secret`, `_HelperClass`) makes it private to its **library** (typically a single `.dart` file plus any `part` files). Top-level functions, other classes, and unit tests in the same library can access `_` members, while external libraries importing the file cannot.

interviewQuestions.title: What is the difference between `import`, `export`, and `part`/`part of`?
interviewQuestions.content: `import` consumes another library, `export` re-exposes symbols in barrel files, and `part` splits one single library (including its `_` private scope) across multiple files.

blocks.text: `import` brings symbols into the current file's namespace (supporting `show`, `hide`, and `as` prefixes). `export` forwards symbols from sub-files out of a package's entry/barrel file. `part` and `part of` merge multiple files into **one logical library** sharing imports and `_` private access—useful mainly for code generators (`freezed`, `json_serializable`) rather than general structuring.

interviewQuestions.title: What is `dart:ffi` and how does it differ from Flutter Platform Channels?
interviewQuestions.content: `dart:ffi` enables synchronous, zero-serialization calls directly into C/C++/Rust shared libraries, whereas Platform Channels serialize messages asynchronously.

blocks.text: `dart:ffi` (Foreign Function Interface) binds Dart directly to C-compatible native symbols in `.so`, `.dylib`, or `.dll` libraries. Unlike Flutter's asynchronous `MethodChannel` (which marshals data across platform threads), `dart:ffi` executes synchronously with near-zero call overhead—ideal for SQLite, audio DSP, cryptography, or Rust/C++ engines (and pairs with `Isolate.run` if the native call is blocking).
