languages.title: C
languages.description: Low-level programming language that provides deep understanding of memory management and system-level concepts.

insights.title: 01. Program Structure & main()
insights.content: Every hosted C program begins execution at the main() function and returns an exit status.

blocks.text: A minimal C program includes standard headers with #include, defines int main(void) as the entry point, and returns 0 to indicate successful termination to the operating system.

insights.title: 02. printf() & Format Specifiers
insights.content: printf() writes formatted output to stdout using placeholders like %d, %f, %c, and %s.

blocks.text: Format specifiers tell printf() how to interpret each argument. Width and precision modifiers such as %.2f or %05d control alignment and decimal places.

insights.title: 03. scanf() & Safe Input Reading
insights.content: scanf() reads formatted input into variable addresses and returns the number of items matched.

blocks.text: Always pass the address of scalar variables using & and check scanf()'s return value to verify valid input. For strings, limit width to prevent buffer overflow.

insights.title: 04. Variables & Primitive Data Types
insights.content: C provides core scalar types—char, int, float, and double—with signed/unsigned modifiers.

blocks.text: Choosing the right type balances range and memory footprint. Use int for general integers, unsigned types for bitmasks or non-negative sizes, and double for general floating-point math.

insights.title: 05. sizeof Operator & Type Limits
insights.content: sizeof returns the compile-time byte size of a type or expression as size_t.

blocks.text: Type sizes in C vary across platforms (for instance, long is 4 bytes on Windows x64 and 8 bytes on Linux x64). Use <limits.h> and %zu when printing sizeof values.

insights.title: 06. const Variables & Typed Literals
insights.content: const enforces read-only access at compile time, while suffixes type literals explicitly.

blocks.text: Prefer const over magic numbers to make intent clear and let the compiler catch accidental mutations. Suffixes like U, L, LL, and f prevent unintended integer or double promotions.

insights.title: 07. Arithmetic Operators & Integer Division
insights.content: Dividing two integers truncates toward zero; cast at least one operand for floating-point division.

blocks.text: C evaluates +, -, *, /, and % according to standard precedence. Watch out for 7 / 2 == 3 in integer arithmetic; casting (double)a / b forces floating-point division.

insights.title: 08. Relational & Logical Operators
insights.content: Comparisons evaluate to 1 (true) or 0 (false), and && / || short-circuit left to right.

blocks.text: Short-circuit evaluation guarantees the right operand of && is skipped if the left is 0, and the right operand of || is skipped if the left is non-zero—essential for null and bounds guards.

insights.title: 09. Bitwise Operators Basics
insights.content: Bitwise &, |, ^, ~, <<, and >> manipulate individual bits inside integer values.

blocks.text: Always perform bitwise operations on unsigned types to avoid sign-bit undefined behavior during shifts. Use OR to set bits, AND with ~ to clear bits, and XOR to toggle bits.

insights.title: 10. Compound Assignment & ++/--
insights.content: Prefix ++x increments before yielding the value; postfix x++ yields the old value first.

blocks.text: Never modify the same variable more than once between sequence points (like i = i++ + ++i), as that causes undefined behavior. Keep ++ and -- in clean, standalone expressions.

insights.title: 11. Ternary & Comma Operators
insights.content: The ternary operator cond ? a : b selects between two expressions inline.

blocks.text: Use the ternary operator for concise conditional values, and remember the comma operator evaluates left-to-right and yields the rightmost expression (commonly seen in for-loop headers).

insights.title: 12. if / else if / else Conditionals
insights.content: Conditional branches execute the first matching block whose condition evaluates non-zero.

blocks.text: Always wrap branch bodies in braces {} even for single lines to prevent dangling-else bugs and accidental misindentation errors.

insights.title: 13. switch / case & Fallthrough
insights.content: switch dispatches on an integral expression; break stops fallthrough to the next case.

blocks.text: Each case label must be an integer constant expression. Grouping cases without break handles multiple inputs identically, while default catches unmatched values.

insights.title: 14. for Loops
insights.content: for loops bundle initialization, continuation condition, and update in one header.

blocks.text: In C99 and later, declaring the loop counter inside for (int i = 0; ...) limits its scope to the loop body, keeping surrounding variables clean.

insights.title: 15. while Loops
insights.content: while evaluates its condition before each iteration, running zero or more times.

blocks.text: Use while when the number of iterations depends on dynamic state rather than a fixed counter—such as reading until EOF or dividing down a number.

insights.title: 16. do-while Loops
insights.content: do-while runs its body at least once before testing the loop condition.

blocks.text: Ideal for menu prompts or retry loops where an action must execute first and repeat only if a condition holds. Also widely used in multi-statement macros (do { ... } while (0)).

insights.title: 17. break & continue Statements
insights.content: break exits the innermost loop immediately; continue skips to its next iteration.

blocks.text: In a for loop, continue still executes the update expression (e.g., i++) before re-checking the condition. Use break to short-circuit searches once a target is found.

insights.title: 18. Nested Loops & Patterns
insights.content: Placing one loop inside another iterates over 2D grids, pairs, or triangular patterns.

blocks.text: Watch time complexity: two nested loops of size N perform O(N^2) iterations. Notice that break inside an inner loop exits only the inner loop, not the outer one.

insights.title: 19. Function Prototypes & Definitions
insights.content: A prototype declares a function's signature before use so the compiler can type-check calls.

blocks.text: In C, use (void) in a parameterless function prototype—empty parentheses () historically meant unspecified parameters in pre-C23 standards.

insights.title: 20. Pass-by-Value Semantics
insights.content: C passes function arguments by value, meaning the callee receives a local copy.

blocks.text: Modifying a parameter inside a function does not affect the caller's variable unless you pass its memory address (a pointer).

insights.title: 21. Recursion & Base Cases
insights.content: A recursive function calls itself on smaller inputs until reaching a terminating base case.

blocks.text: Every recursive function needs a clear base case to prevent stack overflow. Each call pushes a stack frame holding local variables and return addresses.

insights.title: 22. Block Scope & Variable Shadowing
insights.content: Variables declared inside {} exist only within that block and can shadow outer names.

blocks.text: Local automatic variables are uninitialized unless explicitly assigned. Avoid variable shadowing because it hurts readability and can introduce subtle logic bugs.

insights.title: 23. 1D Arrays & Indexing
insights.content: Arrays store a fixed-size contiguous sequence of same-type elements indexed from 0.

blocks.text: C does not perform runtime bounds checking on array indices. Partial initialization like int arr[5] = {1, 2} automatically zero-fills the remaining elements.

insights.title: 24. Passing Arrays & Aggregation
insights.content: Arrays decay to pointers when passed to functions, so pass the element count separately.

blocks.text: Because sizeof(arr) inside a function measures the pointer size rather than the array length, always supply size_t n alongside const int arr[].

insights.title: 25. 2D Arrays & Matrix Iteration
insights.content: 2D arrays are laid out contiguously in row-major order in memory.

blocks.text: When passing a 2D array to a function, all dimensions except the first must be specified so the compiler knows the row stride for address calculation.

insights.title: 26. C Strings & Null Terminator '\0'
insights.content: C strings are char arrays terminated by a zero byte '\0' marking the end of text.

blocks.text: Always allocate at least length + 1 bytes to hold the trailing '\0'. Forgetting the null terminator causes string functions to read past the buffer into adjacent memory.

insights.title: 27. String Length & Comparison (strlen, strcmp)
insights.content: strlen counts characters before '\0'; strcmp compares two strings lexicographically.

blocks.text: Never compare C strings with == because that compares pointer addresses rather than contents. strcmp returns 0 when two strings are identical.

insights.title: 28. Copying & Appending Strings Safely
insights.content: Prefer bounded functions like snprintf or careful strncpy/strncat over unsafe strcpy.

blocks.text: strcpy and strcat do not check destination buffer capacity. Note that strncpy does not guarantee null-termination if the source reaches n characters, so explicitly set dst[size - 1] = '\0'.

insights.title: 29. Character Classification (<ctype.h>)
insights.content: <ctype.h> provides isalpha, isdigit, isspace, tolower, and toupper for portable character handling.

blocks.text: Always cast char arguments to (unsigned char) before passing them to <ctype.h> functions to avoid undefined behavior on platforms where char is signed.

insights.title: 30. Math Functions (<math.h>)
insights.content: <math.h> supplies sqrt, pow, fabs, ceil, floor, and trigonometric functions for doubles.

blocks.text: When compiling with GCC or Clang on Linux, link the math library with -lm if needed. Use fabs() for floating-point absolute values and abs() from <stdlib.h> for ints.

insights.title: 31. Pseudo-Random Numbers (rand & srand)
insights.content: Seed rand() once with srand((unsigned)time(NULL)) to avoid repeating the same sequence.

blocks.text: Call srand() only once at program startup, not inside a loop. Note that rand() is fine for simple games or demos, but not suitable for cryptography.

insights.title: 32. Command-Line Arguments (argc & argv)
insights.content: argc holds the argument count and argv[] holds C-string pointers for each CLI token.

blocks.text: argv[0] is typically the program name, and argv[argc] is guaranteed to be NULL. Check argc before indexing argv[1] to avoid out-of-bounds reads.

insights.title: 33. Booleans & Fixed-Width Integers
insights.content: <stdbool.h> provides bool/true/false, while <stdint.h> gives exact-width types like uint32_t.

blocks.text: Fixed-width types (int8_t, uint16_t, int32_t, uint64_t) ensure identical bit widths across 32-bit and 64-bit architectures—crucial for binary protocols and embedded systems.

insights.title: 34. Type Aliases with typedef
insights.content: typedef creates a readable alias for an existing type without introducing a new distinct type.

blocks.text: typedef simplifies verbose declarations like unsigned char buffers, structs, or function pointers. Use clear naming conventions so readers still recognize pointer or struct types.

insights.title: 35. Enumerations (enum)
insights.content: enum defines a set of named integer constants, improving clarity over raw numeric codes.

blocks.text: By default, enumerators start at 0 and increment by 1, though explicit integer values can be assigned. Combining enum with switch lets compilers warn on unhandled states.

insights.title: 36. Pointer Basics (& and *)
insights.content: A pointer stores the memory address of another variable; * dereferences it to read or write.

blocks.text: The address-of operator & yields a pointer to a variable, while the dereference operator * accesses the pointee. Always initialize pointers before dereferencing them.

insights.title: 37. NULL Pointers & Defensive Checks
insights.content: NULL represents an empty pointer pointing to nothing; dereferencing it causes undefined behavior.

blocks.text: Initialize unready pointers to NULL, check ptr != NULL before dereferencing, and reset freed pointers to NULL to prevent accidental use-after-free bugs.

insights.title: 38. Pointer Arithmetic & Array Traversal
insights.content: Adding 1 to a T* pointer advances the address by sizeof(T) bytes, not 1 byte.

blocks.text: p[i] is defined in C as *(p + i). Subtracting two pointers within the same array yields ptrdiff_t representing the element distance between them.

insights.title: 39. Pointers vs. Arrays
insights.content: Arrays are fixed memory blocks; pointers are reassignable variables holding addresses.

blocks.text: Although an array expression decays to a pointer to its first element in most expressions, sizeof(arr) returns total array bytes whereas sizeof(ptr) returns only the pointer's size.

insights.title: 40. const with Pointers
insights.content: const int *p protects the data; int * const p locks the pointer address itself.

blocks.text: Read C pointer declarations right-to-left: 'const int *p' is a mutable pointer to a constant int, while 'const int * const p' makes both the pointer and the pointee read-only.

insights.title: 41. Simulating Pass-by-Reference with Pointers
insights.content: Passing &var lets a function mutate the caller's original variable directly.

blocks.text: Functions like swap() require pointers because C only passes arguments by value. Passing addresses avoids copying large structures and allows multiple output values.

insights.title: 42. Multiple Return Values via Out-Parameters
insights.content: Return a status/bool directly and write computed results through pointer out-parameters.

blocks.text: This idiomatic C pattern cleanly separates error reporting from output values, avoiding sentinel values that could collide with valid results.

insights.title: 43. Generic Pointers (void *)
insights.content: void * holds any object address without type information and must be cast before dereferencing.

blocks.text: Generic memory functions like malloc, memcpy, and qsort rely on void *. Never perform pointer arithmetic directly on void * in standard C; cast to unsigned char * for byte offsets.

insights.title: 44. Sorting with qsort() & Comparators
insights.content: qsort() sorts any array using a user-supplied comparator accepting two const void * pointers.

blocks.text: Avoid returning (*a - *b) in integer comparators because subtraction can overflow INT_MIN/INT_MAX. Returning (*a > *b) - (*a < *b) is always overflow-safe.

insights.title: 45. String Traversal with Pointers
insights.content: Walking a char * pointer until *p == '\0' provides fast, clean string processing.

blocks.text: String literals like "hello" live in read-only memory; bind them to const char * so the compiler prevents accidental writes, while char buf[] is mutable.

insights.title: 46. Tokenizing Strings (strtok)
insights.content: strtok splits a mutable string by delimiters by inserting '\0' bytes in place.

blocks.text: strtok mutates the input buffer and keeps hidden static state (making it non-reentrant). Pass the buffer on the first call, then NULL on subsequent calls.

insights.title: 47. Formatting & Parsing with snprintf / sscanf
insights.content: snprintf formats safely into bounded buffers; sscanf extracts typed values from strings.

blocks.text: Always prefer snprintf over sprintf because sprintf cannot prevent buffer overflows. Check sscanf's return count to ensure every field parsed as expected.

insights.title: 48. Structs & Designated Initializers
insights.content: struct groups related fields of different types into a single composite data type.

blocks.text: C99 designated initializers (.field = val) make struct creation order-independent and automatically zero-initialize omitted fields.

insights.title: 49. Nested Structs & Arrays of Structs
insights.content: Structs can contain other structs and be stored contiguously inside arrays for tabular data.

blocks.text: Nesting structs models real domain entities cleanly (such as User containing Date) while preserving flat, cache-friendly memory layout.

insights.title: 50. Pointers to Structs (-> Operator)
insights.content: Use ptr->field as shorthand for (*ptr).field when accessing struct members through a pointer.

blocks.text: Passing structs by const pointer (const User *) avoids expensive copies on large structs while still enforcing read-only access inside the function.

insights.title: 51. Passing Structs by Value vs. Pointer
insights.content: Small structs can be passed and returned by value; large structs should be passed by pointer.

blocks.text: Passing by value copies every byte of the struct onto the stack or registers. Passing const T * gives zero-copy read access, while T * permits in-place mutation.

insights.title: 52. Unions & Tagged Unions
insights.content: A union overlays all its members at the same memory address; pair it with an enum tag for safety.

blocks.text: Because only one union member is active at any time, a tagged union (struct containing an enum kind plus a union) provides type-safe sum types in C.

insights.title: 53. Bit-Fields in Structs
insights.content: Bit-fields pack small integer flags into specified bit widths inside a struct.

blocks.text: Use unsigned int for portable bit-fields. Keep in mind that exact bit ordering (MSB vs LSB) is implementation-defined, so use explicit masks and shifts for wire/file formats.

insights.title: 54. Dynamic Allocation with malloc()
insights.content: malloc(bytes) allocates uninitialized heap memory and returns NULL if allocation fails.

blocks.text: Use sizeof(*ptr) inside malloc(n * sizeof(*ptr)) so the allocation stays correct even if the pointer's type changes. Always verify ptr != NULL before use.

insights.title: 55. Zero-Initialized Allocation with calloc()
insights.content: calloc(count, size) allocates heap memory initialized to all-bits-zero and checks multiplication overflow.

blocks.text: Unlike malloc, calloc guarantees every byte starts at 0 and protects against count * size integer overflow internally.

insights.title: 56. Resizing Allocations Safely with realloc()
insights.content: Never assign realloc(ptr, ...) directly back to ptr; store the result in a temporary pointer first.

blocks.text: If realloc fails, it returns NULL while leaving the original memory block allocated. Assigning directly to ptr overwrites your only reference and leaks the old block.

insights.title: 57. free() & Preventing Dangling Pointers
insights.content: Every heap allocation must be freed once; set pointers to NULL after free() to prevent double-free.

blocks.text: Calling free(NULL) is a safe no-op in standard C, whereas freeing the same address twice or reading freed memory causes undefined behavior and security vulnerabilities.

insights.title: 58. Dynamic 2D Arrays (Contiguous vs. Row Pointers)
insights.content: Allocate a single contiguous rows*cols block for cache locality and one-call cleanup.

blocks.text: A flat contiguous array accessed via m[r * cols + c] (or a VLA pointer int (*m)[cols]) avoids N separate malloc calls and keeps rows adjacent in memory.

insights.title: 59. Dynamic Growable Array (Vector Pattern)
insights.content: Track size and capacity in a struct and double capacity when full for amortized O(1) push.

blocks.text: Doubling capacity rather than growing by 1 on every push avoids O(N^2) copying overhead and keeps reallocation count logarithmic.

insights.title: 60. File I/O Basics (fopen & fclose)
insights.content: fopen opens a FILE* stream in modes like "r", "w", "a", or "rb"; always check for NULL and fclose.

blocks.text: Writing with "w" truncates existing files; "a" appends to the end. Always check fopen's return value and close streams promptly to flush buffers and release OS file descriptors.

insights.title: 61. Reading Text Lines with fgets()
insights.content: fgets reads at most size - 1 characters per call and preserves the newline if it fits.

blocks.text: Unlike legacy gets() (removed in C11), fgets() is buffer-safe. Strip a trailing '\n' using strcspn(line, "\n") when needed.

insights.title: 62. Writing Formatted Text (fprintf & fputs)
insights.content: fprintf writes formatted text to a FILE*, while fputs writes raw strings without format parsing.

blocks.text: Always pass "%s" as the format string when printing untrusted strings with fprintf(fp, "%s", str), or use fputs to prevent format-string vulnerabilities.

insights.title: 63. Binary File I/O (fread & fwrite)
insights.content: Use "rb"/"wb" modes with fread and fwrite to transfer raw bytes or fixed structs.

blocks.text: Binary mode prevents newline translation on Windows. Check that the element count returned by fread/fwrite matches the requested count.

insights.title: 64. Random File Access (fseek, ftell, rewind)
insights.content: fseek moves the file cursor relative to SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR, or SEEK_END; ftell reports its offset.

blocks.text: Seeking to SEEK_END and calling ftell lets you measure a binary file's byte length before allocating a read buffer.

insights.title: 65. Error Handling with errno & perror()
insights.content: Standard library and POSIX functions set errno on failure; perror/strerror explain the code.

blocks.text: Only inspect errno immediately after a function signals failure (e.g., returns NULL or -1), because successful calls do not reset errno to 0.

insights.title: 66. Preprocessor #define Constants
insights.content: #define performs textual token substitution before the compiler parses the source code.

blocks.text: Because #define has no type or scope, prefer const or enum for typed constants and reserve #define for conditional compilation, array sizes in pre-C99, or build configuration flags.

insights.title: 67. Function-Like Macros & Parentheses Pitfalls
insights.content: Always wrap every macro parameter and the whole expansion in parentheses, and beware double evaluation.

blocks.text: SQUARE(1 + 2) expands to 1 + 2 * 1 + 2 = 5 without parentheses, and MAX(a++, b) increments a twice. Prefer static inline functions when type safety is available.

insights.title: 68. Include Guards & Conditional Compilation
insights.content: #ifndef HEADER_H guards prevent duplicate definitions when a header is included multiple times.

blocks.text: Standard #ifndef/#define/#endif guards are portable across every C compiler; #ifdef DEBUG lets you toggle diagnostic logging at compile time via -DDEBUG.

insights.title: 69. Multi-File Modules & extern Declarations
insights.content: Put declarations in .h files and definitions in .c files; extern declares symbols defined elsewhere.

blocks.text: Never define non-inline functions or mutable global variables inside headers, or the linker will report multiple-definition errors when two .c files include the header.

insights.title: 70. The static Keyword (Persistence & Internal Linkage)
insights.content: Inside functions, static keeps state across calls; at file scope, static hides symbols from other translation units.

blocks.text: Marking file-scope helpers and globals static is C's primary encapsulation tool—preventing symbol collisions across .c files and enabling better compiler optimization.

insights.title: 71. Double Pointers (T **)
insights.content: A pointer-to-pointer lets a function re-seat the caller's pointer (e.g., allocating or freeing safely).

blocks.text: Double pointers are essential when inserting at the head of a linked list, writing custom allocators, or creating a safeFree(void **pp) helper that nulls the caller's pointer.

insights.title: 72. Array of Pointers vs. Pointer to Array
insights.content: int *a[3] is an array of 3 int pointers; int (*p)[3] is a single pointer to an array of 3 ints.

blocks.text: Because [] binds tighter than *, parentheses are required for pointers to arrays. Incrementing p advances by 3 * sizeof(int) bytes—matching 2D array row strides.

insights.title: 73. Function Pointers & Callbacks
insights.content: Function pointers store code addresses so algorithms can invoke caller-supplied behavior.

blocks.text: Use typedef to make function pointer signatures clean and readable. Callbacks decouple iteration or event logic from specific actions.

insights.title: 74. Dispatch Tables with Function Pointers
insights.content: Arrays of function pointers replace large switch statements with O(1) indexed dispatch.

blocks.text: Dispatch tables are widely used in state machines, protocol parsers, and interpreters. Always bounds-check the opcode before indexing the table.

insights.title: 75. Opaque Pointers & ABI Encapsulation
insights.content: Forward-declare a struct in the header and define its fields only in the .c file.

blocks.text: Opaque handles prevent callers from depending on internal struct layout, letting libraries evolve internal fields without breaking binary compatibility (ABI).

insights.title: 76. Singly Linked List (Insert, Traverse, Free)
insights.content: A singly linked list links heap-allocated nodes via next pointers for O(1) head insertion.

blocks.text: Save node->next before calling free(node) during cleanup so you don't read freed memory while advancing.

insights.title: 77. Circular Ring Buffer (FIFO Queue)
insights.content: A ring buffer wraps head and tail indices modulo capacity for fixed-memory FIFO queues.

blocks.text: Ring buffers are ideal for audio streams, UART/serial drivers, and producer-consumer queues because enqueue and dequeue run in strict O(1) time with zero allocations.

insights.title: 78. Stack Implementation with Bounds Safety
insights.content: A LIFO stack supports O(1) push, pop, and peek with explicit empty/full checks.

blocks.text: Return bool status codes from push/pop rather than silently ignoring underflow or overflow so callers can handle errors deterministically.

insights.title: 79. Hash Table with Separate Chaining
insights.content: Combine an FNV-1a/djb2 hash function with linked buckets for average O(1) string lookups.

blocks.text: Use unsigned long for hash arithmetic to avoid signed integer overflow UB, and reduce modulo bucket count when indexing.

insights.title: 80. Variadic Functions (<stdarg.h>)
insights.content: va_list, va_start, va_arg, and va_end let functions accept a variable number of arguments.

blocks.text: C variadic functions do not know argument count or types automatically; pass an explicit count, sentinel, or format string, and remember default argument promotions (float -> double, char/short -> int).

insights.title: 81. memcpy(), memmove(), and memset()
insights.content: memcpy requires non-overlapping regions; memmove safely handles overlapping memory blocks.

blocks.text: Passing overlapping buffers to memcpy causes undefined behavior. Use memmove when shifting elements within the same array, and memset to zero or fill byte buffers.

insights.title: 82. Struct Padding, Alignment & offsetof
insights.content: Compilers insert padding bytes to align members on natural boundaries; ordering largest-first shrinks structs.

blocks.text: Use offsetof(Type, member) from <stddef.h> and _Alignof(Type) to inspect exact memory layout. Never assume two structs can be compared with memcmp if they contain padding bytes.

insights.title: 83. Flexible Array Members (C99)
insights.content: An unsized array[] as the last struct member lets header + payload live in one heap allocation.

blocks.text: Flexible array members eliminate a second pointer dereference and second free() call, improving cache locality for variable-length packets or strings.

insights.title: 84. static inline Functions in Headers
insights.content: static inline functions eliminate call overhead for small helpers while keeping type safety.

blocks.text: Unlike plain inline in C99 (which requires an external definition in one .c file), static inline can live safely in headers included by multiple translation units.

insights.title: 85. The volatile Qualifier
insights.content: volatile prevents the compiler from caching or optimizing away reads and writes to an object.

blocks.text: Use volatile for memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) hardware registers, sig_atomic_t flags touched by signal handlers, or variables modified across setjmp. Note: volatile is NOT a thread synchronization primitive.

insights.title: 86. The restrict Pointer Qualifier (C99)
insights.content: restrict promises the compiler that two pointers do not alias the same memory region.

blocks.text: By guaranteeing non-overlapping buffers, restrict lets the compiler vectorize loops and keep values in registers instead of reloading after every write.

insights.title: 87. Bit Manipulation Idioms & Masks
insights.content: Power-of-two checks, lowest set bit isolation, and bitmask flags run in single CPU instructions.

blocks.text: (n & (n - 1)) clears the lowest set bit—useful for both Brian Kernighan's popcount loop and checking whether n > 0 is a power of two.

insights.title: 88. Endianness Detection & Byte Swapping
insights.content: Little-endian stores the least significant byte first; network protocols use big-endian.

blocks.text: Avoid type-punning through unions when avoidable; inspecting bytes via unsigned char * or shifting uint32_t explicitly is completely portable and strict-aliasing safe.

insights.title: 89. Non-Local Jumps with setjmp & longjmp
insights.content: setjmp saves execution context and longjmp unwinds back to it for C-style exception recovery.

blocks.text: Local non-volatile variables modified after setjmp have indeterminate values if longjmp fires, and longjmp skips cleanup code—only use it with explicit resource tracking.

insights.title: 90. POSIX Signals & sig_atomic_t
insights.content: Use sigaction and a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so signal handlers remain async-signal-safe.

blocks.text: Never call printf, malloc, or free inside a signal handler because they are not async-signal-safe. Set a flag and check it cleanly in your main loop.

insights.title: 91. POSIX Threads (pthread_create & pthread_join)
insights.content: pthreads spawn concurrent threads sharing the process heap; pthread_join waits for completion.

blocks.text: Compile with -pthread. Always pass distinct memory or heap-allocated arguments to each thread rather than sharing a changing loop variable address.

insights.title: 92. Mutex Synchronization (pthread_mutex_t)
insights.content: Mutexes guard shared mutable state so only one thread executes a critical section at a time.

blocks.text: Lock mutexes for the shortest duration needed and always unlock on every exit path to prevent deadlocks.

insights.title: 93. Condition Variables (pthread_cond_t)
insights.content: Condition variables let threads sleep efficiently until another thread signals a state change.

blocks.text: Always wait inside a while (!predicate) loop—never a single if—because spurious wakeups can occur even when no signal was sent.

insights.title: 94. C11 Lock-Free Atomics (<stdatomic.h>)
insights.content: <stdatomic.h> provides lock-free atomic counters, compare-exchange, and memory ordering.

blocks.text: Atomic operations avoid mutex overhead for simple flags and counters. Default sequential consistency (atomic_fetch_add) is simplest and safest unless profiling requires relaxed ordering.

insights.title: 95. Type-Generic Macros with _Generic (C11)
insights.content: _Generic selects an expression at compile time based on the static type of an argument.

blocks.text: C11 _Generic powers <tgmath.h> and enables clean polymorphic logging or printing APIs without function overloading.

insights.title: 96. Memory-Mapped Files with mmap() (POSIX)
insights.content: mmap maps file contents directly into virtual memory so reads avoid extra user-space copies.

blocks.text: Always check for MAP_FAILED (not NULL), verify file size > 0, and call munmap() when finished.

insights.title: 97. Processes, fork(), and Pipes (POSIX IPC)
insights.content: fork() clones the calling process; pipe() creates a unidirectional byte channel between parent and child.

blocks.text: Close unused pipe ends in both parent and child so EOF is delivered properly, and waitpid() on child PIDs to prevent zombie processes.

insights.title: 98. POSIX TCP Socket Server Basics
insights.content: A TCP server follows socket -> bind -> listen -> accept and reads/writes client streams.

blocks.text: Set SO_REUSEADDR before bind() so quick restarts don't fail with EADDRINUSE, and convert ports with htons() to network byte order.

insights.title: 99. Common Undefined Behavior (UB) Pitfalls
insights.content: Signed overflow, uninitialized reads, out-of-bounds access, and strict-aliasing violations invoke UB.

blocks.text: Because compilers assume UB never happens, UB can silently break security checks or delete branches under -O2. Check arithmetic bounds before performing signed operations.

insights.title: 100. Memory Hygiene, Sanitizers & Strict Warnings
insights.content: Compile with -Wall -Wextra -Werror and test with AddressSanitizer/UBSan to catch leaks and UB early.

blocks.text: AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address,undefined) detects heap/stack buffer overflows, use-after-free, leaks, and signed overflow at runtime with clear stack traces.

interviewQuestions.title: Difference between `const int *p`, `int * const p`, and `const int * const p`
interviewQuestions.content: `const int *p` is a mutable pointer to constant data, `int * const p` is a constant pointer to mutable data, and `const int * const p` locks both.

blocks.text:
• Reading right-to-left around `*`:
  - `const int *p` (same as `int const *p`): `p` is a pointer to a `const int`. You can reassign `p = &y`, but cannot modify `*p = 5`.
  - `int * const p`: `p` is a `const` pointer to `int`. You can modify `*p = 5`, but cannot reassign `p = &y` (must be initialized at declaration).
  - `const int * const p`: Neither `p` nor `*p` can be modified through `p`.

interviewQuestions.title: How does Pointer Arithmetic work (`ptr + 1`) across different types?
interviewQuestions.content: Adding `n` to a pointer `T *ptr` advances its byte address by `n * sizeof(T)`, and subtracting two pointers of the same array yields the element count (`ptrdiff_t`).

blocks.text:
• Scaling rule: If `int *p` is at `0x1000` (`sizeof(int) == 4`), then `p + 1` is `0x1004`, whereas `char *c` at `0x1000` gives `c + 1 == 0x1001`.
• `void *` arithmetic: Illegal in standard C because `void` has no size (GCC allows it as a 1-byte extension—avoid for portability).
• Pointer subtraction: `p2 - p1` divides the byte difference by `sizeof(T)` and is only valid within the same array (or one-past-the-end).

interviewQuestions.title: Explain Array-to-Pointer Decay (`sizeof(arr)` vs `sizeof(&arr[0])`) and `&arr`
interviewQuestions.content: In most expressions an array `T arr[N]` decays to `T *` pointing to `arr[0]`, EXCEPT as the operand of `sizeof`, `_Alignof`, or unary `&` (`&arr` has type `T (*)[N]`).

blocks.text:
• Exceptions to decay: `sizeof(arr)` gives total array bytes (`N * sizeof(T)`), whereas passing `arr` to a function decays it to a pointer (`sizeof(param)` inside the function equals `sizeof(void*)`!).
• `&arr` vs `arr`: Both evaluate to the same starting address, but `arr + 1` advances by `sizeof(T)` while `&arr + 1` advances by the ENTIRE array size (`N * sizeof(T)`).

blocks.code:
int arr[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(arr)); // 20 (5 * 4 bytes)
int *p = arr;                 // Decays to int *
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(p));   // 8 on 64-bit
int (*pa)[5] = &arr;          // Pointer to whole array of 5 ints

interviewQuestions.title: What is a `void *` pointer, and how is it used for Generic Programming in C?
interviewQuestions.content: `void *` is an untyped generic data pointer that converts implicitly to/from any object pointer; it cannot be dereferenced directly without casting to a concrete type.

blocks.text:
• Properties: Holds any object address (`malloc` returns `void *`, `qsort` / `pthread_create` accept `void *`).
• Restrictions: Cannot dereference `*vp` or perform standard pointer arithmetic directly because the pointed-to size is unknown.
• Portability warning: Function pointers (`int (*)(int)`) are NOT guaranteed by the C standard to convert cleanly to/from `void *` (though POSIX `dlsym` relies on it).

interviewQuestions.title: How do Function Pointers work, and how do you read complex declarations?
interviewQuestions.content: A function pointer stores the entry address of executable code in the `.text` segment, enabling callbacks, dispatch jump tables, and runtime polymorphism; `typedef` keeps complex signatures readable.

blocks.text:
• Right-Left / Spiral Rule: `int (*(*fn)(int))[5]` reads as: `fn` is a pointer to a function taking `int`, returning a pointer to an array of 5 `int`s.
• Best practice: Always `typedef` function pointer types (`typedef int (*Handler)(const char *);`) for clean APIs and dispatch tables.

interviewQuestions.title: When do you use a Pointer to a Pointer (`int **`) in C?
interviewQuestions.content: Use `T **` when a function needs to rebind a caller's pointer (pass-by-reference for pointers), represent a ragged array of strings (`char **argv`), or allocate dynamic 2D arrays.

blocks.text:
• Pass-by-value trap: C passes everything by value, including pointers! Modifying `p = malloc(...)` inside `void alloc(int *p)` only mutates the local copy.
• Fix: Pass `&ptr` to `void alloc(int **p)` so `*p = malloc(...)` updates the caller's pointer.
• Linked lists: Using `Node **curr` (Linus Torvalds' 'good taste' trick) eliminates head special-cases when deleting nodes.

interviewQuestions.title: Compare Dangling, Wild, and NULL Pointers (and Use-After-Free)
interviewQuestions.content: A wild pointer is uninitialized garbage, a dangling pointer points to freed or out-of-scope memory, and `NULL` represents an explicit invalid sentinel.

blocks.text:
• Wild pointer: `int *p;` (uninitialized local)—contains indeterminate stack garbage; dereferencing is immediate UB.
• Dangling pointer: Points to heap memory already passed to `free(p)` (Use-After-Free) or a popped stack frame.
• Mitigation: Always initialize pointers (`= NULL`), set `p = NULL` after `free(p)` where practical, and compile with `-fsanitize=address` in testing.

interviewQuestions.title: What does the `restrict` keyword (C99) guarantee to the compiler?
interviewQuestions.content: `restrict` promises the compiler that for the lifetime of that pointer, no other pointer will access the same underlying memory, enabling vectorization and register caching.

blocks.text:
• Pointer aliasing problem: In `void add(int *a, int *b, int *c)`, the compiler must reload `*b` and `*c` on every loop iteration in case `a` aliases `b` or `c`.
• `restrict` contract: Tells the optimizer the regions do not overlap (e.g., `memcpy(void * restrict dst, const void * restrict src, size_t n)`). Violating `restrict` by passing overlapping pointers is Undefined Behavior!

interviewQuestions.title: Describe the Memory Layout of a Running C Program
interviewQuestions.content: A C process virtual address space consists of Text (code), Initialized Data (`.data`), Uninitialized Data (`.bss`), Heap (grows upward), and Stack (grows downward).

blocks.text:
• Segments from low to high virtual addresses:
  1. Text (`.text`): Compiled machine instructions (read-only, executable, shareable across processes).
  2. `.rodata`: Read-only constants and string literals (`"hello"`).
  3. `.data`: Explicitly initialized globals and `static` variables.
  4. `.bss`: Uninitialized / zero-initialized globals and `static` variables (zeroed by OS at load time).
  5. Heap: Dynamic allocations (`malloc`/`free`), grows toward higher addresses (`brk`/`mmap`).
  6. Stack: Function call frames, locals, return addresses, grows downward.

blocks.code:
int g_init = 5;       // .data
int g_zero;           // .bss
const char *s = "hi"; // s in .data, "hi" in .rodata
void f(void) { int local = 1; int *h = malloc(4); } // local on Stack, *h on Heap

interviewQuestions.title: What is the difference between `.data`, `.bss`, and `.rodata` segments?
interviewQuestions.content: `.data` stores non-zero initialized globals/statics inside the binary file, `.bss` records only the size of zero-initialized globals/statics (saving disk space), and `.rodata` holds read-only literals.

blocks.text:
• `.data` vs `.bss`: Declaring `int big[1000000];` (uninitialized) puts it in `.bss`—it adds 0 bytes to the ELF binary on disk! Declaring `int big[1000000] = {1};` puts 4MB into `.data` inside the executable.
• `.rodata` trap: Modifying a string literal (`char *s = "abc"; s[0] = 'x';`) triggers a Segmentation Fault because `.rodata` is mapped read-only (use `char s[] = "abc";` to copy onto the stack).

blocks.code:
char *ro = "hello";   // Points to .rodata -> ro[0] = 'H' is UB / SIGSEGV
char rw[] = "hello";  // Array on stack initialized from literal -> rw[0] = 'H' is safe

interviewQuestions.title: Compare Stack vs Heap Allocation and explain Stack Overflow vs Heap Fragmentation
interviewQuestions.content: Stack allocation is O(1) pointer movement with automatic LIFO lifetime and small fixed limits (~1-8MB), while Heap allocation is flexible and long-lived but slower and prone to leaks/fragmentation.

blocks.text:
• Stack: Deterministic LIFO cleanup, CPU-cache hot, fast (just moves `RSP`), but limited size (e.g., 8MB on Linux). Deep recursion or huge local arrays (`int buf[10000000]`) cause Stack Overflow.
• Heap: Explicit lifetime (`malloc`/`free`), supports large or runtime-sized buffers, but requires allocator metadata, thread synchronization, and manual cleanup.

interviewQuestions.title: Compare `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, and `free` (including common pitfalls)
interviewQuestions.content: `malloc` returns uninitialized bytes, `calloc(n, sz)` zero-initializes and guards against multiplication overflow, and `realloc` may move the block—always assign `realloc` to a temporary pointer.

blocks.text:
• `malloc(size)`: Leaves memory uninitialized (garbage).
• `calloc(count, size)`: Zeroes all allocated bytes and checks `count * size` overflow.
• `realloc(ptr, new_size)` trap: If `realloc` fails and returns `NULL`, overwriting `ptr = realloc(ptr, ...)` leaks the original block! Always use a temp pointer.
• `free(NULL)`: Guaranteed safe no-op by the C standard.

interviewQuestions.title: How do Memory Leaks and Double Frees happen, and what tools catch them?
interviewQuestions.content: Memory leaks occur when heap pointers are lost without `free()`; double free corrupts allocator metadata (and is an exploitable vulnerability); AddressSanitizer and Valgrind detect both.

blocks.text:
• Leak patterns: Early `return` on error paths before `free()`, overwriting a pointer before freeing, or failing to free nested struct fields.
• Double free: Calling `free(p)` twice corrupts freelist pointers (tcache/fastbin attacks) and triggers UB/aborts.
• Tooling: Compile with `-fsanitize=address,undefined -g` (ASan + UBSan) in CI/dev, or run under `valgrind --leak-check=full`.

interviewQuestions.title: Why does the compiler add Padding to Structs, and how do you minimize `sizeof(struct)`?
interviewQuestions.content: Compilers insert padding bytes so each member sits at an address divisible by its natural alignment and total struct size is a multiple of its largest alignment; order members largest-to-smallest to minimize waste.

blocks.text:
• Hardware reason: CPUs read aligned 4/8-byte words in a single bus cycle; unaligned reads incur multi-cycle penalties or hardware faults (ARM/RISC-V).
• Rules:
  1. Each member offset must be a multiple of its alignment (`alignof(member)`).
  2. Total `sizeof(struct)` is padded to a multiple of the strictest member alignment (so arrays of structs stay aligned!).
• Optimization: Sort fields from largest alignment to smallest (`double`/`void*` -> `int` -> `short` -> `char`).

blocks.code:
struct Bad  { char a; int b; char c; }; // 1 + (3 pad) + 4 + 1 + (3 pad) = 12 bytes
struct Good { int b; char a; char c; }; // 4 + 1 + 1 + (2 pad) = 8 bytes

interviewQuestions.title: Explain `offsetof()`, `__attribute__((packed))`, and C11 `alignas` / `alignof`
interviewQuestions.content: `offsetof(T, member)` computes byte offsets portably, `packed` removes padding (at the risk of unaligned access), and C11 `<stdalign.h>` provides standard `alignas`/`alignof`.

blocks.text:
• `offsetof(type, member)` (`<stddef.h>`): Used heavily in kernel-style `container_of()` macros to recover a parent struct pointer from an embedded list node.
• `__attribute__((packed))` / `#pragma pack(1)`: Removes padding for wire/disk formats, but taking `&s.field` can produce an unaligned pointer causing UB or bus errors—prefer `memcpy` deserialization for network protocols!
• C11 `alignas(64)`: Aligns structs to CPU cache lines (64 bytes) to prevent false sharing.

interviewQuestions.title: What is a Flexible Array Member (FAM) in C99, and why is it better than a pointer?
interviewQuestions.content: A Flexible Array Member (`char data[];` as the last struct member) allows allocating header + variable-length payload in a single contiguous `malloc`, improving cache locality and halving `free()` calls.

blocks.text:
• Syntax: Last member of a struct with >=1 other named member is `T data[];` (do NOT use the pre-C99 `data[0]` or `data[1]` hacks, which trigger UB under bounds checks).
• Benefits: One `malloc(sizeof(Packet) + len)`, contiguous memory for CPU cache, single `free(pkt)`.
• Note: `sizeof(struct Packet)` excludes the flexible array member.

interviewQuestions.title: How do `union`s work in C, and what is a Tagged Union?
interviewQuestions.content: All members of a `union` share the same starting memory address (`sizeof` >= largest member), saving RAM for mutually exclusive variants when paired with a discriminant `enum` tag.

blocks.text:
• Memory sharing: Writing `u.f = 1.0f` overwrites the bytes of `u.i`.
• Tagged Union pattern: Wrap an `enum Tag` + `union` inside a `struct` so code always knows which field is currently active.
• Type punning note: Reading an inactive union member is allowed in C99/C11 (unlike C++ where it is UB!), though `memcpy` remains the clearest, portable type-punning idiom.

interviewQuestions.title: What does `volatile` do in C, and why is it NOT sufficient for multithreading?
interviewQuestions.content: `volatile` stops the compiler from caching or eliding loads/stores because the memory can change externally (MMIO, ISRs), but it provides NO atomicity or CPU memory-ordering barriers for threads.

blocks.text:
• What `volatile` prevents: Dead-store elimination, hoisting reads out of `while (*reg == 0)` loops, and reordering accesses relative to other `volatile` accesses.
• Valid uses: Memory-Mapped I/O (hardware registers), globals modified by Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs), and locals preserved across `setjmp`/`longjmp`.
• Why NOT for threads: `volatile int x; x++;` is still a non-atomic read-modify-write race, and CPUs/compilers can reorder non-volatile memory around it—use `<stdatomic.h>` or mutexes.

interviewQuestions.title: Can a variable be both `const` and `volatile`? Give a real-world example.
interviewQuestions.content: Yes — `const volatile` means your code cannot write to the object (`const`), while external hardware or an ISR can change its value at any time (`volatile`).

blocks.text:
• Meaning: `const` is a compile-time contract enforced on *your code* ('read-only by software'), whereas `volatile` tells the optimizer ('value may change outside normal control flow').
• Classic example: A hardware timer tick counter or read-only device status register mapped into memory—software must only read it, and every read must fetch the fresh hardware state.

interviewQuestions.title: Explain the different meanings of the `static` keyword in C
interviewQuestions.content: `static` gives local variables static storage duration (persisting across calls), gives file-scope globals/functions internal linkage (private to the `.c` file), and in C99 marks minimum array parameter sizes.

blocks.text:
• 1. Inside a function (`static int count = 0;`): Stored in `.data`/`.bss` instead of the stack; initialized once and retains its value across calls.
• 2. At file scope (`static void helper(void)` / `static int state;`): Internal linkage—invisible to other translation units (`.c` files), preventing symbol clashes.
• 3. C99 array parameters (`void f(int arr[static 10])`): Guarantees `arr` is non-NULL and points to at least 10 `int`s.

interviewQuestions.title: Difference between Declaration and Definition (`extern`), and avoiding Multiple Definition errors
interviewQuestions.content: A declaration announces a symbol's type (`extern int g_val;`) without allocating storage, while a definition allocates storage (`int g_val = 0;`); put `extern` declarations in `.h` and definitions in one `.c` file.

blocks.text:
• Trap: Writing `int g_count = 0;` in a header `.h` included by two `.c` files causes a linker `multiple definition of 'g_count'` error!
• Correct pattern: Put `extern int g_count;` in `state.h` and `int g_count = 0;` in `state.c`.
• Note on functions: Function prototypes are implicitly `extern` by default unless marked `static`.

interviewQuestions.title: Why use `static inline` instead of plain `inline` in C header files?
interviewQuestions.content: In C99/C11, plain `inline` in a header does not emit an external symbol if the compiler chooses NOT to inline it (causing linker `undefined reference` errors); `static inline` guarantees self-contained linkage.

blocks.text:
• C99 `inline` quirk (different from C++!): An `inline` definition without `extern` provides an 'inline definition' only—at `-O0` (unoptimized debug builds), the compiler calls the function out-of-line and the linker fails unless one `.c` file has an `extern inline` instantiation.
• `static inline` in `.h`: Gives each translation unit internal linkage; compiles cleanly at `-O0` and inlines away at `-O2`, replacing unsafe `#define` macros with type safety.

interviewQuestions.title: Distinguish Undefined Behavior (UB), Implementation-Defined, and Unspecified Behavior
interviewQuestions.content: Implementation-defined behavior is documented by the compiler (`sizeof(int)`), unspecified behavior picks among valid options without documentation (arg eval order), and UB imposes zero requirements.

blocks.text:
• Implementation-defined: Compiler/target must choose and document it (e.g., `sizeof(long)`, signedness of `char`, right-shift of negative signed int in practice).
• Unspecified: Standard allows multiple valid choices (e.g., evaluation order of `f() + g()`).
• Undefined Behavior (UB): Anything can happen—crash, silent corruption, or compiler deleting security checks because optimizers assume UB never occurs!

interviewQuestions.title: Why is Signed Integer Overflow Undefined Behavior in C, while Unsigned Overflow is Well-Defined?
interviewQuestions.content: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^N per the C standard, whereas signed integer overflow is UB—allowing compilers to optimize away `if (x + 1 < x)` overflow checks completely.

blocks.text:
• Unsigned wraparound: `UINT_MAX + 1u == 0u` is guaranteed.
• Signed overflow UB trap: Checking `if (x + 100 < x)` AFTER adding `x + 100` can be deleted by GCC/Clang at `-O2` because the optimizer assumes signed overflow never happens!
• Safe overflow check: Check BEFORE adding (`if (x > INT_MAX - 100)`) or use C23 `<stdckdint.h>` (`ckd_add`) / `__builtin_add_overflow`.

interviewQuestions.title: Why is `i = i++ + ++i;` Undefined Behavior? (Sequence Points / Sequencing Rules)
interviewQuestions.content: Modifying a scalar object more than once—or reading and modifying it without sequencing—between two sequence points is Undefined Behavior.

blocks.text:
• Sequencing rule: In `i++ + ++i` or `a[i] = i++`, the side effects on `i` and value computations are unsequenced relative to each other.
• Sequence points exist at `;`, `&&`, `||`, `?:`, `,` (comma operator, NOT function argument commas!), and after evaluating function arguments before entering the call.
• Fix: Split increments into separate statements.

interviewQuestions.title: Explain the Strict Aliasing Rule and how to safely do Type Punning
interviewQuestions.content: Strict aliasing forbids accessing an object through a pointer of an incompatible type (allowing register optimizations), with exceptions for `char*`/`unsigned char*` and compatible/signed variants; use `memcpy` for portable type punning.

blocks.text:
• Rule (C99/C11 6.5/7): Compilers assume `int *` and `float *` never alias the same address, so writes via `float *` may not reload cached `*int_ptr` reads.
• Allowed exceptions: `char`/`unsigned char` (can inspect raw bytes of anything), signed/unsigned counterparts, or union/struct containing the type.
• Best portable type-punning: `uint32_t bits; memcpy(&bits, &f, sizeof(bits));`—GCC/Clang optimize `memcpy` of 4 bytes into a single CPU register move with zero overhead and zero UB!

interviewQuestions.title: Explain Integer Promotions and the Signed-to-Unsigned Conversion Bug
interviewQuestions.content: Small types (`char`, `short`) promote to `int` in expressions, and mixing `int` with `unsigned int` (or `size_t`) silently converts the negative signed value into a huge unsigned value.

blocks.text:
• Classic bug: `-1 < 1U` evaluates to `0` (`false`)! Why? Usual arithmetic conversions promote `-1` (`int`) to `unsigned int` (`UINT_MAX`), which is greater than `1U`.
• Common real-world bug: `int len = -1; if (len < sizeof(buf))` converts `-1` to `SIZE_MAX` (`false`), bypassing bounds checks!
• Defense: Enable `-Wall -Wextra -Wsign-compare`.

interviewQuestions.title: Compare `sizeof` vs `strlen`, and what happens in `sizeof(x++)`?
interviewQuestions.content: `sizeof` is a compile-time operator returning byte size (does NOT evaluate its operand except for VLAs), whereas `strlen` scans memory at runtime until `'\0'`.

blocks.text:
• `sizeof("hello")`: Returns `6` (includes null terminator `'\0'`). `strlen("hello")`: Returns `5`.
• Pointer trap: For `const char *s = "hello";`, `sizeof(s)` is `8` (pointer size on 64-bit), NOT `6`.
• Unevaluated operand: `int x = 5; size_t sz = sizeof(x++);` leaves `x == 5` because `sizeof` inspects only the type at compile time.

interviewQuestions.title: Difference between `memcpy` and `memmove`, and how is `memmove` implemented?
interviewQuestions.content: `memcpy` assumes non-overlapping regions (overlapping is UB) for maximum SIMD speed, whereas `memmove` checks overlap direction and copies backward when `dst > src`.

blocks.text:
• `memcpy(dst, src, n)`: Undefined Behavior if `[dst, dst+n)` overlaps `[src, src+n)`.
• `memmove(dst, src, n)`: Safe on overlapping buffers.
• Overlap logic: If `dst > src && dst < src + n`, copying forward would overwrite unread `src` bytes—so `memmove` copies backward from `n - 1` down to `0`.

interviewQuestions.title: Why are `gets`, `strcpy`, and `sprintf` dangerous, and how do you handle C strings safely?
interviewQuestions.content: Unbounded string functions ignore destination buffer sizes and cause stack/heap buffer overflows; use `fgets`, `snprintf`, and `strncpy` pitfalls-aware bounded copies.

blocks.text:
• `gets()`: Removed in C11 because it cannot limit input length.
• `strncpy()` trap: Does NOT guarantee null-termination if `src` >= `n`! Always enforce `dst[n - 1] = '\0'` or use `snprintf(dst, sizeof(dst), "%s", src)` (which always null-terminates when `size > 0` and reports truncation via return value >= `sizeof(dst)`).

interviewQuestions.title: How do you Set, Clear, Toggle, and Test bits using Bitwise Operators in C?
interviewQuestions.content: Use `|= (1U << k)` to set, `&= ~(1U << k)` to clear, `^= (1U << k)` to toggle, and `(x >> k) & 1U` to test bit `k`—always using `1U` to avoid signed shift UB.

blocks.text:
• Always use unsigned `1U << k` (or `UINT32_C(1) << k`): Shifting `1` into the sign bit of a 32-bit signed `int` (`1 << 31`) is Undefined Behavior in C!
• Operations:
  - Set bit `k`: `flags |= (1U << k);`
  - Clear bit `k`: `flags &= ~(1U << k);`
  - Toggle bit `k`: `flags ^= (1U << k);`
  - Test bit `k`: `bool is_set = (flags & (1U << k)) != 0;`

blocks.code:
#define BIT(k) (1U << (k))
uint32_t reg = 0;
reg |= BIT(3);   // Set bit 3
reg &= ~BIT(3);  // Clear bit 3
reg ^= BIT(2);   // Toggle bit 2

interviewQuestions.title: Bitwise Tricks: Check Power of 2, Align Up to Alignment, and Detect Endianness
interviewQuestions.content: `n && !(n & (n - 1))` tests powers of two, `(x + align - 1) & ~(align - 1)` rounds up to power-of-two alignment, and inspecting byte 0 of `uint32_t x = 1` reveals endianness.

blocks.text:
• Power of 2: `n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0` (must guard `n != 0`).
• Align up (when `align` is power of 2, e.g., 16): `(size + (align - 1)) & ~(align - 1)`.
• Endianness: Little-endian stores LSB at lowest address (`*(uint8_t *)&val == 1` for `uint32_t val = 1`); network byte order (TCP/IP) is Big-Endian (`htonl`/`ntohl`).

interviewQuestions.title: What are C Bitfields, and why should you be careful using them for binary protocols?
interviewQuestions.content: Bitfields pack sub-byte integer members inside structs, but bit order (MSB-first vs LSB-first), padding, and plain `int` signedness are implementation-defined across compilers and architectures.

blocks.text:
• Portability pitfalls: The C standard leaves bit ordering within an allocation unit, crossing storage-unit boundaries, and whether `int flag : 1` is signed (`0` or `-1`!) up to the compiler/ABI.
• Best practice: Use explicit `unsigned int` for internal space-saving flags, and use explicit bitwise shifts/masks on `uint8_t`/`uint32_t` for portable wire/hardware formats.

interviewQuestions.title: Walk through the 4 stages of the C Compilation Pipeline
interviewQuestions.content: C source builds through Preprocessing (`.i`), Compilation to Assembly (`.s`), Assembly to Object code (`.o`), and Linking into an executable or library.

blocks.text:
• 1. Preprocessor (`gcc -E`): Expands `#include`, `#define` macros, `#ifdef` conditionals, and removes comments -> `.i`.
• 2. Compiler (`gcc -S`): Parses, type-checks, optimizes, and emits target assembly -> `.s`.
• 3. Assembler (`gcc -c`): Converts assembly into machine-code relocatable object files -> `.o` (unresolved external symbols remain).
• 4. Linker (`ld`): Combines `.o` files and libraries, resolves external symbols, and assigns final virtual addresses.

interviewQuestions.title: Compare Static Linking (`.a`) vs Dynamic Linking (`.so` / `.dll`)
interviewQuestions.content: Static linking embeds library code into the executable at build time (standalone, larger binary), while dynamic linking resolves shared `.so`/`.dll` libraries at load/run time (smaller binary, shared RAM pages).

blocks.text:
• Static library (`.a`, `ar rcs`): Linker copies only referenced `.o` members into the binary. Zero runtime dependency, slightly faster direct calls, but patching the library requires relinking.
• Dynamic/Shared library (`.so`, compiled with `-fPIC -shared`): Loaded by `ld.so` at startup (or `dlopen()` at runtime). Multiple processes share the `.text` RAM pages, and bugfixes drop in via library replacement (watch ABI compatibility!).

interviewQuestions.title: Why do C headers need Include Guards (`#ifndef`), and how do Forward Declarations speed up builds?
interviewQuestions.content: Include guards prevent duplicate type definitions when a header is included transitively multiple times; forward declarations (`struct Node;`) break header cycles and reduce recompile cascades.

blocks.text:
• `#ifndef FOO_H / #define FOO_H / #endif`: Strictly portable C standard guard against multiple inclusion within one translation unit (`#pragma once` is widely supported but non-standard and can fail on symlinked paths).
• Forward declarations: If a header only uses pointers (`struct Context *`), write `struct Context;` instead of `#include "context.h"` to break circular dependencies and speed up incremental builds.

blocks.code:
#ifndef BUFFER_H
#define BUFFER_H
struct Allocator; // Forward declaration avoids pulling allocator.h
typedef struct Buffer Buffer;
#endif

interviewQuestions.title: What are the classic C Macro Pitfalls, and why use `do { ... } while (0)`?
interviewQuestions.content: Function-like macros suffer from operator precedence bugs, double evaluation of side-effect arguments (`MAX(i++, j++)`), and `if/else` dangling-semicolon breakage fixed by `do { ... } while(0)`.

blocks.text:
• Precedence trap: `#define SQ(x) x * x` turns `SQ(1 + 2)` into `1 + 2 * 1 + 2 == 5`! Always parenthesize parameters AND the whole expression: `((x) * (x))`.
• Double evaluation: `MAX(a++, b)` increments `a` twice! Prefer `static inline` functions.
• `do { ... } while (0)`: Wraps multi-statement macros into a single safe statement that consumes the caller's trailing `;` cleanly inside unbraced `if (...) MACRO(); else ...`.

blocks.code:
#define LOG_ERR(msg) do { \
    fprintf(stderr, "ERR: %s\n", (msg)); \
    err_count++; \
} while (0)

interviewQuestions.title: What is a Data Race in C11, and how do Mutexes (`pthread_mutex_t`) prevent it?
interviewQuestions.content: In C11, concurrent unsynchronized access to the same memory location where at least one access is a write is a Data Race (Undefined Behavior); mutexes enforce mutual exclusion and memory visibility.

blocks.text:
• Data Race = UB: Even on architectures with word-sized loads, the compiler can hoist or tear non-atomic reads/writes across threads unless synchronized.
• `pthread_mutex_t`: Guarantees only one thread enters the critical section at a time AND establishes a happens-before memory barrier between unlock and subsequent lock.

interviewQuestions.title: What causes Deadlocks in multithreaded C, and how do you prevent them?
interviewQuestions.content: Deadlock occurs when threads hold locks while waiting in a cycle for each other's locks (Mutual Exclusion, Hold-and-Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait); break it via canonical lock ordering.

blocks.text:
• Classic ABBA deadlock: Thread 1 locks `A` then waits for `B`; Thread 2 locks `B` then waits for `A`.
• Preventions:
  1. Global Lock Ordering: Always acquire multiple locks in a fixed order (e.g., by ascending pointer address or ID).
  2. `pthread_mutex_trylock()` with backoff: Release held locks if the second cannot be acquired.
  3. Keep critical sections tiny and never call unknown user callbacks while holding a mutex.

interviewQuestions.title: How do C11 `<stdatomic.h>` Atomics and Memory Ordering (`acquire`/`release`) work?
interviewQuestions.content: C11 `_Atomic` variables provide lock-free atomic operations and explicit memory fences (`memory_order_acquire`/`release`) to prevent CPU and compiler instruction reordering across cores.

blocks.text:
• Default (`memory_order_seq_cst`): Sequential consistency—safest, strongest global order.
• Acquire/Release pairing: Producer writes payload then stores `atomic_store_explicit(&ready, true, memory_order_release)`; Consumer loads `atomic_load_explicit(&ready, memory_order_acquire)`—guaranteeing all producer writes before the release are visible after the acquire!
• `memory_order_relaxed`: Atomicity only, no ordering guarantees (good for pure stats counters).

interviewQuestions.title: Why must `pthread_cond_wait()` always be wrapped in a `while` loop, not an `if`?
interviewQuestions.content: POSIX condition variables can experience spurious wakeups or stolen wakeups (another consumer grabs the item first), so re-checking the predicate in a `while` loop is mandatory.

blocks.text:
• How `pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mtx)` works: Atomically unlocks `mtx` and puts the thread to sleep; upon wakeup, it re-acquires `mtx` before returning.
• Why `while (!predicate)`: (1) OS signals/futexes allow spurious wakeups without `pthread_cond_signal`; (2) Another thread may consume the condition between `signal()` and re-acquiring `mtx`.

interviewQuestions.title: What makes a POSIX Signal Handler safe? (`volatile sig_atomic_t` & Async-Signal-Safe)
interviewQuestions.content: Inside a POSIX signal handler, only async-signal-safe functions may be called (NO `printf` or `malloc`), and shared flags should have type `volatile sig_atomic_t`.

blocks.text:
• Reentrancy hazard: If a signal interrupts `malloc()` or `printf()` while they hold internal libc locks, calling `malloc()`/`printf()` inside the handler deadlocks or corrupts the heap!
• Safe pattern: Set a `volatile sig_atomic_t stop_flag = 1;` (or write 1 byte to a self-pipe via `write()`, which IS async-signal-safe) and handle cleanup in the main loop.

interviewQuestions.title: Explain `fork()`, Copy-on-Write, `exec()`, and Zombie vs Orphan Processes
interviewQuestions.content: `fork()` clones a process lazily via Copy-on-Write pages, `exec()` replaces the address space with a new program, and un-waited exited children become Zombies until the parent calls `waitpid()`.

blocks.text:
• `fork()`: Returns `0` in the child and child PID in the parent; memory pages are shared read-only via Copy-on-Write until either writes.
• Zombie process: Child has exited, but its exit status sits in the kernel process table because parent hasn't called `wait()`/`waitpid()`.
• Orphan process: Parent exited first; child is re-parented to PID 1 (`init`/subreaper) which reaps it.

interviewQuestions.title: Why are Variable-Length Arrays (VLAs) and `alloca()` risky in production C?
interviewQuestions.content: VLAs and `alloca()` allocate dynamic sizes on the stack without returning `NULL` on failure; an oversized input silently causes Stack Overflow or security vulnerabilities.

blocks.text:
• Risk: `int buf[n];` where `n` comes from untrusted input or exceeds stack space crashes immediately (or jumps past the guard page!). Unlike `malloc()`, VLAs have no error return.
• Standard status: C11 downgraded VLAs to an optional feature (`__STDC_NO_VLA__`); Linux kernel banned VLAs (`-Wvla`).
• Alternative: Fixed-size stack buffer for bounded small `n` or `malloc` + `free`.

interviewQuestions.title: Why is returning a pointer to a local variable UB, while returning a `struct` by value works?
interviewQuestions.content: A local variable's stack storage ends when the function returns (leaving a dangling pointer), whereas returning a `struct` by value copies its contents to the caller's frame or registers.

blocks.text:
• Pointer to local: `int *f(void) { int x = 5; return &x; }` returns the address of a popped stack frame—subsequent calls overwrite it.
• Returning a `struct`: Small structs return in CPU registers (x86-64 SysV ABI returns structs <= 16 bytes in `RAX`/`RDX`), and larger structs use a hidden caller-allocated pointer (RVO-like ABI copy).

interviewQuestions.title: Why can `memcmp(&s1, &s2, sizeof(s1))` fail even when two structs have identical fields?
interviewQuestions.content: Padding bytes inside structs hold indeterminate garbage unless zero-initialized with `memset` or `{0}` (and floats have `-0.0` vs `+0.0` / NaN), so `memcmp` can report false inequality.

blocks.text:
• Padding trap: Assigning `s1.a = 'x'; s1.b = 1;` leaves padding bytes between `a` and `b` uninitialized! Even `memset(&s, 0, sizeof(s))` may not stay zeroed if structs are later copied member-by-member.
• Fix: Write an explicit field-by-field `struct_equal(const S *a, const S *b)` function (also handles `float` NaN/-0.0 and pointer deep equality).

interviewQuestions.title: How do `setjmp()` and `longjmp()` work, and why do non-`volatile` locals break across `longjmp`?
interviewQuestions.content: `setjmp`/`longjmp` perform non-local stack unwinding for C error recovery, and any non-`volatile` local variable modified after `setjmp()` has an indeterminate value after `longjmp()`.

blocks.text:
• Mechanism: `setjmp(env)` saves CPU registers (PC, SP, callee-saved regs) and returns `0`; `longjmp(env, val)` restores them and makes `setjmp` appear to return `val`.
• Register restoration trap: If local variable `x` lived in a CPU register and was modified after `setjmp`, `longjmp` restores old register state—marking `x` `volatile` forces it onto the stack.
• Limitation: Never `longjmp` into a function that has already returned!

interviewQuestions.title: Why prefer `enum` over `#define` for integer constants in C?
interviewQuestions.content: `enum` constants respect scope, survive preprocessing into debugger symbol tables (GDB/LLDB), group related values cleanly, and allow compiler `-Wswitch` exhaustiveness warnings.

blocks.text:
• `#define`: Blind text substitution before compilation—no debugger symbol names, no scope.
• `enum`: Compiler assigns sequential integers, preserves symbolic names in debuggers, and warns on missing `switch` cases (`-Wswitch`).
• Limitation: In C (prior to C23 fixed underlying types `enum E : uint8_t`), `enum` constants have type `int`.

interviewQuestions.title: How do Variadic Functions (`<stdarg.h>`) work, and what are Format String Vulnerabilities?
interviewQuestions.content: Variadic functions (`...`) walk extra arguments via `va_list`, `va_start`, `va_arg`, and `va_end`; passing untrusted input directly as the format string to `printf(user_str)` allows arbitrary memory read/write.

blocks.text:
• `<stdarg.h>` rules: Always pair `va_start(ap, last_named)` with `va_end(ap)`. Default argument promotions apply: `float` promotes to `double`, and `char`/`short` promote to `int`.
• Format string attack: `printf(user_input)` lets an attacker pass `%x.%x.%s.%n` to leak stack memory or write arbitrary values via `%n`! Always write `printf("%s", user_input)`.

interviewQuestions.title: Explain CPU Cache Locality (AoS vs SoA) and False Sharing in Multithreaded C
interviewQuestions.content: Contiguous Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) maximizes 64-byte cache-line utilization over AoS, while False Sharing degrades multithreaded speed when two threads mutate independent variables on the same cache line.

blocks.text:
• AoS vs SoA: Iterating `particles[i].x` in Array-of-Structs (`struct Particle { float x, y, z, mass, ...; }`) wastes cache bandwidth loading unused fields; Structure-of-Arrays (`float x[N], y[N];`) enables dense cache lines and SIMD.
• False Sharing: Even if Thread 1 writes `counters[0]` and Thread 2 writes `counters[1]`, if both sit on the same 64-byte cache line, MESI cache coherency bounces the line between cores!
• Fix: Pad or align per-thread data to `alignas(64)`.

languages.aboutDescription: The foundation of modern computing and systems programming.

roadmap.title: Syntax, Types, Bitwise Ops & Control Flow
roadmap.description: Master fixed-width integers (<stdint.h>), signed/unsigned promotion rules, bitmasks, shifts, and C preprocessor macros.

roadmap.title: Pointers, Arrays & Memory Layout
roadmap.description: Understand pointer arithmetic, array-to-pointer decay, function pointers, const correctness, struct padding, and endianness.

roadmap.title: Dynamic Memory Management & Ownership
roadmap.description: Safely manage stack vs. heap lifetimes with malloc/calloc/realloc/free, prevent dangling pointers and leaks, and design custom arenas.

roadmap.title: Modular Compilation, Headers & Build Systems
roadmap.description: Separate .h interfaces from .c translation units, use include guards, understand static/extern linkage, and automate builds with CMake/Make.

roadmap.title: Data Structures & Generic Macros
roadmap.description: Implement linked lists, hash tables, ring buffers, and type-safe abstractions using opaque structs and C11 _Generic dispatch.

roadmap.title: Undefined Behavior, Sanitizers & Debugging
roadmap.description: Eliminate UB and buffer overflows using -Wall -Wextra -Werror, ASan/UBSan, Valgrind, and GDB/LLDB inspection.

roadmap.title: POSIX Systems Programming & Concurrency
roadmap.description: Work with file descriptors, sockets, signals, POSIX threads/C11 atomics, and cache-friendly systems performance tuning.

versions.title: C23 (ISO/IEC 9899:2024)
changes: Standard nullptr constant, bool/true/false keywords, and typeof/auto type inference
Bit-precise integer types _BitInt(N), binary literals (0b), and digit separators (')
Standardized [[nodiscard]], [[fallthrough]], and [[maybe_unused]] attributes
Empty parameter lists () strictly meaning (void), plus memset_explicit() and #embed

versions.title: C17 (ISO/IEC 9899:2018)
changes: Defect-report maintenance revision resolving ambiguities in the C11 specification
Clarified rules around atomic operations, threads, and memory model edge cases
Deprecated redundant features while preserving full C11 binary/source compatibility
Updated __STDC_VERSION__ macro value to 201710L

versions.title: C11 (ISO/IEC 9899:2011)
changes: Native multithreading (<threads.h>) and standardized atomic memory model (<stdatomic.h>)
_Generic type-generic selection macros for compile-time polymorphism
Compile-time _Static_assert checks and anonymous struct/union members
Unicode string literals and char16_t/char32_t types via <uchar.h>

languages.description: The standard markup language for creating web pages and applications.

insights.title: 01. HTML5 Document Structure
insights.content: Every HTML5 page starts with <!DOCTYPE html> and wraps metadata in <head> and visible content in <body>.

blocks.text: The <!DOCTYPE html> declaration activates standards mode in browsers. Inside the root <html> element (with a lang attribute for accessibility and SEO), <head> holds character encoding, viewport settings, and page title, while <body> renders everything users see.

insights.title: 02. Headings Hierarchy (h1 to h6)
insights.content: Use <h1> through <h6> to create a logical document outline rather than merely resizing text.

blocks.text: Search engines and screen readers rely on headings to navigate page structure. Keep one main <h1> per page for the primary title, and nest <h2> through <h6> sequentially without skipping levels.

insights.title: 04. Semantic Text Emphasis & Formatting
insights.content: Prefer <strong>, <em>, <mark>, and <small> over purely visual tags like <b> and <i> when conveying meaning.

blocks.text: <strong> marks strong importance, <em> adds vocal stress or emphasis, <mark> highlights reference text, and <small> represents side comments or legal fine print. Screen readers adjust intonation for semantic tags.

insights.title: 05. Inline Code, Keyboard Input & Abbreviations
insights.content: Use <code>, <kbd>, <samp>, <var>, and <abbr> to give technical prose precise semantic meaning.

blocks.text: <code> denotes inline code snippets, <kbd> represents user keyboard or voice input, <samp> shows program output, <var> marks mathematical or code variables, and <abbr title="..."> expands acronyms on hover.

insights.title: 06. Quotations & Citations (blockquote, q, cite)
insights.content: Mark extended quotes with <blockquote>, inline quotes with <q>, and referenced work titles with <cite>.

blocks.text: The <blockquote> element accepts a cite URL attribute pointing to the source. Inline <q> automatically wraps text in locale-appropriate quotation marks, while <cite> identifies the title of a book, article, or specification.

insights.title: 07. Hyperlinks, Targets & Safe External Links
insights.content: The <a> element connects documents via href, and external tabs should include rel="noopener noreferrer".

blocks.text: Anchor links navigate between pages or external origins. When opening a link in a new tab with target="_blank", always add rel="noopener noreferrer" to prevent the opened page from accessing window.opener.

insights.title: 08. Fragment Links, Mailto, Tel & Download
insights.content: Links can jump to page sections (#id), trigger email or phone apps, or prompt file downloads.

blocks.text: Using href="#section-id" scrolls to an element with a matching id. Special URI schemes like mailto: and tel: invoke native communication apps, and the download attribute instructs the browser to save same-origin files.

insights.title: 09. Unordered & Ordered Lists (ul, ol, li)
insights.content: Use <ul> when item order does not matter and <ol> when sequence or ranking is meaningful.

blocks.text: Only <li> elements should be direct children of <ul> or <ol>, though lists can be nested inside an <li>. Ordered lists support attributes like start, reversed, and type (1, A, a, I, i) for custom numbering.

insights.title: 10. Description Lists (dl, dt, dd)
insights.content: Use <dl> for term-definition pairs, glossaries, or key-value metadata displays.

blocks.text: A description list wraps terms (<dt>) and their corresponding descriptions (<dd>). One term can have multiple <dd> descriptions, or multiple <dt> terms can share one <dd>.

blocks.code:
<dl>
  <dt>DOM</dt>
  <dd>Document Object Model representing the page tree.</dd>
  <dt>SSR</dt>
  <dd>Server-Side Rendering on each request.</dd>
</dl>

insights.title: 11. Images, Alt Text & Intrinsic Dimensions
insights.content: Always provide descriptive alt text and explicit width/height attributes on to prevent layout shifts.

blocks.text: The alt attribute describes the image for screen readers and displays if the image fails to load; leave alt="" empty for purely decorative images. Setting width and height lets the browser reserve aspect-ratio space before download completes (preventing CLS).

insights.title: 12. Figures & Captions (figure, figcaption)
insights.content: Pair self-contained media, diagrams, or code listings with a semantic caption using <figure> and <figcaption>.

blocks.text: <figure> groups standalone content referenced from the main flow—such as charts, photos, or code blocks—while <figcaption> provides its accessible caption either as the first or last child.

insights.title: 13. Basic Data Tables (table, tr, th, td)
insights.content: Use <table> strictly for tabular data with rows (<tr>), header cells (<th>), and data cells (<td>).

blocks.text: Avoid using tables for page layout. Always use <th> instead of styled <td> for column or row headers so assistive technologies announce relationships properly.

insights.title: 14. Table Sections & Captions (caption, thead, tbody, tfoot)
insights.content: Structure complex tables with <caption>, <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> for clarity and print/scroll behavior.

blocks.text: <caption> must be the first child of <table> and acts as its accessible title. Grouping rows into <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> lets browsers repeat headers on printed pages and scroll the body independently.

insights.title: 15. Table Cell Spanning & Header Scope
insights.content: Use colspan, rowspan, and the scope attribute to merge cells and clarify header associations.

blocks.text: colspan merges cells horizontally across columns, while rowspan merges vertically across rows. Adding scope="col" or scope="row" (and colgroup/rowgroup for multi-column headers) explicitly links headers to their cells.

insights.title: 16. Generic Containers: <div> vs <span>
insights.content: <div> is a block-level container for grouping layout elements, while <span> is an inline wrapper for text.

blocks.text: Both <div> and <span> carry zero semantic meaning and should only be used for styling or scripting hooks when no semantic element (like <section>, <article>, or <mark>) fits.

insights.title: 17. HTML Comments & Character Entities
insights.content: Write developer notes with <!-- ... --> and escape reserved HTML symbols using character entities.

blocks.text: Comments are ignored by the browser renderer (though visible in View Source, so never store secrets there). Use entities like <, >, &, ", and © to render reserved characters safely as text.
