blocks.text: Uppercase naming tells JSX to treat the tag as a custom component rather than a built-in DOM element. Exporting components as named or default exports lets you compose UIs across modular files.

insights.title: 03. Passing and Typing Props
insights.content: Props pass read-only data from parent components down to child components.

blocks.text: In TypeScript, define an interface or type for your component's props object and destructure them in the function parameter. Props are immutable inside the child, ensuring predictable one-way data flow.

insights.title: 04. The children Prop and Composition
insights.content: The special children prop lets wrapper components render arbitrary nested JSX passed between their tags.

blocks.text: Use React.ReactNode to type children in TypeScript so strings, numbers, elements, or fragments are all accepted. Composition with children avoids rigid configuration props and keeps layout containers reusable.

insights.title: 05. Default Props via Parameter Destructuring
insights.content: Assign fallback values directly when destructuring props in functional component signatures.

blocks.text: Modern React relies on standard ES6 default parameter values instead of legacy defaultProps. Default values apply whenever a prop is omitted or explicitly passed as undefined.

insights.title: 06. Conditional Rendering with Ternary and &&
insights.content: Render different UI branches in JSX using ternary expressions, logical &&, or early returns.

blocks.text: Use the ternary operator (cond ? a : b) for if/else branches and && when rendering something only if a condition is true. Be careful with numeric left-hand operands like count && <Badge /> because 0 will render literally—convert to boolean with count > 0.

insights.title: 07. Rendering Lists with map() and Keys
insights.content: Transform arrays of data into JSX elements using Array.prototype.map() with a stable key prop.

blocks.text: React uses the key prop to match elements across renders so it can reorder, insert, or remove DOM nodes efficiently. Always pick a stable, unique identifier from your data such as a database ID.

insights.title: 08. Why Index Keys Cause Bugs in Dynamic Lists
insights.content: Using array indexes as keys breaks component state and animations when items are reordered, inserted, or deleted.

blocks.text: If you prepend or delete an item when key={index} is used, React associates existing child state (like input values or checkboxes) with the wrong data item at that index. Index keys are only safe for static, never-reordered lists.

insights.title: 09. React Fragments (<> and <Fragment>)
insights.content: Fragments group multiple sibling elements without adding an extra wrapper node to the DOM.

blocks.text: Use the shorthand <>...</> for simple grouping inside tables, flexboxes, or grids where extra divs would break layout or HTML validity. Use the explicit <Fragment key={...}> syntax whenever you need to pass a key inside a map().

insights.title: 10. Event Handling (onClick, onChange, onSubmit)
insights.content: React attaches camelCase event handlers directly to JSX elements by passing functions, not calling them.

blocks.text: Pass a function reference like onClick={handleClick} or an inline arrow function like onClick={() => select(id)}. Calling handleClick() directly during render would execute it immediately on every render instead of on user interaction.

insights.title: 11. Synthetic Events and Event Typing in TypeScript
insights.content: React wraps browser events in a cross-browser SyntheticEvent with dedicated TypeScript event types.

blocks.text: Type event handlers with React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>, or React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>. This gives full autocomplete for e.target and e.currentTarget safely.

insights.title: 12. Preventing Default Behavior and Event Propagation
insights.content: Call e.preventDefault() to cancel browser defaults and e.stopPropagation() to stop event bubbling.

blocks.text: Events in React bubble up from the target element to ancestor elements just like native DOM events. Use stopPropagation() when a nested button inside a clickable card shouldn't trigger the card's click handler.

insights.title: 13. Introduction to the useState Hook
insights.content: useState adds reactive local state to a functional component and triggers a re-render when updated.

blocks.text: Calling useState(initialValue) returns a tuple of the current state value and a setter function. Never mutate state variables directly; always call the setter so React schedules a re-render with the new snapshot.

insights.title: 14. Functional State Updates (prev => ...)
insights.content: Pass an updater function to setState whenever the next state depends on the previous state.

blocks.text: Because React batches state updates and closures capture the state from the current render, calling setCount(count + 1) twice in one handler only increments once. Using setCount((prev) => prev + 1) queues updates against the latest pending value.

insights.title: 15. Lazy State Initialization in useState
insights.content: Pass a function reference to useState(() => ...) so expensive initial computation runs only once.

blocks.text: If you write useState(computeExpensive()), the function executes on every single re-render even though React ignores the return value after mount. Passing an initializer function without calling it runs it strictly on the initial render.

insights.title: 16. Updating Objects Immutably in State
insights.content: Create a new object copy with spread syntax (...) instead of mutating properties on existing state.

blocks.text: React compares state references with Object.is; mutating user.name directly leaves the reference unchanged so React skips re-rendering. Always construct a new object when updating flat or nested fields.

insights.title: 17. Updating Arrays Immutably in State
insights.content: Use non-mutating array methods like spread, filter, and map instead of push, splice, or sort.

blocks.text: Methods like push() and splice() mutate the existing array in place. Instead, add items with [...items, newItem], remove items with items.filter(), and update a specific item with items.map().

insights.title: 18. Lifting State Up Between Siblings
insights.content: Move shared state to the closest common parent when two sibling components need to stay in sync.

blocks.text: The parent holds the source-of-truth state and passes both the current value and an update callback down as props. This keeps siblings synchronized without duplicating state.

insights.title: 19. Derived State vs Redundant State
insights.content: Compute values from existing state or props during render instead of storing duplicate synchronized state.

blocks.text: Storing things like fullName or filteredCount in separate useState hooks creates sync bugs and extra renders. Compute derived values as plain variables directly inside the component body.

insights.title: 20. Controlled Form Inputs
insights.content: A controlled input binds its value prop to React state and updates it on every onChange event.

blocks.text: Because React state acts as the single source of truth, you can validate, format, or reset input values programmatically at any moment. Always initialize controlled inputs with a string like "" rather than undefined.

insights.title: 21. Handling Multiple Inputs with One Handler
insights.content: Use the input name attribute with computed property names ([name]: value) to manage form fields in one state object.

blocks.text: Instead of creating a separate useState for every input in a form, group related fields into one object and update the matching key dynamically via e.target.name.

insights.title: 22. Uncontrolled Inputs and FormData
insights.content: Uncontrolled inputs let the DOM store the input value and read it on submit using FormData.

blocks.text: For simple forms without live character-by-character validation, uncontrolled inputs with defaultValue and name attributes avoid unnecessary re-renders while keeping React 19 form actions clean.

insights.title: 23. Inline Styles vs CSS Classes
insights.content: Use className for static or themeable styling and inline style objects only for truly dynamic values.

blocks.text: React's style prop accepts a camelCase JavaScript object rather than a CSS string. Reserve inline styles for computed runtime values like progress percentages or coordinates, and keep layout/hover rules in CSS classes.

insights.title: 24. Pure Components and Avoiding Side Effects in Render
insights.content: A React component should act like a pure function: given the same props and state, it returns the same JSX.

blocks.text: Never mutate external variables, fetch data, or modify the DOM directly inside the component body during render. Keep side effects inside event handlers or useEffect so concurrent rendering stays predictable.

insights.title: 25. Component Lifecycle Mental Model (Mount, Update, Unmount)
insights.content: Every component goes through mounting onto the screen, re-rendering on updates, and unmounting when removed.

blocks.text: React creates state on mount, preserves state across updates while the component stays in the same tree position, and destroys state plus runs effect cleanups when unmounted.

insights.title: 26. StrictMode Double Invocation in Development
insights.content: React StrictMode intentionally double-runs renders and effects in development to expose impure logic and missing cleanups.

blocks.text: Only active in development, StrictMode mounts, unmounts, and remounts components to verify that effects clean up subscriptions properly and render functions have no side effects. Production builds run everything once.

insights.title: 27. Props Drilling and When to Avoid It
insights.content: Props drilling occurs when data is threaded through intermediate components that do not use it themselves.

blocks.text: Passing props 1–2 levels down is completely normal and explicit. When props cross many layers, consider component composition with children or React Context rather than cluttering intermediate APIs.

insights.title: 28. Component Composition with Slot Props
insights.content: Accept JSX elements as named props like header, footer, or icon to build flexible layout shells.

blocks.text: Slot props let callers supply pre-configured JSX nodes instead of forcing a generic component to support dozens of boolean and string options. Type slots as React.ReactNode.

insights.title: 29. Automatic XSS Escaping vs dangerouslySetInnerHTML
insights.content: React escapes text values rendered in JSX by default to protect against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).

blocks.text: Strings interpolated inside {} are rendered as plain text, never parsed as HTML. Only use dangerouslySetInnerHTML with trusted or sanitized HTML (for example via DOMPurify).

insights.title: 30. Conditional Classnames and Dynamic Attributes
insights.content: Combine conditional Tailwind or CSS classes cleanly and toggle boolean HTML attributes like disabled or aria-expanded.

blocks.text: Pass undefined (not false) for optional string attributes you want omitted from the DOM, and join conditional class lists with Array.filter(Boolean).join(" ") or a helper like clsx.

insights.title: 31. Resetting Component State with the key Prop
insights.content: Changing a component's key forces React to unmount the old instance and mount a fresh one with reset state.

blocks.text: Instead of writing complex useEffect cleanup logic to reset form fields when switching selected items (e.g., user A to user B), pass key={user.id} to the editor component.

insights.title: 32. Automatic Batching of State Updates
insights.content: React groups multiple state updates inside events, promises, and timeouts into a single re-render.

blocks.text: Since React 18+, calling multiple state setters inside async callbacks or setTimeout triggers only one render pass, improving performance and preventing half-updated UI states.

insights.title: 33. Organizing React Component Files and Folders
insights.content: Keep components focused, colocate related helpers/types, and split files when responsibilities diverge.

blocks.text: A clean feature folder colocates the component, its subcomponents, custom hooks, and TypeScript types together. Extract subcomponents when a file grows hard to scan or when a piece is reused across features.

insights.title: 34. useEffect Basics and the Dependency Array
insights.content: useEffect synchronizes a component with external systems like timers, DOM APIs, or network requests after render.

blocks.text: The dependency array controls when the effect re-runs: omit it to run after every render, pass [] to run only on mount, or list reactive values ([id]) so the effect re-synchronizes whenever they change.

insights.title: 35. Effect Cleanup Functions (Listeners & Timers)
insights.content: Return a cleanup function from useEffect to remove event listeners, clear intervals, or close sockets.

blocks.text: React runs the cleanup function before re-running the effect on dependency changes and when the component unmounts. Without cleanup, timers and global listeners leak memory and fire stale callbacks.

insights.title: 36. Fetching Data Safely with AbortController
insights.content: Abort in-flight fetch requests inside your useEffect cleanup using AbortController.

blocks.text: Passing controller.signal to fetch cancels outdated network requests when the component unmounts or the query changes, saving bandwidth and avoiding state updates from obsolete responses.

insights.title: 37. Avoiding Race Conditions in Async Effects
insights.content: Use an ignore boolean flag in effect cleanups when an async operation cannot be aborted with AbortController.

blocks.text: If a fast second request finishes before a slow first request, the stale response would overwrite newer UI unless ignored. Setting let ignore = false and flipping it in cleanup guarantees only the latest effect commits.

insights.title: 38. When You Don't Need useEffect
insights.content: Avoid useEffect for deriving values from props/state or handling user-triggered events.

blocks.text: Calculating filtered lists in render or executing submit logic directly inside event handlers eliminates extra render passes and keeps data flow linear. Reserve useEffect strictly for external synchronization.

insights.title: 39. useRef for Accessing DOM Elements
insights.content: Attach a ref created with useRef to a JSX element to call imperative browser APIs like focus() or scrollIntoView().

blocks.text: React assigns the underlying DOM node to ref.current after commit and resets it to null on unmount. Always guard ref.current before calling DOM methods.

insights.title: 40. useRef for Mutable Values Without Re-renders
insights.content: Store timer IDs, previous values, or render counters in useRef when mutating them should not trigger a re-render.

blocks.text: Unlike useState, updating ref.current is synchronous and does not schedule a render. Never read or write ref.current during render when it affects JSX output; use it inside effects or event handlers.

insights.title: 41. Callback Refs for Dynamic DOM Measurements
insights.content: Pass a function to the ref prop to run code immediately whenever a DOM node mounts or unmounts.

blocks.text: Unlike an object ref, a callback ref notifies your component the exact moment a conditionally rendered element appears or disappears, making it ideal for measuring element height or width.

insights.title: 42. Ref Cleanup Functions in React 19
insights.content: React 19 lets ref callbacks return a cleanup function that runs automatically when the element unmounts.

blocks.text: Previously React called callback refs with null on unmount. Returning a cleanup function directly from a ref callback pairs observer setup and teardown cleanly in one place.

insights.title: 43. Passing ref as a Regular Prop in React 19
insights.content: In React 19, function components accept ref directly in props without needing React.forwardRef.

blocks.text: You can type ref?: React.Ref<HTMLInputElement> right alongside your other props and forward it to the inner DOM element. forwardRef is no longer required for new React 19 code.

insights.title: 44. useImperativeHandle for Custom Ref APIs
insights.content: useImperativeHandle customizes the instance value exposed to a parent component through a ref.

blocks.text: Instead of exposing the entire DOM node, restrict the parent to safe imperative actions like focusAndSelect() or reset(). This preserves encapsulation inside reusable input or video components.

insights.title: 45. useContext for Sharing State Deeply
insights.content: Context lets a parent component provide data to any descendant in its tree without passing props through every layer.

blocks.text: Create a context with createContext(defaultValue), wrap a subtree with the Context provider (in React 19 you can render <ThemeContext value={...}> directly), and read it via useContext.

insights.title: 46. Typed Context with a Custom Consumer Hook
insights.content: Wrap useContext in a custom hook that throws a clear error when used outside its Provider.

blocks.text: Initializing createContext with null avoids fake default values and narrows the TypeScript return type automatically inside the custom hook so consumers never need null checks.

insights.title: 47. Splitting Contexts to Prevent Extra Re-renders
insights.content: Separate frequently changing state from stable dispatch functions into two contexts.

blocks.text: Every component calling useContext re-renders when the context value changes. Placing dispatch or action callbacks in their own context prevents button-only consumers from re-rendering on state updates.

insights.title: 48. useReducer for Complex State Transitions
insights.content: useReducer centralizes multi-step state updates inside a pure reducer(state, action) function.

blocks.text: When state fields depend on each other or support multiple distinct actions (add, toggle, reset), a discriminated union of TypeScript actions makes every transition explicit and easy to unit-test.

insights.title: 49. Combining useReducer and useContext for Mini Stores
insights.content: Pair useReducer with two contexts (state and dispatch) to share structured app state without external libraries.

blocks.text: The provider owns useReducer and exposes state and dispatch to descendants. Components can dispatch typed actions from anywhere in the subtree with predictable state updates.

insights.title: 50. useMemo for Expensive Computations
insights.content: useMemo caches the result of a pure calculation between renders until one of its dependencies changes.

blocks.text: Use useMemo when filtering, sorting, or transforming large datasets—or when preserving an object/array reference passed to a memoized child. Avoid wrapping trivial arithmetic in useMemo.

insights.title: 51. useCallback for Referential Equality
insights.content: useCallback preserves a function's reference across renders so memoized children or effect dependencies stay stable.

blocks.text: In JavaScript, inline functions create a new reference on every render. Wrapping a callback in useCallback is mainly useful when passing it to a React.memo child or listing it in a useEffect dependency array.

insights.title: 52. React.memo and When Memoization Actually Helps
insights.content: React.memo skips re-rendering a component when its props are shallowly equal to the previous render.

blocks.text: Memoization adds comparison overhead, so apply React.memo selectively to expensive subtrees that re-render often with identical props—not every small component. (Note: React Compiler automates much of this.)

insights.title: 53. Writing Your First Custom Hook (useDebounce)
insights.content: Custom hooks extract reusable stateful logic into functions starting with 'use' that can call other hooks.

blocks.text: Each component calling a custom hook gets its own isolated state and effects. A useDebounce hook delays updating a rapidly changing search term until the user pauses typing.

insights.title: 54. Custom Hook: useLocalStorage with SSR Safety
insights.content: Persist state to localStorage safely without breaking Server-Side Rendering or hydration.

blocks.text: Initialize state with a safe default so server and initial client HTML match, then hydrate from localStorage inside useEffect or useSyncExternalStore.

insights.title: 55. Custom Hook: useFetch with Loading & Error States
insights.content: Encapsulate loading, error, data, and AbortController cancellation inside a reusable useFetch hook.

blocks.text: Returning a typed { data, error, isLoading } object keeps data-fetching components clean and ensures every consumer cancels stale requests automatically on unmount.

insights.title: 56. Custom Hook: useMediaQuery
insights.content: Listen to CSS media query changes in React using window.matchMedia and useEffect.

blocks.text: Subscribe to matchMedia's 'change' event rather than polling window.innerWidth on every resize pixel. Always remove the listener in the cleanup function.

insights.title: 57. useLayoutEffect vs useEffect for DOM Measurements
insights.content: useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations but before the browser paints, preventing visual flicker.

blocks.text: Use useLayoutEffect when you measure an element's bounding box and immediately adjust a tooltip or popover position. For everything else—like data fetching—prefer non-blocking useEffect.

insights.title: 58. useId for Accessible Form Labels and ARIA IDs
insights.content: useId generates unique, deterministic IDs that stay identical across server and client renders.

blocks.text: Hardcoding id='email' breaks accessibility when a component renders twice on the page, and Math.random() causes SSR hydration mismatches. useId solves both cleanly (never use it for list keys).

insights.title: 59. Portals with createPortal for Modals and Tooltips
insights.content: createPortal renders children into a different DOM node (such as document.body) while keeping React context and event bubbling intact.

blocks.text: Portals let modals, drawers, and tooltips escape parent overflow:hidden or z-index stacking contexts without breaking React's component tree or Context consumers.

insights.title: 60. Error Boundaries with getDerivedStateFromError
insights.content: Error Boundaries catch JavaScript errors anywhere in their child component tree during render and show a fallback UI.

blocks.text: React requires a class component implementing static getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch to act as an Error Boundary. Error Boundaries do not catch async or event-handler errors.

insights.title: 61. Recoverable Error Boundaries with Reset Keys
insights.content: Add a reset mechanism to an Error Boundary so users can retry rendering a crashed widget without reloading the page.

blocks.text: Passing an onReset callback or resetting internal error state when a resetKey prop changes lets users recover cleanly from transient network or data errors.

insights.title: 62. Higher-Order Components (HOC) Pattern
insights.content: A Higher-Order Component is a function that takes a component and returns an enhanced component.

blocks.text: While custom hooks replaced most HOCs for sharing logic, HOCs remain useful for cross-cutting wrapper behaviors like analytics tracking or injecting layout guards around arbitrary components.

insights.title: 63. Render Props Pattern and Inversion of Control
insights.content: Pass a function as a prop (or children) so a container controls data or state while the caller controls rendering.

blocks.text: Render props give consumers complete freedom over the markup rendered for each item or mouse/scroll coordinate, without forcing a rigid UI template inside the shared component.

insights.title: 64. Controlled vs Uncontrolled Component Dual Pattern
insights.content: Design reusable UI components that support both controlled (value + onChange) and uncontrolled (defaultValue) usage.

blocks.text: Check whether value !== undefined to determine controlled mode. If uncontrolled, manage internal state initialized from defaultValue; otherwise delegate updates through onChange.

insights.title: 65. Polymorphic Components with TypeScript Generics
insights.content: Build components with an 'as' prop so callers can render a Button as a button, anchor, or custom Link while keeping full type safety.

blocks.text: Using TypeScript generics constrained to React.ElementType merges your component's custom props with the target element's native HTML attributes via ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T>.

insights.title: 66. Lazy Loading Components with React.lazy
insights.content: React.lazy dynamically imports a component bundle only when it is rendered for the first time.

blocks.text: Code-splitting heavy components like rich-text editors, charts, or admin modals shrinks the initial JavaScript bundle and speeds up First Contentful Paint.

insights.title: 67. Code Splitting Routes and Heavy Widgets with Suspense
insights.content: Wrap lazy-loaded routes or feature panels in <Suspense fallback={...}> to show instant loading UI.

blocks.text: While the browser downloads the split JavaScript chunk, Suspense displays the fallback spinner or skeleton cleanly, then swaps in the resolved component without blocking sibling UI.

insights.title: 68. React 19 Actions and Async Transitions
insights.content: React 19 lets startTransition accept async functions and calls them 'Actions' with automatic pending state.

blocks.text: Inside startTransition(async () => ...), React tracks isPending automatically across async awaits, batches resulting state updates, and keeps the UI responsive while mutations run.

insights.title: 69. useActionState for Form Submission State and Errors
insights.content: useActionState manages form action results, validation errors, and pending status out of the box.

blocks.text: Pass an action function (prevState, formData) => nextState and an initial state. Binding the returned formAction to <form action={formAction}> tracks isPending and exposes the latest returned state.

insights.title: 70. useFormStatus for Nested Submit Button Pending UI
insights.content: useFormStatus lets child components inside a <form> read the parent form's submission status without prop drilling.

blocks.text: Import useFormStatus from 'react-dom'. Note the critical rule: it reads the status of an ancestor <form>, so it must be called inside a child component rendered within that form.

insights.title: 71. useOptimistic for Instant Optimistic UI Updates
insights.content: useOptimistic displays an immediate optimistic state during an async action and automatically reverts if it fails.

blocks.text: Pass the authoritative state and an updateFn(current, optimisticValue). Calling addOptimistic inside a Transition updates the UI instantly while the server request finishes in the background.

insights.title: 72. The use() Hook for Reading Promises in Render
insights.content: React 19's use(promise) suspends rendering until the promise resolves and integrates directly with Suspense and Error Boundaries.

blocks.text: Unlike useEffect, use() reads an already-created promise (e.g., passed from a Server Component or cache) cleanly during render. Avoid creating new promises inside render every time—pass a cached or prop promise.

insights.title: 73. Conditional Context Reading with use(Context)
insights.content: Unlike useContext, React 19's use(Context) can be called conditionally inside if statements or loops.

blocks.text: Because use() is not restricted by the top-level-only Hook call-order rule for Context, you can short-circuit with an early return before reading a Context value.

insights.title: 74. React 19 Document Metadata (<title>, <meta>) in Components
insights.content: React 19 natively hoists <title>, <meta>, and <link> tags rendered inside any component up to document <head>.

blocks.text: You no longer need third-party libraries like react-helmet for basic head tags in React 19 client or SSR apps—render standard HTML metadata tags directly inside your page component.

insights.title: 75. React 19 Stylesheet and Script Precedence Hoisting
insights.content: React 19 manages stylesheet loading order via the precedence prop and deduplicates async <script> tags automatically.

blocks.text: By adding precedence='default' or 'high' on <link rel='stylesheet' />, React ensures stylesheets load before revealing Suspense boundaries so unstyled content never flashes.

insights.title: 76. React Compiler Mental Model and Automatic Memoization
insights.content: React Compiler statically analyzes pure components and hooks at build time to insert fine-grained memoization automatically.

blocks.text: When your code follows the Rules of React (pure render, immutable props/state), the compiler caches values and JSX subtrees without manual useMemo, useCallback, or React.memo boilerplate.

insights.title: 77. Rules of React (Idempotency, Immutability, Hook Rules)
insights.content: Components and hooks must be idempotent, treat props/state as immutable, and call hooks unconditionally at the top level.

blocks.text: Never call hooks inside conditions, loops, or nested functions, because React tracks hook state by call order. Never mutate props or state objects after passing them to React.

insights.title: 78. useTransition for Non-Blocking UI Updates
insights.content: useTransition marks expensive state updates as low-priority transitions so urgent typing and clicks stay instantaneous.

blocks.text: If switching tabs or filtering thousands of items slows down input responsiveness, wrap the heavy state update in startTransition while keeping the input update urgent.

insights.title: 79. useDeferredValue for Responsive Search Filtering
insights.content: useDeferredValue defers updating a slow part of the UI while keeping controlled inputs snappy.

blocks.text: Unlike debouncing, useDeferredValue has no fixed timer delay—React renders the urgent input immediately, then renders the deferred value in the background and cancels stale work if the user keeps typing.

insights.title: 80. Concurrent Rendering and Interruptible Work
insights.content: Concurrent React can pause, interrupt, or abandon background renders so high-priority user interactions never stutter.

blocks.text: Because React splits transition work into small chunks and yields back to the browser main thread, typing or clicking interrupts stale low-priority renders rather than queuing behind them.

insights.title: 81. useSyncExternalStore for External Subscriptions
insights.content: useSyncExternalStore safely subscribes React components to external mutable stores or browser APIs without tearing.

blocks.text: Provide a subscribe function, a client getSnapshot function, and an optional getServerSnapshot for SSR. This is the official hook for reading stores outside React or APIs like navigator.onLine.

insights.title: 82. Building a Tiny Pub/Sub Store with useSyncExternalStore
insights.content: Create a lightweight global store outside React using a listener Set and useSyncExternalStore.

blocks.text: External stores trigger re-renders only in components subscribed to them, and work seamlessly across non-React modules like WebSocket handlers or API clients.

insights.title: 83. useInsertionEffect for CSS-in-JS Libraries
insights.content: useInsertionEffect runs before any DOM mutations or useLayoutEffect so runtime CSS-in-JS libraries can inject <style> tags safely.

blocks.text: If styles are injected in useLayoutEffect, layout measurements could read stale styling and trigger extra reflows. Library authors use useInsertionEffect strictly to insert dynamic style rules.

insights.title: 84. Compound Components Pattern with Context
insights.content: Compound components share implicit state through Context so callers compose subcomponents like <Tabs.List> and <Tabs.Panel>.

blocks.text: Attaching subcomponents as properties on the parent component yields a clean, declarative API with zero props drilling and flexible markup order.

insights.title: 85. Headless UI Hooks and Prop Getters
insights.content: Headless hooks encapsulate keyboard navigation, ARIA attributes, and state while rendering zero opinionated markup.

blocks.text: Returning prop-getter helpers like getTriggerProps() lets consumers wire accessibility and interaction logic into any styling system or custom JSX element.

insights.title: 86. React.cloneElement Pitfalls and Modern Alternatives
insights.content: Avoid React.cloneElement because it creates fragile implicit prop contracts; prefer Context, render props, or wrapper components.

blocks.text: cloneElement breaks if a consumer wraps a child in a Fragment or helper component. Sharing state via Context or passing render callbacks keeps composition predictable and type-safe.

insights.title: 87. Suspense for Data Fetching and Render-as-You-Fetch
insights.content: Start fetching data before or alongside rendering and let Suspense show fallbacks while promises resolve.

blocks.text: Instead of fetch-on-render (waiting for a component to mount before calling fetch inside useEffect), initiate the promise early and unwrap it with React 19's use() inside a Suspense boundary.

insights.title: 88. Avoiding Network Waterfalls with Parallel Promise Preloading
insights.content: Initiate independent data promises simultaneously at the route or parent level so requests run in parallel.

blocks.text: When a parent awaits data A before rendering a child that fetches data B, requests stack sequentially. Starting both promises upfront and passing them to children via use() eliminates the waterfall.

insights.title: 89. Nested Suspense Boundaries and Reveal Order
insights.content: Place inner Suspense boundaries around slower secondary widgets so fast primary content appears immediately.

blocks.text: A single top-level Suspense waits for the slowest promise inside it. Nesting a dedicated Suspense around comments or recommendations lets the main article stream in without delay.

insights.title: 90. Profiler API and Identifying Render Bottlenecks
insights.content: Wrap any subtree in <Profiler> to measure actualDuration and baseDuration programmatically.

blocks.text: The onRender callback reports why and how long a component tree took to commit, helping you pinpoint slow renders in real staging environments alongside React DevTools Profiler.

insights.title: 91. Virtualizing Long Lists (Windowing Concept)
insights.content: List virtualization renders only the rows currently visible in the scroll viewport instead of thousands of DOM nodes.

blocks.text: By calculating startIndex and endIndex from scrollTop and rowHeight—or using libraries like @tanstack/react-virtual—memory usage stays constant even for 50,000+ rows.

insights.title: 92. Preventing Stale Closures and Memory Leaks in Hooks
insights.content: Stale closures occur when an interval or listener captures an outdated state variable from an earlier render.

blocks.text: Fix stale closures by including dependencies accurately, using functional state updaters (prev => prev + 1), or storing latest callbacks in a ref when an external subscription shouldn't restart.

insights.title: 93. Separating Non-Reactive Logic from Effects
insights.content: Keep callbacks or theme values out of effect reconnection cycles by reading latest values through a ref (or useEffectEvent).

blocks.text: If a chat socket connects per roomId, changing notification sound settings shouldn't disconnect and reconnect the socket. Sync the latest callback to a ref in render/effect and invoke it inside the stable effect.

insights.title: 94. Hydration Mismatches and Client-Only Deferral
insights.content: Hydration mismatches happen when server-rendered HTML differs from the client's first render pass.

blocks.text: Never branch directly on window, Date.now(), or locale formatting during the initial render. Defer client-only UI until after mount via useEffect, or apply suppressHydrationWarning strictly on small dynamic text like timestamps.

insights.title: 95. Accessible Focus Management and Escape Handling in Modals
insights.content: Move focus into an opened dialog, close on Escape, and restore focus to the trigger when the dialog closes.

blocks.text: Keyboard and screen-reader users rely on explicit focus management in portals and custom overlays. Pair role='dialog' and aria-modal='true' with a ref to focus the dialog container on open.

insights.title: 96. Testing React Components with Accessible Queries
insights.content: Test components the way users interact with them by querying roles, labels, and visible text rather than CSS classes.

blocks.text: Prefer getByRole, getByLabelText, and getByText from @testing-library/react. Testing implementation details like internal state names makes tests brittle during refactors.

insights.title: 97. Testing User Interactions and Async UI States
insights.content: Use userEvent for realistic clicks/typing and findBy* queries to await asynchronous UI updates.

blocks.text: Unlike fireEvent, @testing-library/user-event dispatches full browser interaction sequences. Use await screen.findByText(...) when asserting content that renders after a promise resolves.

insights.title: 98. Testing Custom Hooks with renderHook
insights.content: renderHook tests stateful custom hooks in isolation without writing throwaway wrapper components.

blocks.text: Wrap state-mutating calls returned by the hook inside act(() => ...) so React flushes updates before you assert result.current.

insights.title: 99. Error Handling: Event Handlers vs Render Errors
insights.content: Use try/catch for imperative event/async errors and Error Boundaries for declarative render-phase crashes.

blocks.text: React Error Boundaries catch thrown errors during render and lifecycle commits, whereas clicks and async submits require explicit try/catch state handling (or propagating async errors via state if critical).

insights.title: 100. Production Architecture: Feature-Sliced React Apps
insights.content: Structure large React codebases by domain features with explicit public exports and shared UI primitives.

blocks.text: Keep cross-cutting primitives in shared/ui, isolate each feature's components, hooks, and API logic inside features/<domain>/, and expose only a clean index.ts barrel API to prevent tangled circular imports.

interviewQuestions.title: How do you compare previous and current prop values in a functional component? (useRef vs useState)
interviewQuestions.content: Use useRef to store the previous value across renders without triggering an extra re-render; using useState causes an unnecessary second render cycle.

blocks.text:
• Tracking Previous Props/State: Create a custom `usePrevious(value)` hook backed by `useRef` and `useEffect`. Because `useEffect` runs *after* commit, `ref.current` holds the previous render's value during the current render, then updates afterward.
• Why `useRef` instead of `useState`? Mutating `ref.current` is synchronous and does NOT schedule a re-render.
• Can `useState` be used? Technically yes (storing `[prev, setPrev]`), but calling `setPrev` inside `useEffect` or during render forces an immediate extra render pass on every prop change, hurting performance and risking infinite render loops if not guarded carefully.

interviewQuestions.title: How do you close a modal when clicking outside but keep it open when clicking inside?
interviewQuestions.content: Attach a mousedown/pointerdown listener on document inside useEffect, and check if modalRef.current && !modalRef.current.contains(event.target).

blocks.text:
• Where to register the event: Register `mousedown` (or `pointerdown`) on `document` inside a `useEffect` only while `isOpen` is `true`, and always clean up with `removeEventListener`. Using `mousedown` avoids edge cases where dragging text from inside the modal and releasing outside triggers a `click` outside.
• How to detect inside vs outside: Attach a `ref` to the modal dialog container (`modalRef`), then check:
  `if (modalRef.current && !modalRef.current.contains(event.target as Node)) onClose();`
• Bonus: Also listen for the `Escape` key for accessibility, or use a backdrop overlay `onClick` with `e.stopPropagation()` on the modal content.

interviewQuestions.title: Why can Context API become problematic and cause unnecessary re-renders in large apps?
interviewQuestions.content: Every component consuming a Context re-renders whenever the Provider's value reference changes, even if that component only uses an unchanged slice of the value.

blocks.text:
• Why Context causes re-renders: React Context has no built-in selector mechanism. Whenever the Provider's `value` object changes reference (e.g., any field updates), *every* descendant calling `useContext(MyContext)` re-renders—even if it only reads `user.name` and `theme` changed.
• Why it hurts in large apps: Placing rapidly changing state (forms, filters, real-time data) in a single root Context triggers wide subtree re-renders.
• Mitigations:
  1. Split Contexts by update frequency (e.g., `StateContext` vs `DispatchContext`, or `AuthContext` vs `ThemeContext`).
  2. Memoize the Provider `value` with `useMemo`.
  3. Use Redux Toolkit or Zustand when components need fine-grained slice subscriptions.

interviewQuestions.title: When does memoization (React.memo, useMemo, useCallback) help vs hurt?
interviewQuestions.content: Memoization helps for expensive computations and stable props passed to heavy memoized children; it hurts when applied blindly to cheap renders with unstable dependencies.

blocks.text:
• When it HELPS:
  - `useMemo` for genuinely expensive derived data (sorting/filtering thousands of rows).
  - `useCallback` / `useMemo` to preserve referential equality for props passed to `React.memo` children or effect dependency arrays.
• When it HURTS:
  - Wrapping trivial JSX or cheap primitives adds memory retention and shallow-comparison overhead on every render.
  - If a parent passes a new inline object/function anyway without `useCallback`, `React.memo` still runs the comparison *and* still re-renders—strictly slower than no memoization.

interviewQuestions.title: What is React Fiber, and how does it enable incremental and interruptible rendering?
interviewQuestions.content: React Fiber is the reconciliation engine introduced in React 16 that represents UI work as a linked-list tree of fiber nodes, allowing React to pause, prioritize, and resume rendering across frames.

blocks.text:
• Why Fiber Replaced the Stack Reconciler: The legacy Stack Reconciler traversed the Virtual DOM recursively in a single synchronous call stack, blocking the main thread on large trees.
• Linked-List Tree Structure: Each Fiber node holds `child`, `sibling`, and `return` (parent) pointers plus `alternate` (linking the current tree and work-in-progress tree for double buffering).
• Two-Phase Execution: The Render/Reconciliation phase builds the work-in-progress tree asynchronously and can be paused or aborted; the Commit phase applies DOM mutations synchronously in one pass so the UI is never half-updated.

interviewQuestions.title: How does React's reconciliation algorithm use the `key` prop, and why are array indices risky as keys?
interviewQuestions.content: Keys give sibling elements a stable identity across renders so React can reorder, insert, or destroy the exact matching fiber rather than mutating the wrong instance.

blocks.text:
• Diffing Heuristic: React compares trees level by level ($O(n)$). When element types match, React preserves the component instance and updates props; for dynamic lists, `key` identifies which item moved, was added, or was removed.
• Why Index Keys Break: If items are inserted at the start, sorted, or filtered, array indices shift. React then associates old state (e.g., uncontrolled input values, focus, animations) with the wrong item.
• When Index Keys Are Safe: Only when the list is static, never reordered/filtered, and items have no local state or unique IDs.

interviewQuestions.title: What is Concurrent Rendering in React 18/19, and how does interruptible rendering improve responsiveness?
interviewQuestions.content: Concurrent rendering allows React to prepare multiple UI versions in memory and yield to high-priority browser events like typing or clicks before committing.

blocks.text:
• Interruptible Work: Unlike synchronous rendering, concurrent features (`useTransition`, `useDeferredValue`, `<Suspense>`) mark updates with priority lanes. If a user types while a heavy list is rendering, React pauses the background render, handles the keystroke, and restarts or resumes.
• No Torn UI: Work happens off-screen on the work-in-progress Fiber tree; the real DOM is only updated during the synchronous Commit phase.
• Opt-in by Feature: Concurrent execution activates automatically when you use concurrent APIs, not blindly for every `setState`.

interviewQuestions.title: How does `useTransition` prioritize urgent updates over non-urgent UI transitions?
interviewQuestions.content: `useTransition` marks a state update as a low-priority transition and exposes `isPending` so urgent interactions like typing stay responsive.

blocks.text:
• How It Works: `const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()` lets you keep urgent state (like an input's controlled value) synchronous while wrapping expensive downstream updates (like filtering 10,000 rows or switching tabs) in `startTransition`.
• React 19 Async Actions: In React 19, `startTransition` also supports async functions, keeping `isPending` true until the awaited work finishes.
• Caution: Never wrap the controlled text input's own `setQuery` inside `startTransition`, or typing itself will feel lagged.

interviewQuestions.title: When should you use `useDeferredValue` instead of `useTransition` or debouncing?
interviewQuestions.content: `useDeferredValue` defers a value you receive (such as props) when you don't control the state setter, without imposing an artificial fixed timer delay like debouncing.

blocks.text:
• `useDeferredValue` vs `useTransition`: Use `useTransition` when you own the `setState` call; use `useDeferredValue(value)` when the value comes from props or an external hook.
• `useDeferredValue` vs Debounce: Debouncing waits a fixed time (e.g. 300ms) even on fast machines and doesn't interrupt an already-started render. `useDeferredValue` starts immediately in the background, yields to user input, and adapts to device speed.
• React 19 Initial Value: `useDeferredValue(value, initialValue)` accepts an optional initial value for the first render before deferring updates.

interviewQuestions.title: How does automatic state batching work in React 18+, and when should you use `flushSync`?
interviewQuestions.content: React 18+ batches all state updates regardless of where they originate (promises, timeouts, native events) into a single re-render; `flushSync` opts out when immediate DOM measurement is required.

blocks.text:
• React 17 vs 18+: Previously, React only batched updates inside React event handlers, so two `setState` calls inside `fetch().then()` or `setTimeout` caused two renders. React 18+ batches them automatically via `createRoot`.
• Opting Out with `flushSync`: Wrap a state update in `flushSync(() => setOpen(true))` when you immediately need to read updated DOM layout (e.g., scrolling a newly added chat message into view right after state update).
• Trade-off: `flushSync` forces a synchronous render and hurts batching performance, so use it sparingly.

interviewQuestions.title: How does React 19's `useActionState` simplify async form submissions and pending/error states?
interviewQuestions.content: `useActionState` wraps an async form action, automatically manages the `isPending` transition flag, and returns the latest resolved state or validation error.

blocks.text:
• Signature: `const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(actionFn, initialState, permalink?)`.
• Built-in Transition & Sequencing: Calling `formAction` runs `actionFn(prevState, formData)` inside a transition, eliminating manual `isLoading` / `error` `useState` boilerplate and `e.preventDefault()`.
• Progressive Enhancement: Passing `formAction` to `<form action={formAction}>` works seamlessly with Server Actions and even before hydration if a permalink is provided.

interviewQuestions.title: How does `useFormStatus` from `react-dom` work, and what is its most common usage pitfall?
interviewQuestions.content: `useFormStatus` reads the submission status (`pending`, `data`, `method`) of a parent `<form>`, and the main pitfall is calling it in the same component that renders `<form>`.

blocks.text:
• Parent Form Requirement: `useFormStatus()` only tracks a `<form>` rendered *above* the calling component in the tree. Calling it directly inside the component that renders `<form>` always returns `pending: false`.
• Reusable Submit Buttons: It enables generic `<SubmitButton />` components without prop-drilling `isSubmitting`.
• Returned Fields: Provides `{ pending, data, method, action }` while the form action is executing.

interviewQuestions.title: How does `useOptimistic` work in React 19, and how do you avoid losing user draft input on failure?
interviewQuestions.content: `useOptimistic` projects a temporary UI state during an async action and automatically reverts to the source-of-truth state when the action settles; drafts should stay in separate local state.

blocks.text:
• Lifecycle: `const [optimisticState, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(sourceState, updateFn)`. Calling `addOptimistic(input)` inside a transition/action shows the optimistic UI immediately; once the transition ends, React discards the temporary projection and displays `sourceState`.
• Rollback Behavior: If the server mutation fails and `sourceState` was never updated, the UI reverts cleanly without manual rollback code.
• Draft Input Trap: Never bind an active text input directly to optimistic state that resets on failure—keep the input's draft in local state or uncontrolled `FormData` and clear it only on success.

interviewQuestions.title: How does React 19's `use()` API read Promises and Context conditionally, and what triggers infinite loops with it?
interviewQuestions.content: `use(resource)` integrates with Suspense to unwrap Promises and read Context even inside conditionals or loops, but passing an uncached inline Promise causes an infinite render loop.

blocks.text:
• Why Conditionals Work: Unlike `useContext` or `useState`, `use()` is not bound to the fixed hook call-order array, so it can run after early returns or inside `if` blocks (though still only inside components or custom hooks).
• Promise Integration: When given a pending Promise, `use(promise)` suspends the component to the nearest `<Suspense>` boundary and passes rejections to the nearest Error Boundary.
• Infinite Loop Trap: Calling `use(fetch(...))` directly inside render creates a brand-new Promise on every render attempt, re-suspending infinitely. Pass a memoized/cached Promise or one created in a Server Component or loader.

interviewQuestions.title: How does the React Compiler automate memoization, and why does strict immutability matter even more with it?
interviewQuestions.content: The React Compiler is a build-time Babel/compiler plugin that automatically memoizes component outputs and hook values, relying on strict purity and immutability to compute safe cache dependencies.

blocks.text:
• Fine-Grained Auto-Memoization: Instead of manual `React.memo`, `useMemo`, and `useCallback`, the compiler analyzes data flow at build time and caches sub-expressions and JSX chunks based on reactive dependencies.
• Rules of React Are Mandatory: The compiler assumes components are pure and props/state are immutable during render. Mutating an array or object in place (e.g., `items.push(x)` or mutating a prop) causes stale cached UI or forces the compiler to bail out.
• Gradual Adoption: When migrating legacy code, `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` compiler rules flag violations so problematic components can be fixed or opted out.

interviewQuestions.title: How did React 19 simplify passing `ref` to function components and cleaning up ref callbacks?
interviewQuestions.content: React 19 allows function components to accept `ref` directly as a regular prop without `forwardRef`, and ref callbacks can now return a cleanup function.

blocks.text:
• No More `forwardRef` Boilerplate: `function Input({ ref, ...props })` works natively in React 19, removing wrapper noise and simplifying TypeScript generics.
• Ref Cleanup Functions: Returning a function from a callback ref (`ref={(node) => { ... return () => cleanup(); }}`) runs on unmount or before the ref attaches to a new node, replacing the `if (node === null)` pattern.
• Breaking TS Note: In React 19 types, callback refs must not implicitly return anything other than `void` or a cleanup function (e.g., avoid `ref={el => (myRef.current = el)}` without braces).

interviewQuestions.title: What does `<React.StrictMode>` check in development, and why does it double-invoke renders and effects?
interviewQuestions.content: StrictMode intentionally double-invokes render functions, reducers, initializers, and Effects in development only to expose impure logic and missing effect cleanups.

blocks.text:
• Double Render Check: Invoking component bodies, state updaters, and `useMemo` callbacks twice catches accidental mutations or side effects during render.
• Double Mount/Unmount Effect Cycle (React 18+): React runs setup -> cleanup -> setup once on mount in dev to verify that effects clean up subscriptions, timers, and listeners properly (preparing apps for features like `<Activity>` and Fast Refresh).
• Production Impact: Zero—all StrictMode double-invocations are stripped in production builds.

interviewQuestions.title: How do you prevent race conditions and stale responses when fetching data inside `useEffect`?
interviewQuestions.content: Use an `AbortController` or a boolean `ignore` flag inside the `useEffect` cleanup function so outdated responses from slower requests never overwrite newer state.

blocks.text:
• Why Race Conditions Happen: If `userId` changes from `1` to `2`, request 1 might resolve *after* request 2 and overwrite the UI with User 1's data.
• Solution 1 (`AbortController`): Pass `signal` to `fetch` and call `controller.abort()` in the cleanup to cancel the in-flight HTTP request.
• Solution 2 (Boolean `ignore` Flag): Even with `AbortController`, pair or guard non-abortable promises with `let ignore = false` and check `if (!ignore)` before calling `setState`.
• Note: Prefer router loaders, React Query/RTK Query, or Server Components for app data fetching when available.

interviewQuestions.title: What is the timing difference between `useEffect` and `useLayoutEffect`, and why does `useLayoutEffect` warn in SSR?
interviewQuestions.content: `useLayoutEffect` fires synchronously after DOM mutations but before browser paint, preventing visual flicker for layout measurements, whereas `useEffect` runs asynchronously after paint.

blocks.text:
• Execution Order: Render -> DOM update -> `useLayoutEffect` (synchronous, blocks paint) -> Browser Paint -> `useEffect` (asynchronous).
• When to Use `useLayoutEffect`: Measuring element dimensions (`getBoundingClientRect`) and immediately repositioning tooltips/popovers so the user never sees a 1-frame jump.
• SSR Caveat: Server rendering has no DOM layout; React warns if `useLayoutEffect` runs on the server. Guard with `useEffect` where possible, or gate layout logic behind client mount/Suspense.

interviewQuestions.title: What is `useInsertionEffect` used for, and why is it restricted to CSS-in-JS library authors?
interviewQuestions.content: `useInsertionEffect` runs synchronously before any DOM mutations or `useLayoutEffect` hooks, allowing CSS-in-JS libraries to inject `<style>` tags before layout measurements happen.

blocks.text:
• Timing: Runs before `useLayoutEffect` and before refs are attached, ensuring injected stylesheets exist before any component reads computed styles or layout.
• Constraints: You cannot schedule state updates or reliably access DOM refs inside `useInsertionEffect`.
• Audience: Normal application code should never call `useInsertionEffect`; it exists specifically for runtime CSS-in-JS libraries (like Emotion or styled-components).

interviewQuestions.title: How does `useSyncExternalStore` prevent UI tearing in concurrent renders when subscribing to external stores?
interviewQuestions.content: `useSyncExternalStore` forces synchronous, consistent reads from non-React stores (like Redux or `window.matchMedia`) so concurrent renders never show mismatched values from the same store.

blocks.text:
• What Is Tearing? In a paused concurrent render, an external store might mutate mid-render; Component A reads the old value and Component B reads the new value, producing an inconsistent screen.
• How `useSyncExternalStore` Fixes It: Takes `(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot?)`. If the snapshot changes during a render, React restarts the render synchronously.
• SSR Support: `getServerSnapshot` supplies the deterministic initial snapshot during server rendering and hydration to prevent hydration mismatches.

interviewQuestions.title: When should you use `useImperativeHandle`, and how do you expose a minimal imperative API?
interviewQuestions.content: `useImperativeHandle` customizes the ref object exposed to a parent component so you only reveal specific methods (like `focus()` or `reset()`) instead of the entire underlying DOM node.

blocks.text:
• Encapsulation: Exposing a raw `<input>` ref lets parents mutate styles or DOM attributes arbitrarily. `useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ focus, clear }), [])` restricts access to an explicit contract.
• React 19 Syntax: Combine directly with the `ref` prop without needing `forwardRef`.
• Rule of Thumb: Prefer declarative props first; reserve imperative handles for focus management, media playback, scrolling, or triggering third-party canvas/animation APIs.

interviewQuestions.title: Why should you use `useId` instead of `Math.random()` or module counters for accessibility IDs?
interviewQuestions.content: `useId` generates deterministic, tree-position-based unique IDs that match between server SSR and client hydration, unlike `Math.random()` or mutable module counters.

blocks.text:
• Hydration Safety: `Math.random()` produces different strings on server and client, causing hydration errors; module-level counters break with concurrent/streaming rendering order.
• Stable Across Renders: `useId()` derives IDs from the component's position in the React tree, guaranteeing uniqueness even when multiple instances render.
• Not for List Keys: Never use `useId()` for `key` props in lists—keys must come from your data IDs.

interviewQuestions.title: What are the best practices for designing reusable, composable custom hooks?
interviewQuestions.content: Well-designed custom hooks isolate one cohesive concern, return ergonomic tuple or object shapes, keep returned callbacks stable, and avoid hiding surprising side effects.

blocks.text:
• Single Responsibility: Extract hooks around clear capabilities (`useDebounce`, `useMediaQuery`, `useDisclosure`) rather than dumping unrelated component state into one giant hook.
• Return Shape Choice: Return a tuple (`[value, setValue]`) when callers will rename items or use multiple instances; return an object (`{ data, isLoading, refetch }`) when there are 3+ values.
• Latest Callback Pattern & Cleanup: Always clean up listeners/timers inside internal effects, and avoid forcing callers to wrap every inline callback in `useCallback`.

interviewQuestions.title: What are the trade-offs between controlled and uncontrolled form components in React?
interviewQuestions.content: Controlled inputs store value in React state for instant validation and UI coupling, while uncontrolled inputs let the DOM hold the value via refs or FormData for minimal re-renders.

blocks.text:
• Controlled Inputs: `value` + `onChange` keeps React as the single source of truth—ideal for live formatting, conditional disabling, or synchronized fields, at the cost of re-rendering on every keystroke.
• Uncontrolled Inputs: Use `defaultValue` + `ref` or native `<form action={...}>` with `FormData`. Great for large forms and performance-sensitive inputs (e.g., React Hook Form uses refs under the hood).
• Never Switch Modes: Passing `undefined` then a string to `value` switches from uncontrolled to controlled and triggers a React warning.

interviewQuestions.title: How do Error Boundaries work in React, what errors do they miss, and how do you reset them?
interviewQuestions.content: Error Boundaries are class components implementing `getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch` that catch render/lifecycle errors in descendants, but not async or event-handler errors.

blocks.text:
• Why Still Class Components? React still requires a class component (or a library like `react-error-boundary`) with `static getDerivedStateFromError` to render fallback UI and `componentDidCatch` for error logging.
• What They Do NOT Catch: Event handlers (`onClick`), asynchronous callbacks (`setTimeout`, unawaited promises), SSR errors, and errors thrown inside the Error Boundary itself.
• Resetting State: Pass a changing `resetKey` (or `key` prop) or expose a `resetErrorBoundary` callback so users can retry without a full page reload.

interviewQuestions.title: How does `<Suspense>` coordinate async loading states and prevent waterfall spinners?
interviewQuestions.content: `<Suspense>` declaratively displays a fallback while any child suspends (via `React.lazy`, `use()`, or Suspense-enabled frameworks), letting you place loading boundaries strategically.

blocks.text:
• Boundary Placement: Wrapping small independent widgets in separate `<Suspense>` boundaries allows fast sections to appear immediately while slower ones stream in; wrapping a group coordinates them under a single skeleton.
• Transition Integration: Updating state inside `startTransition` avoids hiding already-visible content behind a fallback—React keeps showing the old UI until the new tree is ready.
• Anti-Pattern: Triggering fetches inside children *after* they mount creates network waterfalls; initiate promises before or at the route level.

interviewQuestions.title: How do React Portals behave with DOM hierarchy versus React synthetic event bubbling?
interviewQuestions.content: `createPortal` renders a child into a different DOM node (like `document.body`), yet events inside the portal still bubble up through the React component tree.

blocks.text:
• DOM vs React Tree: Portals break out of parent CSS `overflow: hidden` or `z-index` stacking contexts by mounting into an external DOM container.
• Event Bubbling Surprise: Because React attaches event delegation to the root, an `onClick` inside a portal still bubbles to its React parent component—even though it is not a DOM descendant.
• Best Practice: Always guard or call `e.stopPropagation()` when a modal/popover inside a portal shouldn't trigger parent card click handlers.

interviewQuestions.title: What is React's SyntheticEvent system, and how did event delegation change in React 17+?
interviewQuestions.content: React wraps native browser events in a cross-browser `SyntheticEvent` and delegates listeners at the React root container instead of `document` (since React 17).

blocks.text:
• Cross-Browser Normalization: `SyntheticEvent` exposes a uniform API (`e.preventDefault()`, `e.stopPropagation()`, `e.nativeEvent`).
• React 17+ Root Delegation: Previously React attached handlers to `document`, causing conflicts when micro-frontends or jQuery widgets ran on the same page. Now handlers attach to the root DOM container (`createRoot(rootEl)`).
• Pooling Removed: Event pooling (where `e.target` became null inside async callbacks unless `e.persist()` was called) was completely removed in React 17+.

interviewQuestions.title: What causes hydration mismatches in SSR React applications, and how do you resolve them properly?
interviewQuestions.content: Hydration mismatches happen when the HTML generated on the server differs from the client's first render pass, often due to browser-only APIs, timestamps, or invalid HTML nesting.

blocks.text:
• Common Causes: Reading `window`, `localStorage`, `Date.now()`, or `Math.random()` directly during render; browser extensions modifying the DOM; or invalid nesting like `

...

` that the browser auto-repairs. • Proper Fixes: Keep the initial client render identical to the server render, then read browser-only state inside `useEffect` or `useSyncExternalStore`. Use `useId()` for dynamic IDs. • Last Resort: `suppressHydrationWarning` only silences direct text/attribute mismatches on a single element (like a localized timestamp) and should not hide structural bugs.

interviewQuestions.title: How does Selective Hydration with `<Suspense>` improve Time to Interactive (TTI) in React 18/19?
interviewQuestions.content: Selective Hydration lets React hydrate separate `<Suspense>` subtrees independently as their JS chunks arrive and even prioritizes hydrating whichever subtree the user clicks first.

blocks.text:
• Before React 18: Hydration was all-or-nothing—the entire page's JS had to download and hydrate before any button became interactive.
• Streaming + Selective Hydration: Each `<Suspense>` boundary can stream HTML early and hydrate independently without blocking other parts of the page.
• Click Prioritization: If a user clicks a component inside an unhydrated `<Suspense>` boundary whose JS has loaded, React synchronously prioritizes hydrating that boundary first and replays the interaction.

interviewQuestions.title: What is the architectural difference between React Server Components (RSC) and traditional SSR?
interviewQuestions.content: Traditional SSR renders Client Components to HTML once on the server and still ships all their JS for hydration; RSCs execute exclusively on the server and ship zero component JS to the browser.

blocks.text:
• Zero Client Bundle for RSC: Server Components can import heavy markdown parsers, database clients, or secrets without adding a single byte to the client bundle.
• No Hydration for RSC: They render to a serialized RSC payload (not hydrated on the client), whereas Client Components (`"use client"`) are both SSR-rendered to HTML and hydrated in the browser for interactivity.
• Complementary, Not Exclusive: Modern frameworks run RSCs and SSR together—RSCs fetch data and compose Client Components only at interactive leaves.

interviewQuestions.title: What values can cross the Server-to-Client (`"use client"`) boundary in RSC, and how does the donut pattern work?
interviewQuestions.content: Props passed from a Server Component to a Client Component must be serializable (no functions or class instances), while the donut pattern passes Server Components as `children` slots inside Client wrappers.

blocks.text:
• Serializable Props Only: Primitives, plain objects, arrays, Dates, Maps/Sets, Promises, JSX elements, and Server Function references can cross the boundary; regular functions, Symbols, and DOM nodes cannot.
• The Donut Pattern: A Client Component cannot directly `import` a Server Component (doing so turns it into a Client Component). Instead, pass the Server Component as `children` or a JSX prop from a parent Server Component.
• Why It Matters: You can wrap server-rendered content inside interactive client providers, modals, or animated containers without shipping the server children's JS.

interviewQuestions.title: How do you implement the Compound Components pattern in React for flexible, declarative APIs?
interviewQuestions.content: Compound Components share implicit state through a parent Context so callers can compose subcomponents (`<Tabs.List>`, `<Tabs.Panel>`) in arbitrary layouts without prop explosion.

blocks.text:
• Core Mechanism: A parent component holds state and provides it via Context; attached subcomponents consume that Context and fail fast if rendered outside the parent.
• Benefits: Avoids passing 15 configuration props (`renderHeader`, `tabIcon`, `panelClass`), supports custom wrappers/markup between subcomponents, and keeps JSX readable.
• Real-World Examples: Radix UI, Headless UI, `<select>/<option>`.

interviewQuestions.title: How do Render Props compare to Custom Hooks, and when are render props still useful?
interviewQuestions.content: Custom Hooks replaced Render Props for sharing stateful logic without wrapper hell, while Render Props remain useful for delegating custom item rendering in libraries like virtualized lists or tables.

blocks.text:
• Why Hooks Won for Logic: Hooks compose flatly without nesting callbacks or adding wrapper nodes to the React tree.
• Where Render Props Still Shine: Inversion of control over *rendering*—such as `renderItem={(item, index) => ...}` in virtual scrollers, data grids, or headless comboboxes where the library supplies computed props/measurements per row.

interviewQuestions.title: How does component composition (`children` or slot props) prevent unnecessary re-renders without `React.memo`?
interviewQuestions.content: Passing expensive JSX via `children` from a parent keeps those element references unchanged when a stateful wrapper re-renders, so React skips re-rendering the children automatically.

blocks.text:
• Why It Works: React skips re-rendering a child element if its exact JSX element object reference (`props.children`) is identical to the previous render.
• Moving State Down vs Wrapping: If a scroll-position or mouse-tracker state lives inside `<ScrollTracker>{expensiveTree}</ScrollTracker>`, updating `scrollY` only re-renders `ScrollTracker`; `expensiveTree` was created by the parent and stays unchanged.
• Advantage Over `React.memo`: Zero prop-comparison overhead and cleaner component boundaries.

interviewQuestions.title: What is state colocation vs. lifting state up, and how does it improve app performance?
interviewQuestions.content: State colocation keeps state as close as possible to the components that actually read it, reducing re-render blast radius and coupling, while lifting state up shares it only when siblings require synchronization.

blocks.text:
• The Cost of Over-Lifting: Putting modal open flags or search input strings at the top `App` level causes large subtrees to re-render on every keystroke.
• Colocation Principle: Start state in the lowest leaf component that needs it; lift it up to the nearest common ancestor only when another sibling needs it.
• Bonus: Colocated state resets naturally when its owning subtree unmounts.

interviewQuestions.title: Why is syncing props or state into another `useState` via `useEffect` an anti-pattern?
interviewQuestions.content: Copying derivable values into `useState` inside `useEffect` introduces an extra render pass with stale intermediate data and risks state desynchronization.

blocks.text:
• The Problem: On prop change, React renders once with the old derived state, paints/commits, runs `useEffect`, and triggers a second render.
• The Fix: Compute derived values directly during render (e.g., `const fullName = first + " " + last`), and only wrap genuinely expensive computations in `useMemo` if profiling shows a bottleneck.

interviewQuestions.title: When should you prefer `useReducer` over `useState`, and how does separating State and Dispatch contexts help performance?
interviewQuestions.content: `useReducer` centralizes complex multi-field state transitions into a pure reducer; splitting State and Dispatch into two Contexts lets action-triggering components avoid re-rendering when state changes.

blocks.text:
• When `useReducer` Fits: Multiple interdependent values (e.g., `status`, `data`, `error`, `step`) that transition together, or when next state depends cleanly on complex action payloads.
• Dual-Context Pattern: Because `dispatch` from `useReducer` has a guaranteed stable identity forever, putting `dispatch` in its own Context lets buttons/forms dispatch actions without subscribing to state updates.

interviewQuestions.title: How can changing a component's `key` prop cleanly reset its internal state without `useEffect`?
interviewQuestions.content: Passing a unique `key` (such as `userId`) forces React to unmount the old component instance and mount a fresh one with initial state whenever the key changes.

blocks.text:
• Why It's Cleaner: Instead of writing a `useEffect` that manually resets five `useState` fields whenever `userId` changes, `<ProfileEditor key={userId} userId={userId} />` guarantees a completely fresh component tree.
• Caveat: Only use this when you truly want a full reset (including child state and DOM focus), because unmounting destroys DOM nodes and re-runs mount effects.

blocks.code: <EditUserForm key={selectedUser.id} user={selectedUser} />

interviewQuestions.title: How do `React.lazy` and dynamic `import()` work with `<Suspense>` for code splitting?
interviewQuestions.content: `React.lazy` defers loading a component's JS bundle until it first renders, suspending to the nearest `<Suspense>` fallback while the chunk downloads.

blocks.text:
• Named vs Default Exports: `React.lazy` expects a module with a `default` export; wrap named exports via `.then(m => ({ default: m.Chart }))`.
• Preloading & Error Handling: Always wrap lazy boundaries with an Error Boundary in case chunk loading fails offline or after a deployment, and trigger `import(...)` on hover/intent when instant transitions matter.

interviewQuestions.title: How does list virtualization (windowing) solve performance bottlenecks for large datasets?
interviewQuestions.content: Virtualization renders only the visible slice of rows (plus a small overscan buffer) inside the viewport instead of thousands of DOM nodes, keeping memory and layout costs constant.

blocks.text:
• Why Big Lists Slow Down: Rendering 10,000 DOM rows bloats memory, layout recalculation, and reconciliation time even if only 15 rows are visible.
• How Windowing Works: Libraries like `@tanstack/react-virtual` calculate scroll offset, position a tall spacer container for accurate scrollbars, and render only visible indices.
• Watch Out For: Dynamic row heights (measure via `ResizeObserver`), keyboard navigation/accessibility, and Ctrl+F browser search limitations on offscreen items.

interviewQuestions.title: How do you diagnose slow renders and wasted re-renders using React DevTools Profiler?
interviewQuestions.content: React DevTools Profiler records commit flamegraphs and ranked charts showing each component's render duration and the exact reason it re-rendered (props, state, hooks, or parent).

blocks.text:
• Step 1 — Enable "Why did this render?": In Profiler settings, record why components rendered to separate cascading parent renders from actual state changes.
• Step 2 — Flamegraph & Ranked View: Gray bars indicate skipped subtrees; yellow/red bars highlight expensive components dominating commit time.
• Step 3 — Production Profiling: For accurate timings without dev overhead, use React's `<Profiler id="..." onRender={...}>` or the profiling build.

interviewQuestions.title: What causes stale closures in React hooks (`useEffect`, timers, listeners), and how do you fix them?
interviewQuestions.content: A stale closure occurs when a callback created in an earlier render captures outdated state/props variables because its effect or listener did not re-subscribe or use a ref/functional updater.

blocks.text:
• Root Cause: Every render creates a fresh scope of local variables. If `useEffect(..., [])` registers a `setInterval` or `window` listener on mount, that callback forever closes over the initial render's variables.
• Fixes:
  1. Include all referenced reactive values in the dependency array.
  2. Use functional state updates (`setCount(c => c + 1)`) when computing next state from previous state.
  3. Store the latest callback in a ref or use `useEffectEvent` when you must not restart a subscription.

interviewQuestions.title: How does `useEffectEvent` solve the conflict between reactive Effect dependencies and non-reactive event logic?
interviewQuestions.content: `useEffectEvent` extracts non-reactive logic from an Effect so it always reads the latest props/state without forcing the Effect (like a WebSocket or analytics log) to reconnect when those values change.

blocks.text:
• The Dilemma: Inside a chat room `useEffect([roomId])`, logging `theme` on connection forces `theme` into the dependency array—causing the socket to disconnect and reconnect whenever the user toggles dark mode.
• How `useEffectEvent` Helps: Wrapping the log/callback in `useEffectEvent` keeps it reading fresh `theme` values while excluding it from the Effect's dependency array.
• Rules: Effect Events can only be called inside Effects (never passed down to children or called during render).

interviewQuestions.title: How does React 19 natively handle document metadata (`<title>`, `<meta>`) and stylesheet precedence?
interviewQuestions.content: React 19 lets components render `<title>`, `<meta>`, `<link>`, and `<script async>` anywhere in the tree, automatically hoisting them to `<head>` and managing stylesheet deduplication and Suspense order.

blocks.text:
• Built-in Head Hoisting: Rendering `<title>` or `<meta>` inside a feature component hoists it cleanly to `document.head` on both SSR and client renders without third-party wrappers like `react-helmet`.
• Stylesheet Precedence: `<link rel="stylesheet" href="..." precedence="default" />` deduplicates shared stylesheets and makes `<Suspense>` wait for the sheet to load before revealing content, preventing FOUC (flash of unstyled content).

interviewQuestions.title: What problem does React's `<Activity>` (Offscreen) component solve compared to conditional rendering (`&&`) or `display: none`?
interviewQuestions.content: `<Activity mode="hidden">` hides a subtree visually and cleans up its effects while preserving its React state and pre-rendering hidden tabs at low priority.

blocks.text:
• Conditional Rendering (`show && <Tab />`) destroys internal component state (scroll, form drafts) when hidden.
• CSS `display: none` preserves state, but keeps Effects, subscriptions, and high-priority re-renders active in the background.
• `<Activity>` Best of Both Worlds: When `mode="hidden"`, React cleans up effects (like video playback or timers), preserves component/DOM state, and defers background updates at idle priority—ideal for multi-tab interfaces and instant back navigation.

interviewQuestions.title: What are the most common causes of memory leaks in React applications, and how do you prevent them?
interviewQuestions.content: Memory leaks in React stem from uncleaned global event listeners, timers, WebSockets, Observers, and retained DOM/closure references after a component unmounts.

blocks.text:
• Common Culprits:
  1. `window.addEventListener` / `IntersectionObserver` / `ResizeObserver` without `removeEventListener` or `disconnect()` in effect cleanup.
  2. Uncleared `setInterval` / `setTimeout` holding references to large state objects.
  3. Unclosed WebSockets, RxJS/store subscriptions, or third-party chart/map instances.
• Detection: Use Chrome DevTools Memory Heap Snapshots (compare detached DOM nodes before and after navigating away).

interviewQuestions.title: How do you implement accessible focus management, keyboard navigation, and ARIA live announcements in React?
